He also shares why land investing has shifted toward improving a property’s highest and best use, and how consistent marketing and purpose-built land data support deal flow.

flippers? Direct mail is a marketing
method where we send two-page letters to
land owners in a particular county to
inquire about their land. The goal is to
grab their attention with this letter by
giving them an option to liquidate their
property quickly. By using direct mail,
we can target specific areas of the
country and reach out to potential

Enchanted Farms is a real estate investment company headquartered in Key West, FL. They needed a better marketing strategy to meet their goal of $20,000 in revenue a month selling land, so they tried direct mail. 

Owner Mike Mazzella mailed 8,000 letters total to land owners throughout the U.S. As a result, Mike generated $40,000! He recommends direct mail marketing to other professionals in the real estate industry. 

Interested in doing a similar campaign for your business? We have worked with over 100,000 businesses and can help you too! Contact us at 1-800-442-0112 or visit rocketprint.com for free letter or postcard samples from your industry.

Land Flipping Empire "Off The Porch" Interview

We recently sat down with Jeffrey Altidort & Deandre Anderson of the Land Flipping Empire for an exclusive “Off The Porch” interview! During our conversation they talked about how they came up with the idea for their business, explain how they met, Deandre’s shares of his story from the streets to sports to entrepreneurship, jumping off the porch when he was 12, Jeff graduating from college, getting fired from their jobs, Deandre explains how he got into entrepreneurship, ‘Rich Dad Poor Dad’ changing their lives, Deandre recalls his first deal, explains what house wholesaling is, how they got into flipping land, Jeff making $5k on his first land deal, reveal they don’t need a license to flip properties, people reaching out to them to learn, what to expect when people sign up for their program, being hands on with their members, having their own app, helping people make 6 figures, reveal the hardest parts of flipping land & being an entrepreneur, being able to work remotely, and much more!

metadata.title: How to Flip Vacant Land for Profit | The Land Flipping Business Explained
metadata.author: Hidden Money
metadata.shortDescription:
How do investors actually turn vacant land into profit?

In this episode of Hidden Money, we take you inside the land flipping business and explore how investors find undervalued vacant land, negotiate purchases, evaluate properties, and resell them for a potential profit.

From researching land and contacting property owners to due diligence, closing costs, and resale strategies, we break down the entire process step by step.

But land flipping isn’t as simple as buying cheap and selling high. What are the hidden costs? How do investors identify profitable opportunities? And what mistakes can turn a promising deal into a financial loss?

In this episode:

 How the land flipping business really works
 Finding undervalued vacant land
 Researching properties before buying
 Contacting landowners and negotiating deals
 Due diligence and potential red flags
 Understanding purchase costs, taxes, and closing expenses
 How investors resell vacant land
 Calculating potential profit margins
 Common land flipping mistakes beginners should avoid
 The risks, challenges, and realities of land investing
 Land flipping can offer interesting opportunities in real estate, but  profits are never guaranteed. Location, market demand, property restrictions, acquisition costs, and resale strategies all play important roles in determining whether a deal makes financial sense.

Welcome to Hidden Money, where we investigate overlooked investments, real estate opportunities, online businesses, side hustles, AI, and unconventional ways people build wealth.

This video is for educational and informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, tax, or legal advice. Investment returns and profits are not guaranteed, and financial losses are possible. Always conduct your own research and due diligence before making investment decisions.

#LandFlipping #VacantLand #LandInvesting #RealEstateInvesting #RealEstateBusiness #InvestmentOpportunities #SideHustles #WealthBuilding #Entrepreneurship #OnlineBusiness #FinancialFreedom #RealEstate #HiddenMoney

segments.text: Land flipping is a real estate
investment strategy where you buy vacant
undeveloped land at below market prices
and resell it quickly for a profit.
Unlike house flipping, you're not
renovating anything.
You're simply finding owners who don't
want their property anymore and
connecting them with buyers who do.
The appeal is simple. Lower entry costs,
no tenants, no maintenance, and deals
you can often close from your laptop.
But make no mistake, this isn't a
get-rich-quick scheme.
It requires research, patience, and a
willingness to learn from mistakes.
Today, we're walking through the entire
process, from finding your first
property to cashing your first check.
The first step is sourcing leads.
Most land flippers target rural counties
where property records are public and
owners are often out of state or
inherited the land.
You can pull lists from county assessor
websites, use paid services like
DataTree or AgentPro 24/7, or even drive
through rural areas noting for sale by
owner signs.
Look for red flags that signal
motivation, delinquent taxes,
out-of-state mailing addresses,
properties owned for decades, or
estates.
Your goal is to find someone who views
the land as a burden, not an asset.
A 10-acre parcel in a rural county might
be worth $15,000,
but the owner hasn't paid taxes in years
and just wants it gone.
Before you contact anyone, do your
homework.
Pull the property's legal description,
zoning, and tax history from the county.
Check if utilities, water, electric,
sewer, are accessible, because land
without utilities is harder to resell.
Use Google Earth to examine the terrain.
Is it flat, wooded, swampy?
Visit the county planning department's
website to confirm zoning allows
residential or commercial use.
Search for liens, easements, or
restrictions in the public records.
You're looking for clean title and
buildable land.
A common mistake is skipping this step
and buying landlocked property or
parcels with environmental restrictions.
Even 15 minutes of research can save you
thousands.
Once you've identified a target
property, reach out to the owner.
Most flippers use direct mail,
handwritten letters, or postcards work
surprisingly well.
Your message is simple. I'm interested
in buying your land in County X.
Would you consider selling?
When they respond, listen more than you
talk.
Ask why they own it, what their plans
are, and if they'd consider an offer.
Negotiation in land deals is usually
straightforward because many sellers
inherited the property or bought it
decades ago for next to nothing.
If the land is worth 15,000 and you
offer 6,000 cash with a quick close,
many will say yes.
Your offer should be 30 to 50% of market
value to leave room for profit and cover
your costs.
You've got a verbal agreement, now comes
due diligence.
Hire a title company to run a title
search and confirm there are no hidden
liens, back taxes, or ownership
disputes.
Budget around $500 to $1,000 for title
work and closing costs.
If the title is clean, draft a purchase
agreement.
You can find templates online or hire a
real estate attorney for a few hundred
dollars.
Many land deals close with owner
financing or a simple warranty deed.
Pay any outstanding back taxes as part
of the purchase, it's often negotiable.
Once the deed is recorded at the county,
the land is yours.
Total time from offer to close can be as
little as 2 weeks if you're paying cash.
Now you own the land, time to sell.
List it on Zillow, Craigslist, Facebook
Marketplace, and specialized sites like
Land Watch or Land and Farm.
Price it at or slightly below market
value for a fast sale.
If you bought it 6,000 and market value
Offer owner financing to attract more
buyers. Many land buyers can't get bank
loans, so you become the bank,
collecting monthly payments with
interest.
Take professional photos. Write a
compelling description highlighting road
access, utilities, and nearby
attractions.
Respond quickly to inquiries.
Most land flips sell within 60 to 180
days.
When it sells, you net the difference
minus holding costs and taxes.
Let's talk real numbers.
You can start land flipping with as
little as 3 to 5,000 dollars.
That covers your first property purchase
in a low-cost rural county, plus title
and closing fees.
Add a few hundred for marketing, mail
campaigns, online ads, and listing fees.
If you're reselling at 12,999
a property you bought for 6,000 and
spent 1,000 on acquisition and
marketing, your gross profit is around
Do two deals like that and you've nearly
doubled your starting capital.
Scale up by reinvesting profits.
Some flippers close 10 to 20 deals a
year, netting 50,000 to 100,000 in
profit.
Land flipping profits are taxed as
ordinary income, not capital gains,
because you're buying and selling
quickly.
That means your profit gets taxed at
your regular income tax rate, which can
be 22 to 37% depending on your bracket.
Keep meticulous records. Every expense,
from title fees to mileage, can be
deducted.
Consider forming an LLC to protect
personal assets and simplify
bookkeeping.
Consult a CPA who understands real
estate. They can help you navigate
deductions, estimated quarterly taxes,
and self-employment tax.
Ignoring taxes is the fastest way to
lose your profits.
Plan for 30 to 40% of your net profit to
go to taxes and you'll avoid surprises
come April.
New land flippers make predictable
mistakes.
First, buying without visiting or
researching, you end up with landlocked
or wetland parcels you can't sell.
Second, overpaying because you didn't
comp the market. Always check recent
sales of similar parcels.
Third, underestimating holding costs
like property taxes and insurance.
Fourth, failing to verify access. If
there's no legal road access, the land
is nearly worthless.
Fifth, ignoring liens and title issues,
which can cost thousands to resolve.
Sixth, rushing the sale and pricing too
high out of greed.
Avoid these and you're ahead of most
beginners.
Land flipping isn't risk-free.
Markets can shift and rural land can sit
unsold for months or years if priced
wrong or located poorly.
You'll tie up capital in holding costs,
taxes, insurance, maintenance while
waiting for a buyer.
There's also competition. More investors
are entering the space, driving up
acquisition costs in some counties.
Environmental issues, zoning changes, or
economic downturns can kill a deal.
And if you rely on owner financing, you
become a lender, which means managing
payments and potential defaults.
Success requires patience, discipline,
and a willingness to walk away from bad
deals.
Treat it like a business, not a gamble,
and you'll reduce your risk
significantly.
So, is land flipping worth it?
If you're willing to learn, do the
research, and approach it
systematically, yes.
It offers lower barriers to entry than
other real estate strategies, no tenants
or repairs, and the freedom to work
remotely.
But, it's not passive income, it's
active deal making.
You'll spend hours researching
properties, negotiating with sellers,
and marketing to buyers.
Your first deal will be the hardest.
After that, you'll refine your process
and move faster.
Start small, reinvest your profits, and
build systems.
Land flipping won't make you rich
overnight, but done right, it can become
a steady source of income and a stepping
stone to larger real estate investments.
Now you know how it really works, time
to take action.

metadata.title: Before Your Next Land Deal: 7 Things to Know - REWBCON 2022 with Seth Williams
metadata.author: REtipster
metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to get started as a land investor? Take your first steps here: https://welcome.retipster.com/5-day-email-course/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=lim&utm_content=pBstDNy9IuM
Join Our Community: https://welcome.retipster.com/newsletter/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=lim&utm_content=pBstDNy9IuM
Land Investing Masterclass: http://landinvestingmasterclass.com?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=lim&utm_content=pBstDNy9IuM

Vacant land is one of the most overlooked and misunderstood real estate investments on earth. In this session, you'll learn how the land flipping business model works and why it carries less risk, requires less investment, with less competition while also offering more profit and growth potential than any other real estate investing niche today. Get ready for a paradigm shift!

Various links and websites are mentioned in the presentation:
Delinquent Tax List Tutorial: https://retipster.com/delinquent-tax-list
DataTree Tutorial: https://retipster.com/findingmotivatedsellers1
7 Ways to Make $1,000/mo from Land: https://youtu.be/oTnf8nymjQg
Land Investing Category on REtipster: https://retipster.com/category/land-investing/
REtipster Forum: https://retipster.com/forum
REtipster Facebook Group: https://retipster.com/facebookgroup

This presentation was from REWBCON in Phoenix, AZ, on March 11, 2022. 

Want to attend the next REWBCON? Use promo code "SETH" and get a $50 discount on your ticket: https://retipster.com/rewbcon

00:20 – Intro
00:48 – What exactly is a paradigm shift? If you think land is a bad investment, please watch this :)
02:30 – How Seth got into land and spot where the opportunity lies in this business
05:36 – Can competition ruin your land investing business?
08:09 – What is a good deal?
09:15 – Seth goes through his first done deal and shares examples of how he leveled up his land game
13:17 – Why would somebody sell their property for less than its worth?
14:18 – Why everyone can start their own land investing business - Are there low barriers to entry?
15:23 – Different strategies for how to find motivated sellers
19:20 – Seven ways to make $1,000 per month from land
23:00 – The pros and cons of seller financing land deals
25:16 – Key takeaways
27:36 – Land investing is a life-changing business
29:12 – Where can you learn more about the land investing business?
30:44 – Looking for a course that gives you everything you need to know from A to Z?

segments.text: I'm Seth Williams.
And we're going to be talking about land investing today.
Are there any, active land investors in the room right now?
Okay.
How many of you maybe have heard of land flipping, but you've never really done anything with it?
Like you're kind of familiar with the concept.
How many of you know nothing about this?
Like you've never even heard of it.
Okay, cool.
Any of you've ever been to REtipster before?
Are you familiar with the site or?
Okay, awesome.
Both of you have been there.
That's great.
Well, here's a question for you.
How many of you like things that are boring?
Okay.
Well, I'm not asking that because I'm wondering if you're going to like this presentation,
but I'm asking that because sometimes some of the most important and influential
and life changing things are things that are lackluster and dull and boring.
And today we're going to be talking about a type of real estate that it gets passed over
and is overlooked by a lot of people, most people really.
But I think it's because they don't know how to step back and see the full business model
from end to end of why it makes sense and how it works.
And one way to look at this is sort of like a paradigm shift.
Do you guys know what a paradigm shift is?
Ever heard of that?
Well, I'll give you an example of one.
So once upon a time there was a blind woman
and she got onto a crowded bus and there was standing room only.
And there was a man on the bus who saw the blind woman and he gave up his seat to her.
So, do you think that was a good or a bad thing for him to do good?
No, it was actually a really, really bad thing.
It was so bad he got fired from his job because he was the bus driver.
All right. So that right there is | what we call a paradigm shift.
So, you thought you knew what was going on, right?
You thought you knew this was a good thing, but you didn't know the whole story.
You didn't have all the information.
And once you did have all the information, it all changed.
A good thing, became a bad thing.
It's kind of like seeing how a magic trick is done, where once you see the illusion,
you can't be fooled by it again.
And that's what I hope you'll take away today from what we're talking about here.
So if we quick rewind the clock back to June, 2007,
this is me and my wife on our wedding day.
And... I know, right?
And this was one of the happiest days of our lives,
but there was sort of this lingering issue that you don't see in that picture.
She and I used to have a lot of tension.
I always wanted to be an entrepreneur.
I had all these grand dreams to be job free and all this stuff, but she didn't like that.
She wanted to just live a normal life, just have an 08:00 to 05:00 job, live in a normal house.
And that was fine.
And every time I would tell her about my dreams to do like house flipping.
It was just like, "No, don't do that, Seth."
She didn't want me to go into debt or hurt us. In hindsight, like she was kind of right.
I didn't know what I was doing.
And there was a lot of risk to that, but I felt like she was holding me back
and she felt like I was going to hurt us.
And it was just this underlying problem that was always there.
It was around this time that I discovered the land business.
When you guys hear about land, for those of you who are not active land flippers,
when you guys hear about land, like, do you see dollar signs flashing?
Like when you think of rural dirt, is it like "Yes, money?"
Because I didn't see that.
I didn't see any way to make cash flow or income from dirt out in the middle of nowhere.
And especially when I would look at listings on like the MLS,
it was like why would anybody do this?
This is crazy.
One of the big issues with why I didn't see it and why a lot of people don't see the opportunity
is because they don't understand how to find deals on land.
And this is sort of the key component that makes everything else work.
Because, if you're looking in the right places, you can find motivated sellers that will
sell for prices that like you wouldn't even believe.
it's stuff that I had never seen before.
if you're looking for properties that have a first sale sign of the front yard
or people who have the property listed, that's usually not who you want to talk to
because these people just by nature of the fact that they have a sign like this in their yard,
it shows that they care and they understand what it's worth.
And they actually have an intention of getting that market value out of it.
What we want to do is look where nobody else is looking and look where it's not evident.
And it's getting easier and easier to find these people through things like direct mail,
through different data services, where we can pull very specific lists.
There are even other types of lists that you can get that are harder to get,
but are very effective.
Through this we can reach out to people and say, hey, I'm looking to buy land.
Do you want to sell land? Give me a call.
Or you can send them an offer on the first piece of mail you send them.
Are there any household sellers in the room?
Okay.
If there were, they would probably be like, "What? Are you serious? Direct mail?"
Like no way, that doesn't work.
It's because houses are much, much more competitive than land.
I mean, it's like a different world.
A lot of household sellers spend tens of thousands of dollars per month on mail.
And sometimes they don't get anything from it.
It's just a very saturated business, especially now like more so than it's ever been.
This kind of brings me to the next key attribute of land is that land investors have relatively
very little competition to deal with.
Back when I got started around 2009, at that point in time, there was no competition. Period.
Like if I ever made an offer to anybody, there was nobody else that knew about the deal.
I wasn't competing with 20 other buyers who are offering over asking price.
These days, things are a little bit different.
I can't tell you that it's no competition anymore.
Other people have definitely caught on and there is competition, but even so
it's far, far different from the world of household selling and pretty much any other type of real estate

In this episode, I sat down in person with Alex Reese from Acrewell, a rising star in the land investing world and an absolute YouTube powerhouse. We talk through his journey from eating peanuts in a CVS to flipping hundreds of land deals, building a media brand, and creating a deep educational product for land buyers.

Alex shares the highs, the lows, and the big mindset shifts that got him out of debt and into building real wealth. He also drops a ton of wisdom on soil issues, due diligence, price-per-acre myths, seller psychology, and how YouTube changed the game for him.

If you're into land investing, building a brand, or just want to hear some crazy land deal stories—you’ll get a ton from this one!

How to 10X Your Income as a Land Investor: https://welcome.retipster.com/webinar-invite/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=Zu8LEqQ-L0w

If you’ve ever wondered what the typical “lifecycle” looks like for a vacant land deal, I put together a detailed framework for all the aspiring land flippers out there to clarify how the process works.

Of course, this is just one model that can be followed. This is how I do it, but not every land investor goes through these exact motions (though, from what I’ve seen, most of us follow a similar set of steps). As I’ve been working in this business over the past decade, this is the most systematic and sustainable way I’ve been able to nail down so far.

1:01 - How Land Flippers Create Win-Win-Win Scenarios
2:26 - Step 1: Market Research
5:01 - Step 2: Direct Mail Marketing for Motivated Sellers
7:35 - Step 3: Lead Processing
8:14 - Step 4: Due Diligence
10:35 - Step 5: Closing the Acquisition
13:22 - Step 6: List, Promote and Sell the Property
16:23 - Seller Financing (Optional)
20:27 - Learn more at http://landinvestingmasterclass.com/

segments.text: Hey guys, what's up?
This is Seth Williams from retipster.com
In this video we're going to talk about the land flipping life cycle.
I know a lot of times I hear from other real estate investors
or people who are thinking about getting into real estate
and they hear this idea of land investing
and they just kind of go blank,
like they don't get it, they don't understand it.
They don't get how you can make money from just buying and selling dirt like this.
So my goal in this video is to address that and really give you a high level overview
of what this whole process looks like.
By the time we get to the end of this, you may be in a spot where you're like,
"Man, this is exactly what I've been looking for. This is awesome".
Or you might also be in a spot where you're like,
"Okay, this is not at all what I thought it was. This is not the right fit for me. No thanks".
So however, you end up, my goal is just to make you understand what this entails.
When it comes to flipping land through this particular business model,
it's all about finding a highly motivated seller who is basically apathetic, doesn't want their property,
and they're willing to sell it to you at a price that is far below market value.
Most land investors who are following this business model might make an offer
anywhere from like 5% to 30% of market value
and then immediately turn around and resell that property at a price
anywhere from like 50% to 80% of market value.
So the end buyer who ends up purchasing this property from you is walking away with a great deal.
You're making some really good money in the process
because you've got a pretty nice profit margin built into that.
And the person you're buying it from
they're also winning because in many cases they've lost interest in the property.
They can't afford it, they don't want it.
And if you're talking to a motivated seller who is not willing to sell their property that low of a price,
then it's probably not the right person for you to be talking to anyway.
So it really does set up a win-win-win scenario through every land deal you do,
which is a pretty cool and kind of fun thing about this business.
This land flipping business model is really pretty simple.
There's not a whole lot of complexity to it,
and that's part of why I've always loved it so much.
But it's also important not to confuse simplicity with ease.
There's going to be problems to solve. An issue you have to navigate through.
But believe me, you can totally do it.
So without further ado, let's get into it.
All right.
So the first thing to talk about, if you're brand new to this business
or if you've never done a land deal before, it all starts with market research.
This is all about understanding which markets around the country are going to
make it easiest for you to sell these properties.
So when you've been in this business long enough,
you're inevitably going to find that not all markets are created equal.
For the most part, it's not that hard to find land deals
no matter where you're looking at the country,
if you're pulling the right kinds of lists and following the right process and your marketing.
But what can be more of a bottleneck is getting properties sold.
Some markets are going to make the selling process much easier than others
and the reason it's easier in some markets is
because these areas are just frankly more desirable
for one reason or another or maybe several reasons.
There are a lot of land buyers out there that want to buy the properties in these markets.
It could be reasons such as tourism.
Say if you're talking about a place where a lot of people like to go on vacation,
maybe they come from all over the world just because
this area is known as a really cool, fun, beautiful place to be.
Or it could it be that the population is growing
or there isn't job growth with a very low unemployment rates.
There could be low crime and a lot of other attributes
that just make this area a really nice place to be.
It's important to distinguish, we're not just talking about the places that you find that are desirable.
We're talking about the areas where your target customers
or the other land buyers in the United States find desirable.
So while that's really easy to do,
it's important not to mistake your wants and desires
with the wants and desires of your actual customers
who are going to end up buying it from you.
So that obviously begs the question, how do you find out which areas are actually desirable
and how do you quantify that?
How do you find credible sources of data to prove that you're looking at a market
where people actually want to be?
Well, the good news is there's lots of free websites out there that have this information
and you can find it pretty easily.
Some of the websites you might want to check out are bestplaces.net
citidata.com
niche.com
You can use websites like this to find information
like the job growth in that market.
You can also check out things like the crime rate,
population growth over the past 10 years,
population growth over the past 20 years and a lot more.
And it's not just about looking at each one of these isolated pieces of data.
It's about taking this information on the market that you're considering working in
and comparing it to the national averages.
Is your market doing better than the national average
or is it doing worse
or is it just kind of on par with everybody else?
And obviously you want the areas that are doing better than the national average.
And you want to do this at both the state and the county level of the markets you're considering working in.
So once you figure out what markets you want to work in,
it's all about starting your marketing process to find highly motivated sellers.
People who own vacant land properties that
they do not want and they're willing to sell at a crazy low price.
And pretty much the universally agreed upon method for doing this is through direct mail.
It's definitely not the only way to do it.
But in terms of scalability and efficiency of your time for what we're trying to do,
direct mail just works undeniably well.
But even within the realm of direct mail, there's still a lot of different directions
you can go in terms of how you pull your list, where you pull it from,
how you filter the recipients on that list,
what kind of mail piece you send out,
what service you use to send out that mail piece.
There's a lot of different variables to this.
It's not just about direct mail, it's about how you do direct mail.
So one of the most common and least time consuming ways to do this is
with something called the "Blind Offers".
And this is kind of a jargon term in the land investing business,
but at a high level, "Blind Offers" are exactly what they sound like.
You send out a bonafide purchase agreement
as your first piece of mail that you send out to your recipients.
And obviously you can't research every single property in meticulous detail
before you send out thousands of these blind offers to people.
So you need to learn some best practices
in terms of how to make sense of the data that's out there
and how to come up with an offer price that makes sense based on the market
in which you're working.
And there's a lot that goes into this strategy in order to make it work.
A lot more than I can cover in this video alone.
So below this video I'm going to link to a few of the resources that can help you along the way
if you're interested in pursuing this particular approach.
If you really want to evaluate each deal one by one and send out an offer
that makes a lot more sense on a case by case basis
there are definitely better ways to accomplish this,
but the drawback is it's going to require a lot more of your time.
So if you're somebody who doesn't have a whole lot of time,
but you do have the budget to send a lot more mail,
then blind offers probably are your best bet simply because it's a lot more scalable
and you don't have to play games with the seller leading them on
or making them think you're going to pay a much higher price than you actually are.
So pretty much I get three types of responses when I send out a blind offer to people.
I get acceptances,
I get people who reject or just don't respond to the blind offer,
or I get people who will respond and try to renegotiate for a higher offer price.
Obviously, many, many people are not going to accept your offer.
That's just something you should expect.
But the nice thing about blind offers is that you don't have to have a lot of this back and forth
where they think you're going to make an offer that you're not actually going to make.
All right, so after you've sent out your direct mail campaign,
whether that's in the form of blind offers
or some kind of neutral message on a postcard or something like that,
the next step is lead processing.
You have to pay attention to and respond to the people
who are doing what you told them to do in your mail piece.
Follow-up is key to every type of real estate investing and land is no exception.
Be prepared to respond to emails, letters, and voicemails from people
who basically just want to confirm that your offer is legitimate
and how they can move forward with closing and get paid.
If people want to negotiate with you for a better price than what you offered them,
it's totally up to you as to whether or not you want to pursue those conversations.
You can if you really hungry for deals and you want to get things closed or you can just say no.
If people do accept your offers, it's up to you to keep the ball rolling and move forward
to your due diligence process to make sure you actually understand what you're about to buy.
All right, so when you've got a lead who has said a yes
and they're willing to move forward with selling their property to you
at the crazy low-ball price you offered them.
The next stage is to do your homework and make sure you totally understand
the full scope of what you're about to purchase.
And the reason this is important is because vacant land,
well, for the most part it's pretty simple.
There can be some squirly things with these types of properties that don't come up with
houses and improved properties with buildings on them.
And the whole idea here is to make sure that the offer price you sent them still make sense
with any inherent risks that come to light.
And if it doesn't, you might have to go back to them and say,
“Hey seller, we found this issue with your property that we just learned about.
We need to adjust our offer price”.
And at that point you can either go your separate ways and not do the deal
or if the seller is still motivated, they can agree to that lower offer price
and buy it even cheaper than your original offer was.
So what exactly are you looking for in this process?
Well, I've got a really detailed blog post that goes over
15 of the most common things that are known to derail land deals.
These are things that a lot of times they're a hiding beneath the surface and are not easy to see,
but they're still really important to know about them before you move forward
with buying a property.
I'm going to link to that blog post beneath this video if you want to check it out.
And I will say that in some parts of the country,
some of these issues are not a very common thing.
So it's not like you need to have an anxiety attack every time you're doing due diligence,
but just be aware that in certain geographic locations,
certain issues are going to be much more important to look for it than others.
Due diligence is really one of the most important parts of the acquisition process
and it's also one of the easiest things to overlook and get lazy about.
I know firsthand that can be kind of tedious to go through each one of these steps
and make sure you understand what you're buying.
But believe me, if there's going to be an issue with a property you're going to buy,
you definitely want to know about that before you take title to the property
and you send your money to that seller.
The last thing you want to do is wake up tomorrow and realize you own a property
that you just paid way more for it than you should have
because there's a giant glaring issue that's going to make it a lot harder for you to sell.
It's not a fun place to be.
So do yourself a huge favor on every deal you do.
Make sure you're doing your homework before you take title to that property.
So after your due diligence checks out
and you have a full understanding of what kind of property you're actually purchasing,
the next step is to move forward with closing the deal.
The easiest way by far to handle this process is to simply take your signed purchase agreement
between yourself and the seller and give it to a local title company
or closing attorney depending on what state you're in.
And title companies and closing attorneys are definitely
not the fastest or cheapest way to get this job done,
but they bring a huge value to the table,
especially when they do their job well and do it reasonably quickly.
They handle all the title work, which is a really big part of your due diligence.
They facilitate the signing of documents,
they make sure everybody's schedules are coordinated and lineup
and they also disperse the funds,
which is another huge part of the value that they bring to the table
because if you don't have a title company or a closing agent in place to do this,
it creates kind of an understandable trust issue between yourself and the other party.
And you can certainly get over that,
but it's a lot harder to do when you don't have this third party closing agent involved in the process.
So a good closing agent adds a ton of value.
However, under certain circumstances, like for example, if you're buying a property that
only costs a few hundred dollars,
the idea of paying a closing agent more than the cost of the property itself,
just to close the deal kind of starts to throw the economics of the deal out of whack.
It doesn't mean you can't or shouldn't do it,
but I mean understandably you might start to question - Is that really makes sense?
Is there a cheaper, faster way for me to do this on my own?
And the answer is yes, there is.
It is going to require a bit of learning for you to understand how title work works,
how to understand these documents, how to put them together.
And also there are some states where you legally cannot do this on your own.
You have to hire an attorney to do that.
And I've actually got a separate blog post that discusses how all that works.
So be sure to check out that beneath this video as well.
But assuming you are working in a state where you are legally allowed to complete these
documents on your own,
it is possible to conduct a self-closing and do all this stuff in house
And I think the big obstacles you'll have to work,
they were first of all just understanding and completing the documentation correctly,
which is kind of a big deal.
Aside from that, you also have to figure out how to exchange funds with the other party
in a way that they're going to trust you and you're going to trust them to perform.
And even with that, there are some third party services you can get involved
to kind of be a mediator in this process that's slightly less expensive than a title company,
but still it's one of those obstacles you'll have to work through
if you don't work with a professional closing agent.
But just keep in mind you can go either way.
It's just a matter of how much profit is on the bone with the deal you're working on.
If there's a huge profit margin, then it's kind of a no brainer.
A title company or closing attorney is going to take a ton of work off your hands.
They're probably going to do a better job than you can anyway
and they'll solve a lot of problems and make things a lot easier as you go through the process.
So once all the closing documentation has been signed, notarized and recorded,
you are the new official owner of the property.
And now it's time to turn around and resell this thing
at a significant markup and make your money and you want to do it as quickly as possible.
So when it comes to selling land, there's really three major things to think about.
Possibly four depending on your situation.
And we'll get into that in just a minute.
So the first thing to think about in the selling process is
marketing to find buyers for your property.
As soon as you take title to that property,
your number one goal is to let the world know
that you have an amazing property for sale at a great price
and the opportunity is not going to last long.
This is the message you want to get out as many places as you can.
And personally, I like free things, so I like to list my properties
on websites like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist and Zillow for sale by owner.
Now these websites certainly have their quirks,
but still there are a lot of people on these websites every single day.
It's a great way to get a lot of exposure.
Another option is to try to find a good real estate agent who specializes in selling vacant land.
And in my experience, these aren't actually that easy to find in some markets.
They are kind of few and far between.
And of course, any agent you talk to is probably going to say
that they're amazing at their job regardless of whether they actually are.
So this can be kind of tricky to find one,
but if you can find one, it can be very effective
at almost totally outsourcing the selling process
and just putting the job on somebody else's plate
so that they can spend their time dealing with this instead of you.
If you can find a great agent who knows how to sell land quickly
and they have a big buyers list
it can be an awesome way to really kick your selling process in the high gear.
We've actually got a blog post about how to find these types of land specialized agents.
I'm going to go ahead and link to that beneath this video as well.
Now the next important component of the selling process is lead processing.
Just like when you're doing your marketing to find motivated sellers,
when you're listing your property for sale,
people are going to be responding to your listing and sending you emails
and phone calls and other messages from other mediums
and it's up to you or some kind of a hired assistant to stay in touch
with these people and respond to them, answer their questions,
and don't just stop answering their questions, but asking them
"If this isn't the right property for you, what kind of property are you looking for?"
And then adding them to your buyers list because who knows,
they may be the perfect buyer to snatch up your next property in a matter of days if not hours.
And remember the more of a connection you're able to build with somebody,
the higher likelihood they may actually end up doing a transaction with you at some future date.
So there's always potential value in every conversation you have.
And then the final step in the selling process is just like in the acquisition process - Closing.
Depending on how big the deal is and how complicated you want to make it,
you can either close the thing yourself
or you can find a good local closing agent to handle all this for you.
And like we talked about earlier, there are definitely benefits and drawbacks to both approaches.
So it's up to you to decide what makes the most sense for the deal that you're working on.
And then once the paperwork is signed, notarized and recorded,
you can take your money and move on to the next deal
and keep going through the land flipping life cycle all over again.
So another really important thing that can have a huge positive impact
on your land investing business is seller financing.
You remember that possible fourth thing I mentioned earlier?
That's what we're going to talk about here.
So seller financing is an incredible tool,
especially when you use it in the land investing business.
It can help you make a lot more money.
It can help you sell your properties faster and create a lot of streams of income that
just bring a lot more financial predictability to your business.
And even though seller financing is pretty cool for a lot of reasons,
it's not without its headaches.
So the idea with seller financing is essentially you're going to become the bank and the transaction.
And the reason this is important is because, especially with vacant land,
a lot of land buyers are going to have a really hard time
finding a bank to finance their purchase of vacant land
unless they have an immediate plan to improve that property.
If they just want to buy the land and own it and not do anything with it.
A lot of banks want nothing to do with that
because vacant land is kind of a difficult asset to value
and it just throws a huge wrench into their underwriting process.
So if you're willing to step in and actually be the lender in the form of seller financing,
it provides a huge solution to your buyers.
It allows a lot more potential buyers to purchase the property from you
because if they don't have all the cash in their bank account, they can't buy the thing.
But if you're willing to finance it for them, that just allows a deal to be done
when it otherwise wouldn't be able to happen.
And when you set up a seller finance deal like this,
it's up to you to dictate whatever terms you're willing to accept
so you can determine what kind of interest you're going to charge.
If any, you can determine how much of a down payment you want to collect upfront.
If any, you can collect payments over 12 months, 36 months, 60 months.
It's kind of up to you and there's a lot of things you can do to play with it
and make the deal viable for both you and your end buyer.
And of course, the beautiful thing is, remember you bought this thing free and clear
so you don't have any loans on it.
And yet all the money you're making from this buyer who you're extending seller financing to
is making payments for months and months and months and you don't have any other loans
that you have to pay off in the process.
So a lot of this is pure profit.
And you can even set this up so that the initial down payment you get from this buyer
completely pays off all the money you have invested into the deal.
So right out of the gate you're already made whole and a lot of these payments are just
funneling profit into your bank account on autopilot.
Now I'll be the first to tell you, you absolutely do not need to offer seller financing
in order to make it in the land business.
But for those land investors who are willing to jump into this realm with both feet,
it can be pretty instrumental at adding a lot of stability and just predictable cash flow
to their ongoing business operation.
And it can also play a big role in helping them sell their properties faster and for more money.
But keep in mind when you create these streams of income from seller finance land deals,
it is sort of like passive income but it is going to pay off at some point,
usually within one year to three years to five years,
however long you set the term of your loan.
So if you want this income to keep coming in indefinitely you'll have to keep buying
more properties and selling them with seller financing.
This is not like permanent sources of cash flow.
So that's a really important thing to distinguish
and just keep in mind if you want to do this
seller financing thing in the land business.
And for those out there who do want to work a land flipping business full time,
this kind of seller financing thing can be a pretty big deal
because when you need to live on the income from your land business,
it's a little bit harder to do that when you're just relying
on these big spikes of income when you have a cash sale.
But when you have a whole lot of buyers
who are making consistent monthly payments to you in the form of seller financing,
you could easily build up a base of these types of deals to cover a lot of your overhead.
Just to know that no matter what,
you're most likely going to have this source of income for this month.
Now that doesn't mean this income is guarantee.
You will definitely come across some borrowers who will pay late.
Some people will stop paying, so it's not a totally trouble-free ride.
But still, if you can get like dozens of these kinds of deals paying you on a monthly basis,
even when you do have people who drop off, you can always repossess those properties,
keep all the money that you made from the first defaulting borrower, resell them
and start the cash flowing process all over again.
And they can even be more profitable when people do default
because it allows you to do that.
And there you have it guys.
Those are all the steps included in the land flipping life cycle.
Of course, there's a lot of nuances and details buried
within each one of these steps I just mentioned.
There's a ton of other stuff I can talk about and I actually do talk about it
in the Land Investing Master class that we offer inside the REtipster Club.
This is a full blown 12 module course with a lot of bonuses,
a lot of free coaching calls we do every month
and a members only forum where you can get a lot of your questions answered
and I've laid up pretty much everything I know
and have ever learned about the land business.
It's seriously a treasure trove of information.
So if you've ever wanted that kind of A to Z course, that just lays it all out there,
that's where you can go to check it out.
But even if you're not interested in that,
I really hope you were able to learn a lot of the high-level concepts about
how this land flipping life cycle works when we're following this kind of business model.
As you can see, it's pretty simple,
but that doesn't mean there's not wrinkles tied into each step along the way.
So it's just about understanding how to overcome some of those obstacles.
If you want to take a deep dive and learn everything there is to know about this business model,
head over to retipster.club and check out the land investing masterclass.
Thanks again for watching.
I hope this was helpful.

Show Notes: https://retipster.com/291-landon-bleau/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=podcast&utm_content=Uaqe67xWZN0

Landon Bleau built his land investing business incredibly fast, but the way he did it involved taking some risks I definitely wouldn't recommend for everyone.

He went roughly $45,000–$50,000 into credit card debt, with most of that money going straight into land marketing. Within months, he had paid it back, quit his corporate finance job, and built a land business that he could run remotely.

But that's only part of the story.

In this conversation, I wanted to understand what Landon's operation actually looks like behind the scenes today.

We talk about why he sold every rental property he owned, how the land market has changed since 2024, why minor subdivides now generate a huge percentage of his gross profit, and why texting is producing roughly 3X the return on ad spend of his direct mail.

We also dig into his handwritten blind offer strategy, how he uses Claude Code to price land and analyze millions of text messages, how his five-person team operates, and what happened when he scaled his marketing so aggressively that his net profit fell off a cliff.

There's a lot here for land investors trying to build a more scalable and profitable operation without confusing revenue with actual take-home profit.

I still remember the first time I heard about buying vacant land. My reaction was the same as most people’s.

It sure didn’t seem that exciting, and I couldn’t understand how anyone could actually make money from a vacant land property as an investment.

However, part of that “lack of excitement” comes from a lack of understanding of how the land-flipping business works and the huge opportunity it represents.

I’m Seth Williams from REtipster.com, and in this video, I’m breaking down the entire land flipping life cycle. If you’ve ever wondered how land investors buy and sell properties for massive profits, this is your crash course on how it works.

We’ll cover:
✅ How to find motivated sellers who will sell their land for pennies on the dollar
✅ The best markets for flipping land and how to identify them
✅ Direct mail, cold calling, and other marketing strategies to find land deals
✅ How to analyze and research properties to avoid costly mistakes
✅ The pros and cons of seller financing and how it can boost your profits
✅ How to sell land fast and maximize your earnings

This is the ultimate guide for beginners who want to learn how to start a profitable land investing business. By the end of this video, you’ll know if land flipping is right for you!

I'm excited to have Steve Hodgdon on the show today. He's a smart guy with years of experience in land investing and real estate. Rather than overpromising, Steve gives straight-shooting advice about the real complexities of this business.

We have a free-flowing conversation about some of the less glamorous but oh-so important fundamentals—doing your homework on deals, choosing partners wisely, and how to leverage technology to make better decisions. AI is a big part of the discussion, but he also cautions that the human element is still key to verifying deals, and legwork is still king.

Steve's not flashy, but I appreciate his thoughtful approach and how generous he is about sharing hard-won knowledge. Whether you're an operator looking for funding or interested in backing other investors yourself, this chat breaks down some key ideas that any land flipper can apply right away.

@HonestWealthBuilders 

What if the most valuable asset in your land investing business isn't the land you own, but the customers you've already sold to?

In this episode of the REtipster Podcast, I sit down with **Abi Asija**, co-founder of Gokce Capital, a land investing business he started with his wife, Erica, in 2018.

Since then, they've completed nearly 800 land deals, built a seven-figure business, and grown a team of 20 people.

But what really caught my attention wasn't how many properties they've sold. It was how differently Abi thinks about growing a land business.

While many land investors try to automate everything and avoid talking to customers, Abi has taken the opposite approach. His team proactively calls existing buyers, checks in on their progress, and looks for ways to build relationships that turn into repeat business.

I had a lot of questions about this strategy. Is it worth the extra payroll? Do customers actually want to be called every month? How can you tell whether these relationships are generating more revenue?

We had a pretty spirited conversation about it, and I pushed back on several of his ideas.

In this episode, you'll learn:
- How Abi and Erica grew their land business from a small New York City apartment
- Why 80% of their land sales involve seller financing
- How they encourage buyers to pay off loans early
- The difference between customer service and customer success
- How customer lifetime value can change the economics of land investing
- Why they hired three additional employees for buyer relationships and faster lead response
- How their 60-second response rule helps them capture more sales
- Why Abi tries to scare off job applicants during the interview process
- What he would do if he had to restart a land business with only $10,000

metadata.title: Minor Partition vs. Subdivision in Land Development
metadata.author: Cody Bjugan
metadata.shortDescription:
Minor partitions are getting some attention online right now—splitting a parcel into 2–3 lots. I started there myself 20+ years ago, and it’s a great way to get your feet wet in land with development potential.

But here’s the truth: when you compare the return on effort (ROE) between minor partitions and full subdivision entitlements, the difference is massive. Today, most of my projects average 200–250+ lots, and the impact—both financially and on solving the housing shortage—is on a completely different level.

In this video, I’ll break down:
✅ What a minor partition actually is
✅ How it differs from a subdivision entitlement
✅ Why larger projects create bigger paydays and more community impact
✅ Why I focus on entitlements that solve the housing shortage crisis
✅ How you can start small, but eventually graduate to larger deals

At the end of the day, whether it’s 3 lots or 300 lots, the key is this: land is the foundation of real estate. My mission is to help people understand the value of God’s asset—land—and how entitlements unlock that value.

If you found this valuable, make sure to subscribe!

metadata.title: Backyard Subdivision, What Most People Get Wrong
metadata.author: Peter Kelly Property
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about subdividing your backyard, but worried it could turn into a financial nightmare?
💥 Join Australia’s #1 Property Developer Network (Free): https://www.littlefishnetwork.com.au/
🎯 1-on-1 Mentoring: https://www.littlefishproperty.com.au/mentoring/
📞 Book a Call with Pete: https://www.littlefishproperty.com.au/strategy-session/

👉 Talk to our property development consultants:
https://www.littlefishproperties.com.au/property-development-consultants/

Most backyard subdivisions fail not because the land is too small, but because people miss the real traps that don’t show up until it’s too late. In this video, Peter Kelly breaks down exactly how to subdivide your backyard the right way — without getting screwed.

If you already own a property or you’re considering buying one with subdivision potential, this video will show you what actually matters before you commit a dollar.

No fluff.
No jargon.
Just real-world advice from someone who does this for a living.

🔥 You’ll learn
→ Whether subdividing your backyard actually makes financial sense
→ The biggest mistakes homeowners make before they even start
→ How the position of your existing house can kill a subdivision
→ The minimum vehicle access that actually works in the real world
→ Why outdoor space matters more than most people realise
→ The difference between separate titles vs shared driveways
→ Hidden costs with services, easements, and site constraints
→ Why building behind an existing home costs more than people expect
→ How to run a simple feasibility that protects you from bad deals
→ What fast-track planning rules don’t tell you
→ The exact team you need to avoid expensive mistakes

📣 Powered by: Little Fish Property: https://www.littlefishproperties.com.au/
🔗 Follow Pete: https://www.instagram.com/peterkellyproperty/

👇 Chapters
00:00 Intro
00:58 Why You Want to Subdivide
02:12 Can Your Block Handle a Backyard Subdivision?
03:55 Vehicle Access: The Make-or-Break Factor
05:00 Anything to Retain
05:11 Outdoor Space: Making Both Home Livable
06:54 Driveways, Titles & Common Property
08:07 Services, Easements & Hidden Site Constraints
09:27 Build Logistics: The Hidden Costs
10:10 Running the Numbers
11:06 Fast-Track Planning Rules
11:48 The Team You Need to Get This Right

#BackyardSubdivision
#PropertyDevelopmentAustralia
#SubdivideLand
#DualOccupancy

segments.text: You might be looking at your backyard
thinking, "If I could put another home
out there, that would completely change
the value of this property. Or could it
actually tank the value of the existing
home and leave you with a second home
that no one really wants to live in?"
Wow. That's exactly what we're going to
break down in this video. How to
subdivide your backyard properly so you
don't make one of the biggest mistakes
of your life. Because let's face it, on
paper, it feels simple. You already own
the land. You already have the house.
How hard can adding another home really
be? But this is exactly where people get
caught, even when the block looks
perfect at first glance. A backyard
subdivision can be a smart and lowrisk
way to lift the value of a property you
already own. or it can quietly become
one of the most frustrating and
expensive projects that you'll step into
if you don't understand how these work
in the real world. Let's get into it.
First thing I always ask people is why
they want to do it. Not in a deep
emotional sense, just the practical
reason. Are they thinking about building
something out the back and selling it to
make a profit? Are you looking to hold
both dwellings and create a second
income stream? or are you thinking you'd
like to live in one and rent the other
or eventually move into the new house
and keep the front one as an investment?
Your answer matters because it
completely changes what a good outcome
looks like. If it's a pure investment
play, the numbers need to make sense.
You want to see a reasonable margin
there after all your costs, interest,
tax, and some buffer for risk. If it's
more of an owner occupier move, you
might be more comfortable with a
slightly slimmer financial return
because you're also improving your
lifestyle. Maybe you end up with a brand
new home out the back. And the benefit
of that outweighs chasing a higher
profit. Either way, being clear on your
reason up front keeps you honest. It
stops you from pushing a backyard
subdivision onto a block that simply
can't deliver the outcome you're aiming
for. Once you're clear on the reason for
doing this, the next question is what
the block itself is actually telling
you. The most overlooked factor is the
position of your existing house. Most
people look at the total land size and
think that if you've got 600 or 700
square m, surely I can fit something out
the back. But the location of the
existing house determines what's
genuinely possible. If your house is
sitting in the middle of the block, it
can be very hard to give either home a
meaningful backyard once you start
dividing the land. If it's pushed too
far forward to one of the side
boundaries, you may not have enough
width down the side for proper vehicle
access. If the house is too close to the
front setback, which is the required
distance from the street to the front of
your home, it reduces the space that you
have to work with. And if the house has
parts that stick out towards the side
boundary, like a room or extension, that
can narrow the side access. All of this
affects how cars get through, how the
driveway fits, and what you can design
on the block. It's not just about
squeezing a second dwelling in. It's
about whether you end up with two
genuinely functional houses rather than
one good home and one that feels
compromised. Two quality homes will
always outperform a good one and a poor
one in value and in rent. So when I look
at a backyard subdivision, the first
thing I study is the position of the
existing home. How it relates to its
boundaries and what this means for
access, layout, and the livability of
the home at the rear. That leads into
the next big deal breaker, which is the
vehicle access. If you cannot get cars
to the back safely and comfortably, you
do not have a project. In most cases,
you want around 4 m of clear width down
the side for a driveway that feels
realistic in the real world, not 3 m
that only works if nobody opens a car
door or drives anything bigger than a
hatchback. Actual usable width that
feels good. Then you need to think about
parking for both houses. Planning rules
are usually straightforward here. As a
simple guideline, a two-bedroom home
normally needs one car space, and three
bedrooms and more will mean you need two
car spaces. And that applies for both
the front and the rear home. A lot of
people get excited about the new home
and forget about the front one. They
don't realize the existing house no
longer has compliant parking once they
start carving up the block and going
into town planning and the whole plan
falls apart. So, you need to be honest
with yourself about the access. How wide
is it really once you allow for the
boundary walls, services, and anything
you need to retain? What are you
actually left with? and can you get cars
in and out the way that still feels
functional dayto-day and it's not a
stretch. Once access is dealt with, the
next thing you need to look at is the
outdoor space. Each home needs proper
outdoor space. That's just a planning
term for a decent outdoor area that
people will actually use. Somewhere you
can still sit outside, have a table and
chairs, let the kids play, or set up a
barbecue. not a skinny strip of concrete
that technically ticks a box, but nobody
ever wants to spend time out there. What
often happens is with backyard
subdivisions is by the time that you
allow for a driveway and the turning
room for the cars, garages, carports,
and the setbacks that you need off the
boundaries, the area that's left for the
outdoor living gets tight very quickly.
If the rear home ends up with a
courtyard that feels like an
afterthought, buyers notice that
immediately. Tenants notice it, valuers
notice it, and it will pull down both
your sale price and your rent. The same
applies to the front. If you carve out
too much land off the existing home and
the outdoor area ends up feeling awkward
or half finished, you're hurting the
value of the house that you already own.
So again, you're not just asking, can I
technically fit this? You're asking,
would I be happy living in either of
these homes once they are finished? By
the way, if you're serious about doing a
project like this and you want to learn
from other people who are actually in
the game, make sure you join our
Littlefish Network. It's our free
property developer community with
thousands of like-minded people sharing
their wins, challenges, and lessons
every day. Takes about 2 minutes to sign
up. I'll drop a link in the description.
Now, let us talk about the driveways and
titles because this is another big one.
The premium outcome is when each home
has its own separate driveway and its
own access. The front one keeps its
driveway. The back one has its own
perhaps from a side street or if you're
on a corner if you're lucky enough to
have that, but both homes will have
their own private access. That means
that each house sits on its own lot with
its own land with no shared driveway
area that appears as common property on
the title. Buyers love that. It feels
more like a standalone home and less
like something that has been split. When
that is not possible, you move into a
shared driveway setup where both homes
use the same access and often park
around the back. That can still work. It
is very common but it is slightly lower
quality outcome in terms of privacy and
how it feels daytoday. It also means
that you are creating common property
which is just shared land that both
owners have responsibilities over.
Neither option is automatically right or
wrong but you just want to be clear
about which one you are creating and how
that flows into your end values and your
feasibility. Services are another area
that people routinely underestimate.
Every new home needs its own legal
service connections. That means sewer,
water, power, and whatever
telecommunications that are required in
your area. On a fresh site, where you
knock down an old house and build two or
more dwellings together, you plan for
all that from scratch in one go. With a
backyard subdivision, you're working
behind a house that already exists.
There are already pipes in the ground.
There might be an easement which is a
simple strip of land usually along the
back or side fence where the council or
water authority has rights because the
underground services. There might be
trees that need protecting older
driveways that need to be cut up and
existing service pits in awkward spots.
If you want to stage things, for
example, by renovating or living in the
front house now and building the house
out the back later, you still need to
provide services to the new lot to get
your subdivision approved and receive

Neil Clements unpacks the most powerful value-add for land investors: the land subdivision.

Whether you flip, hold, or develop, mastering subdivisions can double—or even triple—your profit without ever laying a foundation.

In this episode we cover:
- Why carving up dirt beats a standard land flip
- The Texas 10-acre exemption that lets you skip approvals
- Key differences between exempt, minor, and major plats
- Cost, timelines, and hidden risks most investors miss
- How to spot a perfect subdivision deal before you buy

0:00 - Intro & why subdivisions matter
0:42 - Value-add vs. a regular land flip
3:18 - Offering full market price—and still winning

6:05 - Minor plats: approvals, costs, timelines
9:59 - Major plats: roads, utilities, six-figure plans

metadata.author: Clay Hepler

You don’t need to flip more land.

You need to flip it smarter

In this 10-minute breakdown, I’ll show you how we bought an 80-acre parcel in rural Minnesota, split it into four 20-acre lots, and walked away with $235,000 in profit — without touching the dirt.

No construction. No utilities. No heavy lifting.

Just a smart play using **road frontage, zoning, and clean contracts.**

If you're trying to flip land faster and with more upside — this is the strategy you need to understand.

---

- Why large parcels scare buyers (and how to fix it)
- How to use subdivision to multiply exit opportunities
- The real value of road frontage (and what happens if you miss it)

segments.text: To subdivide land, check your zoning, talk to the planning office, hire a surveyor to draw a
plat, get health and utility sign-offs, win approval, and record the plat.
Start with your zoning district, minimum lot size, frontage and setbacks. Then ask
planning staff whether your split is minor or major, and get the checklist.
A licensed surveyor draws the plat. If the lots use septic, the
soil work comes before the vote. Collect utility sign-offs, file,
attend any hearing, and record the approved plat.
A minor subdivision is a small split along an existing road, with no
new street. A major subdivision needs a new street, utility lines or
engineering plans, so it gets a longer review.
Each place draws the line differently. Washington defines a short subdivision as four
or fewer lots, and Toledo, Ohio treats up to five lots as a lot split.
Application fees vary widely. Huntsville charges $50 plus 1 dollar per lot
for a minor subdivision, and Toledo charges $150 per split.
Nashville charges $1,375 for a final plat, and
$3,000 for a major subdivision concept plan.
The full cost is a stack of separate quotes: the planning fee, the surveyor, soil
and septic work, any engineering and road work, bonds and recording.
The government application fee is often the smallest line.
Most states bar the sale of a lot in a new
subdivision until the plat is approved and recorded.
You can still sell the whole parcel before you subdivide, and then the
buyer carries the survey, fees, hearings and approval risk.
A small split is usually faster. Toledo says lot split reviews
typically take several weeks once the application is complete.
Huntsville says its subdivision process takes about 120
days start to finish if no obstacles come up.

After construction, you submit a final plat depicting your lots for approval and recording at the courthouse. After recording, you can finally start selling lots or constructing houses or buildings. How much will your subdivision project cost? At a minimum, you need a survey and a plat. Expect to pay application and recording fees, too. A very simple subdivision could possibly be done for under $2,000, but that's rare. Most subdivisions require some type of utility installation, and many also require road construction. Think about it. How will the new tract to get water? And how will you access the plat? In addition, you may encounter impact fees, such as school impact fees. These can total tens of thousands of dollars per lot, depending on your jurisdiction. Unfortunately, you must pay for all of these costs before selling any lots and earning a return on your money. Surprise subdivision headaches to watch out for. Smart real estate investors should familiarize themselves with common subdivision problems. Keep an eye out for these hiccups. Raw land. Developing raw land typically falls under subdivision regulations. Hire a local surveyor or engineer who is familiar with the local regulations to guide you. Extra lot properties. If you purchase property with an extra lot attached, don't assume that extra lot is legal or immediately buildable. Check to make sure it was properly subdivided before constructing another property. If that date is before subdivision regulations were enacted, then your lot is likely grandfathered. In this video I break down how to make real profit from a paper subdivision by taking raw land through the subdivision and entitlement process and selling the finished lots. I also explain timelines, risks, zoning, infrastructure requirements, and what buyers look for when purchasing approved lots. If you want to learn land development, create higher margins, and scale beyond flipping, this will give you a clear path.

0:00 - Intro
1:01 - Why Use Parcel Tagging?
1:16 - How to Start Parcel Tagging?
3:37 - How to Add Tagged Parcels to Your List?
3:57 - Exporting Your List
4:27 - When to Use Parcel Tagging?
5:00 - Get Special Pricing on DataTree!

Have you ever wanted to build a small but very specific list of properties based on their location, and the normal 'Advanced Search' tool just wasn't precise enough to hand-pick the exact properties and property owners you want?

When I'm going after a smaller number of properties in a more precise vicinity, the "freehand" tool in DataTree is PERFECT for this! I call it 'parcel tagging,' and in this video, I'll show you how it works and in what situations I think it makes the most sense to use this approach.

I use this approach when scoping out an area to find location-specific properties that are difficult to hand-pick with the conventional 'Advanced Search' functionality. It's also useful when the other drawing tools aren't precise enough to find those needle-in-a-haystack properties I'm looking for.

videos.full_text: hey everyone this is Max Edson co-founder of Christ and I'm here to walk you through our out-of-county owner the total parcel ratio map and ultimately what this map is providing you with is a breakdown on a percentage basis of those property owners that own a property within a certain County but don't actually live in the county itself and so to get this value what we're doing is calculating the total number of owner records that do not live in the same county as their parcel and dividing that number by the total number of parcels in that county as a whole and so we're able to provide you these values on a county-by-county basis across the United States and the reason why this is important is because it's one of the common theories amongst investors is that the further they are away from the property that they own the more likely they are to potentially sell that property to you and so if you look in the top right hand corner you'll be able to see the legend where the lighter the county is the fewer out of County owners there are and the darker that county is the more out of County owners there are so as an example if you wanted to look into counties that had a higher or greater percentage of Audi County owners what you would want to do is just type in a certain person percentage let's say 40 or higher and it would filter out those counties that don't necessarily meet that criteria and then you could Target those in particular that do so please like share subscribe if you want to learn more and enjoy

metadata.author: Joséphine Saffert
metadata.shortDescription:
Do you ever wonder how developers and investors instantly spot opportunities in a piece of land?

The secret is using tools like Parcel Viewer. Whether you’re checking ownership, zoning, or lot dimensions, this tool can save you hours of research and help you make smarter, faster decisions.

Discover how developers and investors pinpoint opportunities using tools like Parser Viewer! This video provides a step-by-step guide to using interactive maps for property research, focusing on checking land ownership and understanding zoning regulations. Learn how to leverage gis data and information from the county office to enhance your land use analysis.

I’m Josephine, real estate developer and coach, and in today’s video, I’m going to give you a complete walkthrough of how to use Parcel Viewer like a pro - so you can start finding profitable land deals before anyone else.

Learn how to develop your own properties in Developer Academy! 
👉 DM us “START” on Instagram → www.instagram.com/josephinesaffert 

#realestatedevelopment #parcelviewer #realestate

metadata.shortDescription:
Wetlands provide important benefits for landowners, wildlife, and water quality across Mississippi. Through the Wetland Reserve Easement (WRE) program, landowners can restore and protect wetland areas while supporting their land management goals and contributing to healthier watersheds.

In this video, conservation professionals describe services wetlands provide for water conservation. Learn how water holding can help landowners manage water for wildlife while providing environmental benefits such as improved water quality, wildlife habitat, and floodwater storage.

Learn more about wetland conservation and landowner resources: https://extension.msstate.edu/natural-resources/environment/mississippi-land-stewards

metadata.title: Raw Land Traps 2026: Perc Tests, Road Access & Utility Costs Explained
metadata.author: Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision
metadata.shortDescription:
That cheap $8,000 acre could cost you $60,000 more before you build anything, and you might not be allowed to build at all. In this 2026 guide, we break down the three raw land traps that catch tiny home and barndominium buyers: perc tests, road access and utility costs.

⏱️ WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS VIDEO
✅ What a perc test is, what it costs (about $750 to $1,900) and what happens if you fail
✅ Septic system costs, from about $5,000 up to $25,000 or more
✅ Why physical access is not legal access, and how landlocked parcels trap buyers
✅ Utility costs: power extension, wells, septic, driveways and more
✅ Zoning, easements and deed restrictions to check before you buy
✅ A simple 8-step pre-purchase checklist to protect your deposit

📌 CHAPTERS
0:00 The hook
0:30 Subscribe to Barndo Tiny Homes and Vision
0:50 Why raw land is risky
2:30 Trap #1: The perc test
6:00 Trap #2: Road access
9:30 Trap #3: Utility costs
14:00 Bonus traps: zoning, HOAs and easements
15:30 Your pre-purchase checklist
17:00 Final thoughts

🔔 NEW HERE? Subscribe to Barndo Tiny Homes and Vision for real costs, real builds and real lessons every week.

💬 JOIN THE CONVERSATION
What’s the strangest land problem you’ve run into? Tell us in the comments!

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is general information only, not legal, financial or surveying advice. Costs vary a lot by state, county, soil and distance, and the figures shown are typical 2026 ranges from published guides. Always consult a licensed surveyor, attorney, soil tester and your local planning office before buying land.

metadata.title: Perc testing, flood plains, slope, septic - oh my! Bill Bower explains it all to us!
metadata.author: The Jen Holden Group of Compass
metadata.shortDescription:
We are so excited to welcome Bill Bower to chat with us about all things you need to consider when building a new home or renovating an existing home! Especially here in the Annapolis area where we are surrounded by water, there are many considerations that have to take place before you break ground on any home building project.  Bill’s specialty area is the Chesapeake Bay Critical Area and includes:

Residential and Commercial ALTA Surveys
Waterfront development
Development in FEMA flood zones
Buffer Management Plans
Steep slope remediation
Forest clearing mitigation
Invasive species management
Shoreline stabilization
Septic system design
Stormwater management design
Sediment & erosion control design
Yacht Club & Marina redevelopment
Violation abatement
Permitting agricultural structures (horse barns & indoor riding arenas)

If you want to reach Bill directly to discuss your specific surveying and engineering needs, you can reach him at 410-266-5599 ext. 131 or via email, bbower@cpja.com.  As always, the Jen Holden Group is here to help with all your real estate needs. Reach out to us anytime, 443.803.7620 or jen@thejenholdengroup.com!
