metadata.title: What is a FEMA flood zone and does it affect your claim?
metadata.author: PushLeads
metadata.shortDescription:
This video breaks down every major FEMA flood zone type, what each one costs in insurance premiums, what construction rules apply, and how to find, verify, and challenge your designation. It is for homeowners in flood-prone areas, buyers doing due diligence, and restoration contractors who want to understand the claims landscape their customers are navigating.

FEMA's flood zone maps control more than most property owners realize. Your zone letter determines whether flood insurance is legally required, how high your foundation must sit, and what you must disclose at sale. Getting that designation wrong — or not knowing it at all — can mean the difference between a covered claim and a five-figure out-of-pocket loss. This video walks through the full picture in plain language.

- High risk A and V zones carry a 1% annual flood chance, compounding to a 26% chance over a 30-year mortgage, and trigger mandatory flood insurance on any federally backed loan
- Zone VE requires pile or column foundations so wave action passes beneath the structure, prohibits fill as structural support, and demands breakaway walls below base flood elevation
- Zone AE is the most common high-risk designation and has published base flood elevations that make insurance pricing and building requirements precise
- More than 20% of all National Flood Insurance Program claims come from moderate- and low-risk zones where no federal mandate requires coverage
- An elevation certificate from a licensed surveyor, costing $400 to $800, is the single most powerful tool for reducing your premium — every foot above base flood elevation earns a measurable discount
- A Letter of Map Amendment can remove an incorrectly mapped property from a high-risk zone; engineering and survey costs run $1,500 to $5,000 but a successful LOMA can cut premiums by $1,000 or more per year

metadata.title: Before You Buy Cheap Florida Land: 7 Checks That Kill Deals (Perc, Septic, Flood, Access)
metadata.author: Florida Land Facts
metadata.shortDescription:
A Florida lot for under $8,000 an acre looks like a bargain — until one failed check turns it into the most expensive dirt you ever bought. Before you wire a deposit on vacant land in Florida, run these 7 checks, in this order.

This channel is run by a real Florida land buyer and operator working in Highlands County (Sebring), and every video is built on real lots, real documents, and real numbers. In this one: why the perc test decides your septic system before you ever pick a house plan, what a septic system really costs in Florida in 2026 (conventional $3,600–$12,500, typically $10,000–$15,000, and $15,000–$25,000 for a mound system), FEMA flood Zone X vs Zone AE, landlocked lots and easements, zoning surprises, the gopher tortoise and Florida scrub-jay problem in Central Florida scrub, and the utility question nobody asks until it's too late — plus the one bonus document that protects you from all of it.

THE 7 CHECKS
1. Perc test — it decides the septic system you are allowed to build
2. Septic cost — the system can cost 2–3x the price of the land
3. Flood zone — Zone X vs Zone AE on the FEMA map
4. Legal access — never buy a landlocked lot on a handshake
5. Zoning — setbacks, manufactured homes, RV rules, minimum sizes
6. Protected species — gopher tortoise and Florida scrub-jay habitat
7. Utilities — power distance, well, and internet reality
Bonus: a boundary survey before you close

CHAPTERS
0:00 The $8,000-an-Acre Trap
0:41 The 7 Checks (and Who's Behind This Channel)
1:35 Check 1: The Perc Test Decides Everything
2:32 Check 2: What a Septic System Really Costs
3:21 Check 3: Flood Zone — Zone X vs Zone AE
4:18 Check 4: Legal Access and Landlocked Lots
4:59 Check 5: Zoning — What You Can Actually Build
5:42 Check 6: Protected Species (Gopher Tortoise, Scrub-Jay)
6:28 Check 7: Utilities — Power, Water, Internet
7:13 Bonus: Get a Boundary Survey
7:44 The Order of Operations

Next video: What a Florida Septic System REALLY Costs in 2026.

DISCLAIMER
This video is educational content based on real land-buying work in Central Florida. It is not financial, legal, or tax advice. Costs and rules vary by county, parcel, and date — verify everything for your specific lot with the county, the Florida Department of Health, FEMA's flood maps, and a licensed surveyor before you buy.

AI CONTENT NOTE
This video's narration is performed by an AI (synthetic) narrator voice, disclosed here and in the video itself, as YouTube requires. The content, examples, documents, and imagery are based on a real Florida land operator's actual lots and deals in Highlands County, Florida. Some check illustrations (septic, perc test, wildlife, utility poles) are AI-generated illustrative images and are labeled as such on screen; the satellite, county parcel map, and lot photos are real.

you like, and you may still not be
allowed to build on it because the dirt
cannot absorb the water from one toilet.
That is what a septic system asks of the
ground and the test that decides it can
fail on land that looks perfect. I'm a
civil engineer who works in water
utilities and today I'll show you what
the perk test really measures, what
happens when land fails it, and how to
protect yourself in the contract before
you pay for the ground. First, why this
matters at all. If a lot has no sewer
line, the house needs its own treatment
system and that system lives in the
soil. Here is how it works. Wastewater
leaves the house and flows into a buried
watertight tank where solids settle and
grease floats to the top. The liquid in
the middle flows out through a
distribution box into the drain field, a
set of trenches in the soil, and the
last treatment step is the soil itself.
The EPA says the soil removes harmful
bacteria, viruses, and some nutrients
from that water. So a drain field is not
a pipe problem. It is a soil problem. If
the soil cannot take the water, you need
a different, more expensive system. The
tank only separates solids from liquid.
The soil does the real cleaning slowly
every day for the 15 to 40 years the
system is supposed to last. And here is
the part buyers miss. If it fails, the
seller pays nothing. You do. Once you
close, an unbuildable lot is your lot.
In the last official count, the 1990
census, about 25% of Americans used
septic systems. Newer survey numbers are
lower, but the industry disputes them.
Now the test, a percolation test or perk
test times how fast water drains into
the soil measured in minutes per inch.
Here is what Alabama's extension service
describes. Dig at least six holes, 24 to
42 inches deep and 8 to 12 inches wide.
Soak them for at least 4 hours or
overnight. Then measure how fast the
water drops every 5 minutes if it is
fast, every 30 if it is slow. The test
can take 3 to 4 hours and the readings
from the holes are averaged into one
number for the whole drain field area.
So what number fails? That guide says a
rate of 60 minutes per inch or slower is
unacceptable for a standard drain field.
That is tight soil and the water just
sits. The wastewater has nowhere to go
and it comes back up in the yard or in
the house. The opposite matters too. The
same guide says sandy and gravelly soils
are not recommended either and water
that races through gets less treatment.
The perc rate is not the only gate. The
water table, bedrock, or a tight layer
should be at least 4 ft below the
trenches. A lot can look dry in August
and hold water in March. Soil borings
can reveal that with mottled red and
gray soil or standing water in spring.
That is why some counties care about wet
weather testing. A perc test in a dry
August can give you a comfortable number
that March will not honor. The slope
should be under 15% and land that floods
should never be used for a drain field.
One extension guide says 1 acre is
usually the minimum with good soil
because you need the system, a repair
area, and 100 ft from wells. You can
look up your lot in the county soil
survey. It is useful for screening, but
that guide says it cannot replace a test
on the actual ground. Pipes before
plans. Before you picture the kitchen,
find out where the pipes will go because
on this lot the pipe ends in the soil.
Now, who decides? Not the seller and not
the realtor. Usually it is the county
health department and the rules change
from place to place.
In North Carolina's Onslow County, for
example, there are three permits.
First, an improvement permit after the
soil evaluation.
Then a construction authorization, which
is required before you can get building
permits. Then an operation permit after
the installation passes inspection.
Notice the order. You cannot get
building permits until that septic
authorization exists. So the septic
decides the schedule, not the builder.
That first permit states the system type
and the number of bedrooms. A bedroom
count can limit the size of the house
you build. And if the soil is
unsuitable, the county sends a turn down
letter. That one letter can end a plan
that looked finished on paper.
In Indiana's Wayne County, a certified
soil scientist has to profile the soil.
The report is valid for two years and
the permit itself for one.
So an old soil report from the seller
may be stale by the time you buy. Ask
the county how old it is and whether it
is still accepted.
Wayne County also says that if a drain
outlet sits off your property, you need
a recorded easement. A septic plan can
depend on your neighbor's land. In
California's Mendocino County, the
health division defines wet weather
testing and says final approval depends
on several factors, not just the perk
rate. And a test hole in a spot where
the lines cannot be installed will not
be accepted. The number alone never
decides it. I do one-on-one feasibility
reviews and I made a free land and
utility checklist you can start with.
Both links are in the description. So
what if the land fails? It is often not
the end.
It means you need a different system,
like a mound or an aerator, as the
extension guide puts it. One cost guide
says a mound is used when the water
table is high, bedrock is shallow, or
the soil is too dense, and it is built
up above the natural ground.
Those systems cost more. The same guide
puts a conventional system at about
and a mound at $15,000 to $25,000. An
advanced treatment unit, the aerobic
kind, runs $15,000
to $30,000 or more and is often needed
near sensitive waters. Those are one
guide's ranges, not quotes. The same
guide lists the soil evaluation at $150
to $500 and a designer at $1,000 to
$5,000. Wayne County lists a $400 permit
fee. So the real price of a lot with no
sewer is the price plus what your soil
demands. Two lots that look the same can
differ by $10,000 or more. What drives
the price? Soil and water table depth,
bedrock, terrain, the system type and
field size, tank material, labor,
permits, and restoring the yard
afterward.
If a lot fails, you have three choices.
Pay for a different system if the county
allows it. Move the system to a better
spot on the lot or renegotiate or walk
away. All three are cheaper before you
close. That is why the order matters.
Test first, buy second. The test also
helps design. It tells the designer
where the field can go and how large it
must be, which is why the soil comes
before the floor plan. Now, how to
protect yourself. One. Do not trust a
verbal it should perks. The extension
guide says professionals must perform
the tests to get a permit. Two. Put it
in the contract. Make the purchase
contingent on a passing soil evaluation
with enough time for wet weather testing
if your county requires it. Ask your
attorney or agent how to word it because
contingency rules vary by state and I am
an engineer, not a lawyer. Three. Call
the county health department before you
make an offer. Ask if the lot was ever
tested, approved, or turned down and
whether a permit exists. Four. Ask what
else the county requires. Setbacks, lot
size, a repair area, the distance to
wells. In Onslow County, the septic
setback is 10 ft from property lines and
5 ft from the dwelling. Five. Look at
the neighbors. Septic systems and wells
next door are a clue, not proof, because
the soil on your lot is what gets
tested. Six. Ask how many bedrooms the
lot supports. If you want a four-bedroom
house and the approval is for two, that
is a problem you want to find before
closing. Seven. Ask whether sewer could
ever come. A sewer district's will serve
letter says the district can serve a
lot. It does not say the pipe is at your
property line or who pays to extend it.

question changes. Hire a septic
inspector before you buy. EPA says local
rules or your lender may even require
it. Ask whether the system was ever
repaired or replaced and ask the health
department for the as-built drawing. EPA
says that is one way to locate the
system. The inspector checks pumping
records, the age, the sludge and scum
levels, leaks and backups, the tank and
pipes, and signs of drain field failure
like standing water. EPA says a system
can last 15 to 40 years with care and
should be inspected every 3 to 5 years

Vendor sold a landlocked block of land surrounded by the vendor's retained land and adjoining railway land. The purchaser had no legal right of way to any public highway. English High Court held an easement of necessity was implied across the vendor's land because without it, the granted land could not be used at all.

🏛️ RATIO DECIDENDI & KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES
• Core Ratio: An easement of necessity will be implied at common law only where land is completely and absolutely landlocked with zero lawful means of physical access, not for mere convenience.
• Statutory & Doctrinal Anchors: Common law doctrine of easements of necessity; Non-derogation from grant; Pomfret v Ricroft; Clark v Cogge.
• Key Principles & Application: Strict common law rule: Convenience, commercial advantage, or cheaper access is never enough. The land must be physically impassable without access. Contrast with statutory easements under s 88K Conveyancing Act 1919.

🔍 CASE ANALYSIS & DOCTRINAL BREAKDOWN
[Parties to the Dispute]: Plaintiff: Barry (purchaser of landlocked plot). Defendant: Hasseldine (vendor of plot / adjoining servient owner).
[Ancillary Parties]: Air Ministry / Disused Airfield (third party owning adjacent land over which permissive access had previously been granted).
[Material Facts Summary]: A landowner sold a landlocked plot surrounded by his own land and a third party's airfield. Permissive airfield access was revoked. Held: grantee was entitled to an implied easement of necessity across vendor's retained land.
[Chronology of Events]: 1. 1947: Defendant Hasseldine sells triangular plot of land to plaintiff Barry for £475. 2. Plot completely surrounded on two sides by Hasseldine's land, and on the third side by a...
[Procedural History]: High Court of Justice, Chancery Division before Danckwerts J. Action for declaration of an easement of necessity.
[Court's Legal Analysis]: Danckwerts J examined the foundational doctrine of easements of necessity.
[Legal Framework Classification]: Implied Easements of Necessity, Non-Derogation from Grant, Landlocked Parcels, Legal Right vs Precarious Permissive Access.
[Key Judicial Definitions]: Necessity vs Permissive Access: Danckwerts J at 839: 'A way of necessity depends on the absence of any legal right of access...
[Applied Rules & Statutory Provisions]: Common law doctrine of easements of necessity; Non-derogation from grant; Pomfret v Ricroft; Clark v Cogge.
[Substantive Legal Topics]: Easements; Way of Necessity; Implied Grant; Landlocked Land; Non-Derogation from Grant; Permissive Licences; Access to Highway.
[Final Outcome of Appeal/Trial]: Judgment for the plaintiff; declaration that plaintiff was entitled to a way of necessity over defendant's land.
[Substantive Orders Made]: Declared that the plaintiff was entitled to a way of necessity over the defendant's driveway, with inquiry into exact route if parties could not agree.
[Costs Orders]: Defendant ordered to pay the plaintiff's costs of the action.
[Precedent Distinctions & Relations]: Seminal common law authority modernising easements of necessity; distinguished in Case #57 (Manjang v Drammeh) where navigable water access existed;
[Subtext & Commercial Context]: Postwar rural parcel carving where informal friendly access arrangements collapsed when military authorities cordoned off surplus airfield property.
[One-Sentence Case Synthesis]: Easement of necessity benchmark: implied way arises over grantor's land where alternative access across a third party's land was merely a revocable licence.
[Key Pinpoint Citations]: Clark v Cogge (1607) Cro Jac 170; Corporation of London v Riggs (1880) 13 Ch D 798 at 806; Holmes v Goring (1824) 2 Bing 76; Pinnington v Galland (1853) 9 Exch 1 at 12.

segments.text: Barry and Hasseldine In November 1947,
the defendant sold a plot to W. J.
Farmery, retaining surrounding land. The
plot was bounded by the defendant's land
and strangers' properties. At
conveyance, access was obtained over a
disused airfield on a stranger's land
via a permissive right of way.
In October 1949, Farmery conveyed the
plot to the plaintiff, Barry. In 1950,
the stranger fenced off the airfield,
terminating the permissive access.
Barry sued when Hasseldine refused him
access across his retained land to the
highway. The defendant defended the
action on the grounds that a way of
necessity only arises if the granted
land is entirely enclosed by the
grantor's land, and that the permissive
airfield way barred the implication of
necessity. The key property law issue
was whether a way of necessity can be
implied when land is partly enclosed by
strangers' land, and if a permissive way
over a stranger's land defeats the
implication.
Danckwerts, Justice, allowed the claim.
The court held that a way of necessity
is implied by law as an incident to a
grant.
Common sense dictates that if a grantee
has no legal right of access except over
the grantor's land, a way of necessity
must be implied to prevent the land from
being useless. This applies even if the
land is partly surrounded by strangers.
Furthermore, a mere permissive way of
approach cannot defeat the implication,
since permission can be terminated at
any time. The court defined easements of
necessity and landlocked land. The court
considered Gayford and Moffatt and
rejected the contrary obiter in
Titchmarsh and Royston Water Co. The
court granted Barry the specific remedy
of a declaration of a way of necessity
and an injunction restraining
interference.

videos.full_text: Barry and Hasseldine In November 1947, the defendant sold a plot to W. J. Farmery, retaining surrounding land. The plot was bounded by the defendant's land and strangers' properties. At conveyance, access was obtained over a disused airfield on a stranger's land via a permissive right of way. In October 1949, Farmery conveyed the plot to the plaintiff, Barry. In 1950, the stranger fenced off the airfield, terminating the permissive access. Barry sued when Hasseldine refused him access across his retained land to the highway. The defendant defended the action on the grounds that a way of necessity only arises if the granted land is entirely enclosed by the grantor's land, and that the permissive airfield way barred the implication of necessity. The key property law issue was whether a way of necessity can be implied when land is partly enclosed by strangers' land, and if a permissive way over a stranger's land defeats the implication. Danckwerts, Justice, allowed the claim. The court held that a way of necessity is implied by law as an incident to a grant. Common sense dictates that if a grantee has no legal right of access except over the grantor's land, a way of necessity must be implied to prevent the land from being useless. This applies even if the land is partly surrounded by strangers. Furthermore, a mere permissive way of approach cannot defeat the implication, since permission can be terminated at any time. The court defined easements of necessity and landlocked land. The court considered Gayford and Moffatt and rejected the contrary obiter in Titchmarsh and Royston Water Co. The court granted Barry the specific remedy of a declaration of a way of necessity and an injunction restraining interference.

metadata.title: 🎥 Landlocked Land in Florida?! What I Learned While Hunting for Access, Easements & Closest Neighbor
metadata.author: Amber Shah of St. Augustine Realtor
metadata.shortDescription:
🎥 Landlocked Land in Florida?! What I Learned While Hunting for Access, Easements & the Closest Neighbor | Amber Shah Realtor

Today’s real estate adventure took me off the paved roads and into the real-world puzzle of buying land in Florida — because not every property comes with an easy driveway, a cute mailbox, or even legal access. 😳🌳

In this video, I went out to look at a piece of land for a customer, and we quickly discovered one major issue: the property appeared to be landlocked. That means there may not be direct road access to the parcel, which can make buying, selling, financing, building, or even simply walking onto the land much more complicated.

So what did I do?

I started looking for the closest neighbor nearby to try to understand possible access points, existing paths, road frontage, and whether there could be an easement situation that might allow my customer to legally reach the land.

This is the kind of real estate work people do not always see online. It is not just pretty houses, closing photos, and cute signs. Sometimes real estate means boots on the ground, county research, neighbor conversations, property appraiser maps, deed research, surveys, title questions, and learning how land access really works.

🌿 In this video, I talk about:
✅ What it means when land is landlocked
✅ Why access is one of the most important things to verify before buying vacant land
✅ What an easement is and why it matters
✅ Why nearby neighbors may be part of the solution
✅ Why buyers should never assume they can legally access a parcel just because it shows up on a map
✅ Why land buyers in Florida need a knowledgeable Realtor who will actually go look, ask questions, and dig deeper

Buying vacant land in St. Augustine, St. Johns County, Putnam County, Flagler County, Hastings, Palatka, Interlachen, or anywhere in Northeast Florida can be an incredible opportunity — but it also comes with due diligence.

Before buying land, you need to ask questions like:

Does the property have legal access?
Is there road frontage?
Is there an easement?
Is the easement recorded?
Can you build on it?
Is it wetlands?
Is it in a flood zone?
Will a lender finance it?
Can you get utilities?
Can you install septic and well?
Are there zoning restrictions?
Are there deed restrictions?
Is there an HOA?
Can you actually get to the land without trespassing?

Because a cheap piece of land is not always a good deal if you cannot legally access it, build on it, or use it the way you planned.

This is why I always say real estate is part strategy, part research, part intuition, part persistence, and part “let me go knock on a neighbor’s door and figure this out.” That is the Yoga in Sales way: presence over pressure, service over ego, and always be connecting.

If you are thinking about buying land in Northeast Florida, especially in St. Johns County, Putnam County, Flagler County, Hastings, Palatka, Interlachen, Elkton, St. Augustine, or the surrounding areas, call me before you buy. I can help you understand what questions to ask, what red flags to watch for, and how to start researching whether the property is truly usable.

metadata.shortDescription:
Understanding the basics of easements and encroachments is important for preparing for your real estate exam. This real estate exam prep video will discuss the key real estate terms of:

(1) Easements - The legal interest in the land of another defined as a right to use
(2) Encroachments - Tresspassing or intruding upon the land of another, such as tree branches or fences 
(3) Ingress & Egress - To enter and exit
(4) Easement Appurtenant - An easement that runs with the land, such as a shared driveway
(5) Easement of Necessity - Created by law when a landl owner id landlocked and needs access to the real property
(6) Easement by prescription - Rights gained in the land of another by continuous use
(7) Easement in Gross - An easement that does not have a dominent tenant, such as a utility easement

Best of luck with your studies...

metadata.author: Texas Agriculture Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Newsflash:  Property can be landlocked in Texas and there is not a law that requires a neighbor to give automatic access.  What does this mean for a landlocked owner?  In what situations can a landlocked owner seek legal access from a court?  What should a landlocked property owner do?

We have more information on landlocked property on the following episode of Ag Law in the Field:  https://aglaw.libsyn.com/episode-153-cassie-gresham-access-to-property-landlocked-property-myth-busting

For more information on options to gain legal access:  https://agrilife.org/texasaglaw/2018/07/23/questions-from-tiffanys-desk-how-can-i-access-landlocked-property-in-texas/

Why Double Closing Land Deals Rarely Works #doubleclosing #landflipping #realestatetips

In this episode, Steven and Jill explain why double-closing land deals usually fail and what strategy works better instead. They share real stories from investors, legal issues you could face, and why skipping due diligence or trying to resell without owning the property leads to problems. 

If you’re new to land flipping, this honest talk can help you avoid a costly mistake and build a better, long-lasting business model.

On today's Land Academy Show, join Steven Jack Butala (https://www.linkedin.com/in/steven-butala-39853916) and Jill DeWit (https://www.linkedin.com/in/jill-dewit) pull back the curtain on why double closing in land deals often leads to frustration, not profit, and reveal their tried-and-true alternative. 

They'll dismantle common myths about using a buyer's funds, expose the practical and legal traps that derail deals, and show you how to structure transactions with far greater efficiency. If you've ever contemplated a double close to conserve cash or sidestep risk, this episode delivers the unvarnished truth about the math, the pitfalls, and a demonstrably cleaner, more scalable path to closing land deals.

metadata.title: Closing Costs Explained: Lender Policy vs Owner Policy
metadata.author: Clause Gate
metadata.shortDescription:
Today we learn how mortgage insurance choices directly impact your home buying journey by comparing an owner policy with a lender policy. Understanding these closing costs ensures your real estate investment stays fully protected against unexpected legal claims. Many homebuyers miss critical differences during closing, putting their property equity at serious risk. We break down both policy options so you can make smart legal decisions before signing final loan papers. Watch full video, like and subscribe the channel.

#MortgageInsurance #ClosingCosts #Homebuying #RealEstate #Refinance

segments.text: Welcome back to Clausegate, your trusted
source for breaking down complex real
estate and legal concepts into easy to
understand guidance. Buying a home is
one of the largest financial investments
you will ever make in your life. So,
protecting that asset from legal
disputes is critical. When you close on
a real estate transaction, title
insurance plays a central role in
securing your financial peace of mind.
Many home buyers get confused when they
see to different policy fees listed on
their closing disclosures. Those two
distinct options are known as the lender
policy and the owner policy, each
serving a completely different purpose.
Understanding the differences between
these two insurance policies ensures you
make smart choices at the closing table.
Title insurance fundamentally differs
from traditional insurance policies like
home insurance or car insurance because
it protects against past issues rather
than future events. When a property
transfers from one owner to another, a
comprehensive search of public land
records takes place to confirm clear
ownership. However, even the most
thorough public records searches can
mish hidden errors, unrecorded leans, or
fraudulent deeds from decades ago. That
is precisely where title insurance steps
in to shield buyers and financial
institutions from financial loss.
Without proper coverage, an unforeseen
defect in the legal history of the
property could jeopardize your ownership
rights. Exploring how each policy
functions will help you protect your
investment for years to come. A lender
title insurance policy is specifically
designed to protect the financial
interest of the mortgage bank or lending
company funding your loan. When a bank
lends hundreds of thousands of dollars
to help you purchase real estate, they
require assurance that their financial
lean remains valid. If an undiscovered
legal issue arises that challenges
ownership of the land, the bank could
risk losing their financial collateral.
To eliminate this risk, almost every
institutional lender mandates that the
home buyer pay for a lender policy as a
non-negotiable condition of loan
approval. This requirement ensures that
the financial entity providing your
mortgage money stays fully protected
throughout the life of your loan
repayment. It is crucial to understand
that a lender title insurance policy
provides zero direct legal protection
for you as the actual home buyer. The
policy coverage amount matches the
original principal loan balance and
systematically decreases as you pay down
your mortgage. Once you pay off your
loan balance entirely, the lender policy
completely expires, leaving no
continuing protection for the land or
structure. If an ancient air surfaces
claiming ownership of your house, the
lender policy only steps in to protect
the financial institution from financial
loss. The bank gets reimbursed for their
outstanding loan balance, but you could
still lose your home and all your
invested money. In sharp contrast to
lender coverage, an owner title
insurance policy is specifically crafted
to protect the home buyer and their
accumulated equity. Purchasing an owner
policy is typically optional in many
real estate transactions, but skipping
this vital protection leaves your
lifetime savings exposed. An owner
policy covers the full purchase price of
the property, preserving your financial
investment against past legal defects.
Unlike auto or homeowners coverage,
which requires annual premium payments,
an owner title policy requires only a
single one-time fee paid at closing.
That single payment provides continuous
coverage for as long as you or your
legal heirs retain ownership of the
house. The legal protections provided by
an owner title policy shield buyers
against a wide variety of serious hidden
ownership defects. Common examples of
title defects include forged deeds,
illegal transfers by previous owners,
undisclosed heirs claiming rights to the
property, and improper tax filings.
Additionally, unpaid contractor bills
from previous owners can result in
mechanic leans that attach directly to
the land you just purchased. If a
longlost legal heir appears years after
your closing date and claims ownership
of your living space, your owner policy
covers all legal defense fees. Without
an owner policy, you would have to pay
thousands of dollars out of pocket to
defend your legal right to stay. To
highlight the difference, imagine a
scenario where a previous property owner
failed to pay property taxes or forged a
signature on a deed. If a court
determines that the deed transfer was
illegal, the entire property transaction
could be declared completely invalid. In
that unfortunate situation, a lender
title policy would pay off the bank for
the remaining mortgage loan balance to
protect their business interest.
However, without an owner title policy,
you would lose all the cash you put into
your down payment and equity payments.
You would effectively be left without a
house while receiving zero financial
compensation for your catastrophic loss.
Calculating the cost of title insurance
policies depends heavily on state
regulations, local customs, and the
final purchase price of your property.
In many real estate transactions,
purchasing both policies simultaneously
unlocks a special discounted rate known
as reissue coverage or simultaneous
issue pricing. Buying both policies
together is significantly cheaper than
purchasing each insurance policy
separately at different points in time.
Depending on the state where you buy
real estate, local custom dictates
whether the seller or the beer pays for
the owner policy. Negotiating who pays
for these closing costs can be an
effective strategy during purchase
agreement discussions. The long-term
benefits of carrying an owner title
insurance policy extend directly to your
family and estate planning decisions.
Should you pass away, your owner title
policy automatically transfers its
coverage to your legal heirs who inherit
the family real estate. This inheritance
feature ensures that your children or
relatives receive the exact same
ownership protections without paying
additional insurance premiums. As your
property appreciates in value over time,
some insurance companies even offer
inflation writers to boost your coverage
limit. Securing long-term protection
ensures that your hard-earned real
estate wealth remains safely preserved
for future generations.
Different states across the United
States operate under varied regulations
regarding how title insurance rates and
policy forms are established. In heavily
regulated states like Texas or Florida,
title insurance rates are set by
government agencies, eliminating price
variance between companies. In other
states, title insurance companies
compete freely, allowing smart consumers
to shop around for lower closing fees
and title services. Regardless of state
rules, consumers possess the legal right
to choose their preferred title company
rather than accepting defaults. Shopping
around for title service providers
empowers you to find competitive rates
while securing quality policy
protection. Real estate investors and
firsttime home buyers alike must avoid
common misconceptions surrounding title
insurance policies and mortgage
requirements.
A frequent misconception is believing
that a clean preliminary title report
guarantees that no future title claims
will ever surface. Another common
mistake is assuming that the lender
policy automatically covers the beer
simply because the beer paid for it at
closing. Dispel these dangerous myths
early in your home buying journey so you
can make informed decisions about your
financial security. Buying a home
without an owner policy is an
unnecessary risk that no smart property
beer should take. When reviewing your
loan estimates, pay careful attention to
how simultaneous issuing fees are
calculated and displayed by your
mortgage lender. If you decide to
purchase both policies, the title
company applies a substantial discount
to the owner policy premium. This
bundled discount makes adding full
equity protection far more affordable
than many firsttime home buyers
originally anticipate. Always ask your
title agent or real estate attorney to
provide a detailed breakdown of
simultaneous policy pricing options.
Taking a proactive approach during
contract negotiations guarantees you
receive every financial discount
available under state law. Navigating
the closing process requires a clear
view of all financial obligations listed
on your closing disclosure document. On
standard paperwork, the lender title
policy is listed under the mandatory
closing costs section required by your
loan provider. The owner title policy
usually appears under the optional
services section, which leads some
misinformed buyers to decline it to save
cash. Experts strongly advise against
skipping the owner policy because the
cost of defending a property lawsuit far
exceeds the initial policy fee. Spending
a few hundred at closing prevents
life-changing financial hardship if an
unknown title defect emerges down the
road. Understanding how title searches
operate explains why title insurance
remains essential despite thorough
preliminary work by legal professionals.
Before closing, a specialized title
company reviews historical deeds, tax
records, court filings, and county
registries for red flags. This process
identifies standard issues like
outstanding mortgages, municipal leans
or recorded easements that must be
cleared before transfer. However, public
records are created and maintained by
human beings, meaning human error can
occur during record filing. forgeries,
missing probate records, and filing
mistakes cannot be discovered through
standard record searches alone. Making
title insurance a vital safety net. When
an unexpected title claim emerges after
closing, filing a claim under your owner
policy initiates an immediate legal
defense. Your title insurance company
assigns experienced legal counsel to
represent your interest in court without
requiring out-ofpocket legal retainer
fees. The insurance provider works
directly with local courts to clear the
title defect or negotiate a financial
settlement with the claimant if the
legal claim cannot be defeated. The
policy reimbures you for covered
financial losses up to your total policy
limits. Having a major insurance firm
backing your property rights ensures you
do not face complex property litigation
alone. Comparing title insurance to
regular hazard insurance highlights why
the two products work together to
protect your primary residential
property. Standard homeowners insurance
protects against future events like
accidental fires, severe windtorm
damage, theft or liability for slip and
fall injuries. Title insurance strictly
protects your legal right of ownership
against events that occurred in the past
prior to your closing date. You need
both types of insurance coverage because
house fires and ownership disputes
present to entirely different financial
threats. Combining strong hazard
insurance with a solid owner title
policy creates complete financial
protection for your residential real
estate. Refinancing an existing mortgage
loan also impacts your title insurance
requirements, creating questions for
property owners undergoing the process.
When you refinance your home, your new
lender will always require you to
purchase a fresh lender title policy.
This requirement exists because the old
mortgage gets paid off entirely,
terminating the original lender policy
that protected your previous bank.
Fortunately, you do not need to
repurchase a new owner title policy when
refinancing your mortgage loan. Your
original owner policy remains fully
active and continues protecting your
equity for as long as you retain
ownership. Every home buyer should view
title insurance as an indispensable
component of a comprehensive personal
financial plan. Protecting your home
equity safeguards the foundation of your
family wealth against hidden legal
challenges that could destroy your
finances. The small upfront cost of an
owner policy delivers decades of
security shielding you from costly
property litigation and lost equity.
Making sure both your lender and
yourself are protected allows you to
move into your new home with complete
confidence. Take time to read your
policy documents carefully so you
understand your specific rights,
exceptions, and coverage limits. In
conclusion, distinguishing between a
lender policy and an owner policy is
essential for anyone purchasing real
estate in the United States. The lender
policy serves the financial institution
by securing their loan balance, while
the owner policy protects your
hard-earned equity and ownership rights.
Choosing to buy an owner title policy
alongside the mandatory lender policy
ensures complete coverage against
historical title defects and legal
claims. Investing in both policies
safeguards your home, your family, and
your financial future against unexpected
legal troubles. Make informed choices at
the closing table to ensure your real
estate journey remains safe and
successful. Thanks for watching the
video. Subscribe this channel. Like the
video if you found the video great.

Ready to learn a land investing strategy that could skyrocket your profits?

In this LIA 2.0 coaching response, I break down how we structure our land double closes, including why we target at least $15,000 in spread, how we negotiate with buyers, and why we've largely moved away from 90-day double-close contracts.

- Why we target a minimum $15,000 spread
- How we negotiate price versus closing terms
- Why we collect earnest money from buyers
- The reason we prefer 120-day double closes
- How we negotiate agent fees on smaller deals
- What new land investors should know about their first double close

metadata.title: Florida Title Insurance Explained - What Buyers MUST Know Before Closing
metadata.author: Casey Joiner
metadata.shortDescription:
Florida Title Insurance Explained - What Buyers MUST Know Before Closing
Featuring Guest Expert: Kirby Williams, Board Certified Real Estate Attorney And Founder of Shoreline Title LLC.

If you're buying property in Florida real estate, you’ve probably heard the term title insurance, but do you really know what it protects you from? 
In this video, Casey Joiner discusses with Florida real estate attorney Kirby Williams of Shoreline LLC Title to break down Florida title insurance in the simplest, clearest way possible, so you can make confident decisions before closing.
Whether you're a first-time buyer, a seasoned investor, or just trying to understand how title insurance works, this conversation will save you money, stress, and potential legal headaches.
From forged deeds to open permits, property line disputes, survey problems, and easement issues, we cover the real situations that buyers run into and why title insurance in Florida matters more than ever.

GUEST:
Kirby Williams
Board Certified Real Estate Attorney And Founder of Shoreline Title LLC
Kirby earned his J.D. in 1997 and has practiced real estate law in Florida and Alabama ever since. Today, he helps close real estate transactions across Walton, Okaloosa, and Bay Counties, bringing decades of legal and title insurance experience to ensure every closing is handled with care, clarity, and full protection for buyers.
Shoreline Title LLC - https://shorelinetitlellc.com/

00:00 Introduction
00:36 Kirby Williams with Shoreline Title LLC
03:48 Why Should I Get Title Insurance
08:16 Permit Issues
10:59 Title Nightmares

32:05 Conclusion

----------------------------------------

https://casey.scenicsir.com/

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS VIDEO:
1. What is title insurance?
2. Do you really need title insurance in Florida?
3. Who pays for title insurance in Florida?
4. Why lenders require title insurance
5. Cash buyers and title insurance: Should you still get it?
6. How title insurance protects you from hidden risks
7. Why surveys are critical in Florida real estate
8. What “illegal lot splits” mean for buyers
9. How beach access easements actually work
10. Real stories of title issues that could cost buyers thousands

WHY TITLE INSURANCE MATTERS IN FLORIDA:
Florida’s booming market, especially along the Gulf Coast and 30A, has created a sharp rise in:
A. Open permits
B. Encroachments
C. Unrecorded easements
D. Older subdivisions with unclear plats
E. Properties with outdated or missing surveys
Without proper title insurance Florida protection, buyers could face huge repair bills, legal disputes, or even lose ownership rights. This video explains exactly why these risks exist and how to avoid them.

Whether you're a first-time homebuyer, a seasoned investor, or buying your dream beach home on 30A, title insurance is far more than just a closing formality. It’s protection for your investment, peace of mind, and future security. Partnering with trusted professionals like Kirby at Shoreline Title ensures you’re not just buying property, you’re safeguarding it.

Back in 2010, President Obama signed the Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (commonly known as Dodd-Frank) into federal law.

This legislation came in response to a massive economic downturn, which was partially fed by the irresponsible lending practices of some, which ultimately led to a great deal of financial hurt for many.

At the time, many people in the real estate investing community started recognizing that this legislation was going to introduce some significant new restrictions that would cause major issues with their ability to sell properties with owner financing.

I still remember seeing forum discussions, blog articles, emails and social media posts from people who were FREAKING OUT about these changes, because for many of them, it was going to add some big new restrictions to the way they were doing business.

Around the same time, I had to wonder how this legislation would affect my business. As a land investor, my real estate investing activity was a bit different than most real estate investors, and I remembered hearing from most other vacant land investors that Dodd-Frank didn't apply to raw land transactions the way it did to 95% of the other real estate deals.

After reading up on it myself, I found much of the same thing. It seemed like there were a lot of exceptions that specifically excluded vacant land from all of the new cumbersome rules that Dodd-Frank brought into the picture... but it wasn't until just recently that I decided to dive much deeper into the fine print to understand the issues the best I possibly could.

In this video, I will give you my purely NON-LEGAL opinion on what Dodd-Frank and the associated regulations have to say about transactions involving vacant land and seller financing. #sellerfinancing #ownerfinancing #realestateinvesting

segments.text: Hey, it's Joe.
This next one is from Sherri Om from Norwalk, California.
Sherri asks, "Thanks for all your great information.
What do I need to do to comply with the Dodd-Frank Act if I'm buying properties cheap and reselling
with seller financing to an end buyer who wants to live in the home?"
Well, first of all, you don't have to buy properties cheap in order to resell them.
You can buy them at full market value.
If you get them on terms, you can actually sell them for a premium and take the profit,
the amount that you sell it over market value, as your profit, and so you don't really need
to worry about that.
As far as the Dodd-Frank Act goes, if you type in Dodd slash Frank into my blog, there's
an article that I did on Dodd-Frank, so I'm not going to go into a lot of detail about
it.
One thing we know about Dodd-Frank is that it's mainly focused on securities, so they're
interested in people that are using private money and whether or not those people need
security licenses and those types of things rather than the type of seller financing that
we do.
Essentially, all we're doing is facilitating a sale.
We're taking control of the property, we're turning around and selling it, we're doing
proper disclosures - we're doing all of the things that the Dodd-Frank is designed to
force companies to do.
So we're already doing those things.
We do it ethically.
We make sure that people understand what's going on, so we don't really have to worry
about Dodd-Frank so much.
Also, Dodd-Frank is many hundreds of pages long and most of the things in Dodd-Frank
have never been contested in court, so we don't know how some of that stuff is going
to play out over the next few years, so we'll just continue to watch that over the next
few years and see if it has an impact on investors like us.
There was an awful lot of fear in the investor community about Dodd-Frank.
As I've said from the very beginning, with most of these things, we've had to make a
tweak or two to make it work, but if you're doing it ethically anyway in the first place
and if you're doing the paperwork properly in the first place, then these things are
already going to be complied with and you're not going to have to worry about them so much.
If you're raising private money, that's a different story.
Then you might need to get a securities license to make that work.
Read my article on the blog: JoeCrumpBlog.com about Dodd-Frank and I think it'll give you
a better understanding of what we're doing with that and how we're complying with it
and what you'll need to do with it as well.
Alright, I hope that helps.
And before I end, the bottom line on this is don't worry so much about regulation - I'm
not saying don't comply - I'm saying don't worry about it - we've always found a way
to make these things work and we've always found a way to continue to do business.
Remember, we're still working in a free market economy.
They're not trying to keep us from doing business - they're just wanting to make sure that the
business that we do is done properly, that it's done ethically, that it's done responsibly
and to make sure that everybody understands what's going on in a deal.
The reason that these regulations come into being is not so that they can chop off the
head of capitalism - the reason is because they want to keep people from abusing their
power and their knowledge over other people, and so if your treat this business responsibly,
if you treat it ethically, and if you do disclose the stuff that you're doing and make sure
that everybody understands what their risks are and what their benefits are when they're
going into a deal, you won't have to worry about very many of these things.
Alright, I hope that helps.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning an RV Storage Lot
metadata.author: The Owner's Math
metadata.shortDescription:
Nobody stores an RV because they lack space. Almost every tenant owns a house with an empty driveway — they're just legally prohibited from parking on it. That rule is the business.

This is the full economics of owning an RV storage facility: why the fence is trivial and the ground is what kills projects, how the stormwater basin and the drive-aisle geometry quietly decide how many spaces you're even allowed to have, and why two identical five-acre parcels can differ by sixty percent in inventory — permanently, set the day the site plan is drawn.

Then the real engine. Why an RV storage lot isn't a storage business at all — it's a compliance business, renting the cheapest lawful place to park a problem a rule created. Why cancelling means selling the vehicle, and selling the vehicle means conceding the life it was bought for. Why the demand rests on an ordinance you don't control and can be voted away at a meeting you're not invited to. We walk the abandoned-vehicle trap, the own-versus-lease-the-land decision, and why success itself can evict you.

Finally, the honest math. One good year, one bad year, in dollars — and why a lot that looks full from the road tells you almost nothing.

You're not building storage. You're building a lawful place to park what a rule evicted from somewhere else.

metadata.title: America’s RV Parks Are Becoming Too Expensive — Full Time Residents Have Nowhere Left to Go
metadata.author: American Fault Lines

segments.text: If you walk through almost any
independent RV park in the Sunbelt on a
Tuesday morning, the first thing you
notice is how quiet it is. These are not
vacationers loading up kayaks or packing
coolers for the lake. You see insulated
skirting wrapped around the bottom of
fifth wheels to keep the winter wind
out. You see 100 lb propane cylinders
sitting upright on wooden pallets
plumbed directly into the side panels
with copper fittings.
You see wooden steps built up to the
front doors, small potted plants on the
picnic tables, and heavy-duty hitches
resting quietly on concrete blocks.
For a long time, this was America's
quiet compromise.
If housing prices in town climbed out of
reach, or if your retirement savings
took a hit, you could buy a solid used
travel trailer, tow it onto a gravel
pad, and hook up to water, sewer, and a
50 amp electrical pedestal.
In many parts of the country, that used
to cost $350 to $500 a month, and that
number often covered your water and
trash.
It gave you independence, dignity, and a
roof over your head that nobody could
pull out from under you. Now, that
compromise is falling apart.
Over the last 4 years, monthly lot rents
at parks across the country have
steadily pushed toward $900, $1,200,
and in some areas more than $1,500 a
month.
That figure usually does not include
metered electricity, which can easily
add another $150 to $300 when
temperatures swing. At the same time,
older parks are being sold off to
corporate investment groups. Long-term
spaces are being converted into
short-term vacation rentals, and strict
new rules are disqualifying older rigs
that working people and retirees rely
on.
That brings us to a difficult question.
When the mobile home park and the RV
park were supposed to be the bottom rung
of private American housing, where do
you go when the bottom rung gets priced
like an apartment? To understand how we
got here, you have to look at how the
mathematics of RV living changed. For
decades, recreational vehicles were
treated exactly like their name
suggested. They were for camping, summer
vacations, and occasional road trips.
But, starting around 2008 and
accelerating sharply after 2020,
millions of Americans began viewing an
RV not as leisure gear, but as an
affordable, permanent residence.
Industry estimates that more than 1
million Americans now live full-time in
RVs. A significant share of those
residents are men and women aged 55 and
older.
Some are traveling trade workers,
pipeliners, and electricians who follow
job sites across state lines. Many more
are retirees living entirely on fixed
social security checks that average
around $1,900
a month.
On paper, trading a high property tax
house or an escalating apartment lease
for a paid-off trailer looks like common
sense.
In real life, it's a different story.
The first pressure point hits right at
the park office.
Up until about 2018, the vast majority
of RV parks in the United States were
small, family-owned businesses.
A retired couple or a local family owned
the land, managed the gravel roads,
pumped the septic tanks, and kept rent
predictable.
If an older resident on social security
had a lean month, the owner usually
worked with them. The park was
essentially an informal neighborhood.
Over the past decade, institutional
investors and private equity firms
realized that independent RV parks were
one of the last fragments of commercial
real estate offering high cash yields.
Unlike apartment complexes, an RV park
owner does not own the living units.
They do not have to replace broken water
heaters, fix leaky roofs, or replace
worn carpeting inside the rigs.
The owner simply leases the dirt, the
utility pedestal, and the gravel
driveway.
The overhead is low, and the tenant
brings their own home.
Between 2020 and 2024, large real estate
investment trusts and private equity
funds bought up hundreds of independent
campgrounds and parks across Florida,
Texas, Arizona, North Carolina, and
Tennessee.
When an investment group purchases a
park, the business model changes
overnight. The goal is no longer steady
modest cash flow. The goal is maximizing
return per square foot.
The corporate playbook follows a very
consistent pattern. First, the park gets
a facelift. The front entrance gets a
fresh coat of paint, new gravel is
spread on the roads, and high-speed
internet is advertised at the gate.
Maybe a pickleball court or an updated
dog run goes in near the office.
Then the property is rebranded from a
campground or mobile park into an
outdoor resort.
Along with that rebranding comes a
letter under the door of every long-term
resident. A monthly rent of $475
becomes $750 in the first year.
By the second year, it reaches $950.
Utilities, which were once bundled into
the flat fee, are split off and metered
individually.
Now, keep that in mind when you look at
a typical monthly budget. Suppose a
retired couple takes in $2,600
a month in combined Social Security
benefits.
When lot rent was $450 with utilities
included, they had $2,150
left for groceries, prescription
co-pays, vehicle insurance, gasoline,
and savings.
When lot rent jumps to $950,
and the park adds a $45 monthly water
and sewer fee, plus an electric bill
that runs $180 in the heat of August,
their baseline shelter cost has jumped
from $450 to nearly $1,175.
That is more than a 150% increase on the
exact same plot of gravel. And the cost
of the dirt is only half the battle.
The other side of the squeeze comes from
park regulations that are quietly
pushing older rigs off the property.
You don't have to look far to see the
10-year rule in action.
Across the country, an increasing number
of private parks enforce an explicit
policy. If your RV was manufactured more
than 10 years ago, you cannot stay
there. In some resort-heavy regions,
that limit is set at seven or even five
years.
The original justification for this rule
made some practical sense.
Park owners wanted to prevent
dilapidated, hazardous, or abandoned
campers from cluttering the lots and
running up unpaid disposal bills.
But today, the 10-year rule is often
applied regardless of condition.
A retiree could have a immaculate 2011
fifth wheel with brand new tires,
spotless fiberglass, and working
systems. And the park management will
flatly deny their application based
solely on the vehicle identification
number.
Think about what that does to an older
owner.
If your rig is a 2012 model, and your
current park increases its rent beyond
what your social security check can
handle,
you cannot simply hitch up and drive
down the highway to an older, cheaper
park.
Many of those alternative parks have
instituted the exact same age limits.
Worse, moving an RV is no longer an
inexpensive proposition. If you live
stationary, chances are you do not own a
heavy-duty 3/4 ton or 1-ton diesel
truck.
Buying and maintaining a modern diesel
pickup capable of towing a 12,000 lb
fifth wheel can easily run $40,000 to
$60,000 used, with insurance and fuel
costs to match. If you have to hire a
commercial hotshot hauler to move your
rig to another county, rates typically
range from $3 to $5 a mile, plus hookup
and leveling fees. A 200-mile relocation
can quickly turn into a $1,000 expense
before you even pay your first month's
deposit at the new location.
And that assumes the trailer can legally
roll down the highway at all.
Many full-time rigs sit on tires that
are 8 or 10 years old. Even if the tread
looks deep, trailer tires degrade
internally from ultraviolet exposure and
dry rot. Replacing four or six
heavy-duty trailer tires before a move
can cost between $800 and $1,500.
For an older resident living month to
month, that single mechanical hurdle can
make leaving physically impossible.
Then there is the legal reality of the
RV itself. This is perhaps the most
vulnerable aspect of full-time RV life,
and it catches many residents completely
off guard.
In almost every state, someone who parks
an RV in a commercial park is not
considered a tenant in the eyes of
property law. They are classified as a
guest, a licensee, or a transient
occupant. That distinction sounds
technical, but here is what that means
in practical terms. If you rent an
apartment or a house under a residential
lease, state landlord-tenant laws
protect you. A landlord must give you
formal written notice, usually 30 to 60
days, before altering your terms or
terminating your lease. If they want to
remove you, they have to file an
eviction action in court, give you a
chance to appear before a judge, and
obtain a court order writ. In an RV
park, those protections often vanish
because the relationship is legally
closer to a motel stay than an apartment
rental.
A park operator in many jurisdictions
can give a long-term resident 72 hours,
or sometimes just 24 hours, to
disconnect their utilities and pull off
the property.
If the resident cannot move the rig in
time, local law enforcement can treat
the situation not as a civil
landlord-tenant dispute, but as simple
trespassing.
The rig can be impounded or towed to a
commercial storage yard where daily
storage fees begin racking up at $50 to
$100 a day.
For an older person whose entire net
worth is tied up in that trailer, an
impound lot is financial ruin.
If you cannot pay the towing bill and
the daily storage fees within 30 to 60
days, the impound company can file for a
mechanic's lien, take title to the
trailer, and sell it at auction or scrap
it.
The resident loses both their shelter
and their personal possessions in a
matter of weeks.
Now, let's take a step back and look at
the municipal level
because private corporate buyers are
only part of the equation.
Local county and city governments are
actively squeezing full-time RVers out
from the other direction.
Across the United States, dozens of
counties that were once friendly to
long-term RV living have rewritten their
zoning codes. In popular Sunbelt
destinations, local city councils have
passed ordinances restricting stays in
commercial RV parks to a maximum of 14,
28, or 60 consecutive days.
Once your time is up, you are legally
required to leave the park, and you
cannot return for another 30 days. City
officials often argue these measures are
designed to preserve tourism revenue,
protect public health, and prevent parks
from becoming unpermitted shantytowns.
But the functional result is clear. It
makes it illegal for an RV park to serve
as permanent housing. Consider what that
means for a full-timer.
A retired veteran who settled into an
Arizona park 5 years ago, built a small
deck, established his primary care
doctor at the nearby VA clinic, and pays
his lot rent every month, can suddenly
find out that a new county ordinance
makes his residency unlawful.
He is told he must pack up every 30 days
and move just to satisfy an ordinance
intended to boost hotel occupancy tax.
Some full-timers try to escape this trap
by buying their own land.
You see this advertised all over rural
America. A half acre or 1 acre lot in
Texas, New Mexico, Missouri, or northern
Florida for $10,000 to $20,000 cash.
People [snorts] buy the parcel thinking
they will park their camper, dig a
septic tank, drill a shallow well, and
live without paying lot rent to anyone
ever again.
In real life, local building codes
almost always block that plan. In the
vast majority of American counties, it
is completely illegal to live
permanently in an RV on your own private
land unless you are actively building a
permitted stick-built home on the
property. Even then, counties often cap
the temporary stay at 6 months or 1
year.
If you pull an RV onto a rural lot you
own outright, hook it to a generator,
and live there quietly.
County code enforcement will eventually
show up with a violation notice.
Fines typically start at $50 to $100 a
day.
If the fines go unpaid, the county
places a tax lien on the parcel. Within
a few years, the very land you bought to
protect your independence can be seized
and sold on the courthouse steps.
To be fair, we have to look at the other
side of this ledger.
Park owners and municipal authorities
are not operating in a vacuum, and
running an RV park in 2026 involves real
operational headaches that many
residents never see.
First, there is the infrastructure cost.
Most independent RV parks in this
country were laid out 40 or 50 years
ago.
They were designed for 16-ft aluminum
campers that drew 15 or 30 amps of
electricity to run a tiny refrigerator
and a couple of interior light bulbs.
Today, a modern 40-ft fifth wheel is
essentially a rolling townhouse. It has
three slide-outs, two or three heavy air
conditioners, an electric water heater,
a residential refrigerator, a microwave,
and multiple televisions. When an entire
row of full-time residents runs their
dual air conditioning units all
afternoon during a heat wave, the
electrical load on an aging park is
enormous. Transformers blow, underground
lines melt, and breaker boxes burn out.
Upgrading an older 50-space park from 30
amp to modern 50 amp commercial service
across every pedestal can easily run
to up qualia, $250,000.
Septic systems face the exact same
problem. An RV park septic field
designed in 1980 was meant for weekend
use. When 60 families live on the system
365 days a year, running washing
machines, taking daily showers, and
dumping chemical-heavy holding tanks,
older septic drain fields fail quickly.
Replacing a commercial-grade septic
absorption field can cost six figures,
and local environmental protection
agencies can shut a park down if a leak
surfaces. Then there is commercial
insurance.
Over the past 3 years, property and
casualty insurance rates for commercial
campground operators have jumped between
30% and 70%, especially in states
exposed to hurricanes, severe storms, or
wildfires.
Add in escalating county property taxes
based on reassessed land values, and an
independent owner's fixed costs are
significantly higher than they were 5
years ago.
Furthermore, park owners face genuine
business risks with long-term tenants
who fall on hard times.
If an RV owner stops paying rent, breaks
an axle, and abandons an old rotted
camper on a space, the park owner is
left with the bill. Disposing of an
abandoned 35-ft travel trailer legally
at a commercial landfill requires hiring
a flatbed tow truck and paying hazardous
waste dumping fees. That process
routinely costs a park owner between
$2,000 and $4,000 per abandoned rig.
There is also the plain math of the
hospitality market.
If a park owner can rent a site to a
traveling vacationer for $75 or $90 a
night on the weekend, they can bring in
$600 to $800 in a single week. A monthly
resident paying $500 a month works out
to less than $17 a night. From a purely
financial standpoint, park operators
have a massive incentive to phase out
permanent residents and cater
exclusively to short-term travelers with
newer, expensive recreational rigs.
Understanding that business calculation
makes sense on a ledger,
but it does nothing to solve the human
reality on the ground.
Picture a retired widower living on
social security in a small town outside
Ocala, Florida.
Suppose he sold his modest stick-built
home 8 years ago after his wife passed
away.
The maintenance on the older house was
too much. The property insurance was
doubling every few years, and after
paying off the remaining mortgage, he
had $45,000 left in the bank. He bought
a clean, used 28-ft travel trailer for
$18,000 and parked it in a quiet, shaded
campground where the rent was $425 a
month, electric included for 5 years.
That setup worked well. He had his
routine, his neighbors, and enough
breathing room on his $1,850
monthly check to afford groceries, keep
gas in his 10-year-old sedan, and put a
little money away every month.
Then the park sells. A regional property
management company takes over.
Within 6 months, the monthly rate jumps
6 months later, it moves to $1,050
plus a separate electric meter that
averages $140 a month. On top of that,
the management informs him that by next
spring, all trailers older than 10 years
must be removed to make way for premium
concrete pull-through sites aimed at
short-term vacationers. His trailer is a
2013 model. It is in good condition, but
it is now 13 years old. He does not have
a truck to pull it. He calls five other
parks within a 50-mi radius, and four of
them tell him they have a strict 10-year
rule.
The fifth park has a 2-year waiting list
for monthly spaces and charges $1,100 a
month anyway.
An apartment in town requires proof that
your monthly income is three times the
rent.
With local one-bedroom apartments
starting at $1,400 a month, his $1,850
check does not meet the income
threshold, even if he could pass the
credit check.
He cannot afford to stay. He cannot
afford to leave, and the home he lives
in cannot legally sit on the ground
where it is parked. That is not an
isolated story.
It is playing out in nearly every state
from coast to coast.
So, where do people go when this
happens? Some full-timers head out west
to public lands managed by the Bureau of
Land Management or the US Forest
Service. This is known as boondocking or
dispersed camping. On designated BLM
land, you can park your rig for free,
but there are strict trade-offs. There
are no electrical hookups, no water
connections, and no sewer dumps. You
rely entirely on solar panels, small
generators, and the water you can haul
in 5-gallon jugs.
More importantly, federal regulations
strictly enforce a 14-day stay limit.
Once your 14 days are up, you must pack
up your entire camp and move at least 25
mi away, and you cannot return to that
same district for several months. For a
fit 30-year-old remote worker with an
expensive lithium battery bank and an
off-road four-wheel drive rig, dispersed
camping is an adventurous lifestyle. For
a 68-year-old retiree dealing with
arthritis, managing insulin in an RV
refrigerator, and needing reliable power
for a CPAP machine, boondocking in the
desert while packing up every 2 weeks is
exhausting, physically demanding, and
potentially dangerous.
Other residents try to make informal
arrangements with private landowners.
They find a farmer or a rural homeowner
with a few acres who is willing to let
them park behind a barn for $300 a month
in cash, running an extension cord and a
garden hose out to the camper.
These arrangements can work for a while,
but they are inherently fragile. All it
takes is one irritated neighbor calling
the county zoning board to report an
illegal dwelling.
An inspector visits, writes a citation,
and the landowner has no choice but to
tell the tenant they have 48 hours to
clear out.
There is no legal recourse, no lease
agreement, and no refund. That leaves
the most desperate option, which you can
see lining the industrial access roads
and frontage streets outside cities like
Phoenix, Las Vegas, and Portland.
Campers with faded decals and flat tires
parked on public asphalt, moving every
72 hours to avoid city parking tickets.
At that point, the vehicle is no longer
a tool for independent retirement
living.
It is simply an unhoused person's last
shelter before sleeping on the pavement.
That brings us to the next question.
What can actually change this
trajectory?
There are a few policy discussions
beginning to surface at state levels,
though progress is slow.
Housing advocates in several western
states have pushed to amend state
landlord-tenant laws to include
long-term RV park residents under
standard manufactured housing
protections.
If an RV resident signs a month-to-month
lease and stays in a park for more than
30 or 60 consecutive days, those
proposals would grant them the same
eviction protections as a tenant in a
standard apartment or mobile home park.
That would mean mandatory 60-day notices
for significant rent increases, clear
legal procedures for lease termination,
and protection against arbitrary rig
limits once a resident is already
established.
A few rural counties are also
experimenting with changing their zoning
codes to allow tiny home and RV villages
on private land. Recognizing that an RV
pad with safe permitted utility hookups
is vastly preferable to people living in
cars or setting up tents along
riverbanks.
Whether those policy changes gain
traction depends entirely on local
politics.
In many communities, existing homeowners
strongly resist having RV parks expanded
or legalized for long-term residency,
fearing that high-density mobile living
will lower nearby property values or
strain local road and emergency
services.
In the meantime, anyone living in an RV
full-time, or anyone considering it as a
retirement plan, has to approach the
road with clear eyes and defensive
financial planning.
First, relying on private RV parks as a
cheap permanent housing solution is no
longer a viable long-term strategy in
most parts of the country.
If you are planning to live full-time in
an RV, your monthly budget must account
for site fees that mirror a small
apartment rents, especially in desirable
climate zones.
Second, maintaining mobility is the only
real leverage an RV owner has. If your
rig cannot move under its own power, or
if you cannot afford to have it towed on
short notice, you are entirely at the
mercy of the park owner's rate hikes.
Keeping tires fresh, wheel bearings
greased, and an emergency towing fund
set aside is not optional. It is the
only thing standing between an
unexpected rate hike and having your
home impounded.
Finally, older Americans considering
selling their homes to live in a camper
must understand the fundamental
difference between depreciating assets
and real estate.
A house, even an older one that needs
maintenance, sits on deeded land that
generally holds or gains value over
time.
An RV is a vehicle.
It loses value every year. Its
components degrade rapidly under
continuous full-time use, and the ground
beneath it belongs to someone else who
can raise the price or ask you to leave
at any moment.
The dream of the open road has always
been a central part of American life.
For decades, it represented freedom,
self-reliance, and the ability to live
comfortably on your own terms, even when
resources were tight. Now, as investment
funds purchase the gravel pads, counties
rewrite the zoning maps, and monthly
park fees rival traditional rent, that
escape hatch is closing fast. The
freedom of having a home with wheels on
it only works if there is an affordable,
welcoming place left to park them. If
you or someone in your family has lived
full-time in an RV over the past few
years, what changes have you seen in
your local lot rents and park rules?
