When lot rent jumps to $950, and the park adds a $45 monthly water and sewer fee, plus an electric bill that runs $180 in the heat of August, their baseline shelter cost has jumped from $450 to nearly $1,175. That is more than a 150% increase on the exact same plot of gravel. And the cost of the dirt is only half the battle. The other side of the squeeze comes from park regulations that are quietly pushing older rigs off the property. You don't have to look far to see the 10-year rule in action. Across the country, an increasing number of private parks enforce an explicit policy. If your RV was manufactured more than 10 years ago, you cannot stay there. In some resort-heavy regions, that limit is set at seven or even five years. The original justification for this rule made some practical sense. Park owners wanted to prevent dilapidated, hazardous, or abandoned campers from cluttering the lots and running up unpaid disposal bills. But today, the 10-year rule is often applied regardless of condition. A retiree could have a immaculate 2011 fifth wheel with brand new tires, spotless fiberglass, and working systems. And the park management will flatly deny their application based solely on the vehicle identification number. Think about what that does to an older owner. If your rig is a 2012 model, and your current park increases its rent beyond what your social security check can handle, you cannot simply hitch up and drive down the highway to an older, cheaper park. Many of those alternative parks have instituted the exact same age limits. Worse, moving an RV is no longer an inexpensive proposition. If you live stationary, chances are you do not own a heavy-duty 3/4 ton or 1-ton diesel truck. Buying and maintaining a modern diesel pickup capable of towing a 12,000 lb fifth wheel can easily run $40,000 to $60,000 used, with insurance and fuel costs to match. If you have to hire a commercial hotshot hauler to move your rig to another county, rates typically range from $3 to $5 a mile, plus hookup and leveling fees. A 200-mile relocation can quickly turn into a $1,000 expense before you even pay your first month's deposit at the new location. And that assumes the trailer can legally roll down the highway at all. Many full-time rigs sit on tires that are 8 or 10 years old. Even if the tread looks deep, trailer tires degrade internally from ultraviolet exposure and dry rot. Replacing four or six heavy-duty trailer tires before a move can cost between $800 and $1,500. For an older resident living month to month, that single mechanical hurdle can make leaving physically impossible. Then there is the legal reality of the RV itself. This is perhaps the most vulnerable aspect of full-time RV life, and it catches many residents completely off guard. In almost every state, someone who parks an RV in a commercial park is not considered a tenant in the eyes of property law. They are classified as a guest, a licensee, or a transient occupant. That distinction sounds technical, but here is what that means in practical terms. If you rent an apartment or a house under a residential lease, state landlord-tenant laws protect you. A landlord must give you formal written notice, usually 30 to 60 days, before altering your terms or terminating your lease. If they want to remove you, they have to file an eviction action in court, give you a chance to appear before a judge, and obtain a court order writ. In an RV park, those protections often vanish because the relationship is legally closer to a motel stay than an apartment rental. A park operator in many jurisdictions can give a long-term resident 72 hours, or sometimes just 24 hours, to disconnect their utilities and pull off the property. If the resident cannot move the rig in time, local law enforcement can treat the situation not as a civil landlord-tenant dispute, but as simple trespassing. The rig can be impounded or towed to a commercial storage yard where daily storage fees begin racking up at $50 to $100 a day. For an older person whose entire net worth is tied up in that trailer, an impound lot is financial ruin. If you cannot pay the towing bill and the daily storage fees within 30 to 60 days, the impound company can file for a mechanic's lien, take title to the trailer, and sell it at auction or scrap it. The resident loses both their shelter and their personal possessions in a matter of weeks. Now, let's take a step back and look at the municipal level because private corporate buyers are only part of the equation. Local county and city governments are actively squeezing full-time RVers out from the other direction. Across the United States, dozens of counties that were once friendly to long-term RV living have rewritten their zoning codes. In popular Sunbelt destinations, local city councils have passed ordinances restricting stays in commercial RV parks to a maximum of 14, 28, or 60 consecutive days. Once your time is up, you are legally required to leave the park, and you cannot return for another 30 days. City officials often argue these measures are designed to preserve tourism revenue, protect public health, and prevent parks from becoming unpermitted shantytowns. But the functional result is clear. It makes it illegal for an RV park to serve as permanent housing. Consider what that means for a full-timer. A retired veteran who settled into an Arizona park 5 years ago, built a small deck, established his primary care doctor at the nearby VA clinic, and pays his lot rent every month, can suddenly find out that a new county ordinance makes his residency unlawful. He is told he must pack up every 30 days and move just to satisfy an ordinance intended to boost hotel occupancy tax. Some full-timers try to escape this trap by buying their own land. You see this advertised all over rural America. A half acre or 1 acre lot in Texas, New Mexico, Missouri, or northern Florida for $10,000 to $20,000 cash. People [snorts] buy the parcel thinking they will park their camper, dig a septic tank, drill a shallow well, and live without paying lot rent to anyone ever again. In real life, local building codes almost always block that plan. In the vast majority of American counties, it is completely illegal to live permanently in an RV on your own private land unless you are actively building a permitted stick-built home on the property. Even then, counties often cap the temporary stay at 6 months or 1 year. If you pull an RV onto a rural lot you own outright, hook it to a generator, and live there quietly. County code enforcement will eventually show up with a violation notice. Fines typically start at $50 to $100 a day. If the fines go unpaid, the county places a tax lien on the parcel. Within a few years, the very land you bought to protect your independence can be seized and sold on the courthouse steps. To be fair, we have to look at the other side of this ledger. Park owners and municipal authorities are not operating in a vacuum, and running an RV park in 2026 involves real operational headaches that many residents never see. First, there is the infrastructure cost. Most independent RV parks in this country were laid out 40 or 50 years ago. They were designed for 16-ft aluminum campers that drew 15 or 30 amps of electricity to run a tiny refrigerator and a couple of interior light bulbs. Today, a modern 40-ft fifth wheel is essentially a rolling townhouse. It has three slide-outs, two or three heavy air conditioners, an electric water heater, a residential refrigerator, a microwave, and multiple televisions. When an entire row of full-time residents runs their dual air conditioning units all afternoon during a heat wave, the electrical load on an aging park is enormous. Transformers blow, underground lines melt, and breaker boxes burn out. Upgrading an older 50-space park from 30 amp to modern 50 amp commercial service across every pedestal can easily run $150,000 to up qualia, $250,000. Septic systems face the exact same problem. An RV park septic field designed in 1980 was meant for weekend use. When 60 families live on the system 365 days a year, running washing machines, taking daily showers, and dumping chemical-heavy holding tanks, older septic drain fields fail quickly. Replacing a commercial-grade septic absorption field can cost six figures, and local environmental protection agencies can shut a park down if a leak surfaces. Then there is commercial insurance. Over the past 3 years, property and casualty insurance rates for commercial campground operators have jumped between 30% and 70%, especially in states exposed to hurricanes, severe storms, or wildfires. Add in escalating county property taxes based on reassessed land values, and an independent owner's fixed costs are significantly higher than they were 5 years ago. Furthermore, park owners face genuine business risks with long-term tenants who fall on hard times. If an RV owner stops paying rent, breaks an axle, and abandons an old rotted camper on a space, the park owner is left with the bill. Disposing of an abandoned 35-ft travel trailer legally at a commercial landfill requires hiring a flatbed tow truck and paying hazardous waste dumping fees. That process routinely costs a park owner between $2,000 and $4,000 per abandoned rig. There is also the plain math of the hospitality market. If a park owner can rent a site to a traveling vacationer for $75 or $90 a night on the weekend, they can bring in $600 to $800 in a single week. A monthly resident paying $500 a month works out to less than $17 a night. From a purely financial standpoint, park operators have a massive incentive to phase out permanent residents and cater exclusively to short-term travelers with newer, expensive recreational rigs. Understanding that business calculation makes sense on a ledger, but it does nothing to solve the human reality on the ground. Picture a retired widower living on social security in a small town outside Ocala, Florida. Suppose he sold his modest stick-built home 8 years ago after his wife passed away. The maintenance on the older house was too much. The property insurance was doubling every few years, and after paying off the remaining mortgage, he had $45,000 left in the bank. He bought a clean, used 28-ft travel trailer for $18,000 and parked it in a quiet, shaded campground where the rent was $425 a month, electric included for 5 years. That setup worked well. He had his routine, his neighbors, and enough breathing room on his $1,850 monthly check to afford groceries, keep gas in his 10-year-old sedan, and put a little money away every month. Then the park sells. A regional property management company takes over. Within 6 months, the monthly rate jumps to $850. 6 months later, it moves to $1,050 plus a separate electric meter that averages $140 a month. On top of that, the management informs him that by next spring, all trailers older than 10 years must be removed to make way for premium concrete pull-through sites aimed at short-term vacationers. His trailer is a 2013 model. It is in good condition, but it is now 13 years old. He does not have a truck to pull it. He calls five other parks within a 50-mi radius, and four of them tell him they have a strict 10-year rule. The fifth park has a 2-year waiting list for monthly spaces and charges $1,100 a month anyway. An apartment in town requires proof that your monthly income is three times the rent. With local one-bedroom apartments starting at $1,400 a month, his $1,850 check does not meet the income threshold, even if he could pass the credit check. He cannot afford to stay. He cannot afford to leave, and the home he lives in cannot legally sit on the ground where it is parked. That is not an isolated story. It is playing out in nearly every state from coast to coast. So, where do people go when this happens? Some full-timers head out west to public lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management or the US Forest Service. This is known as boondocking or dispersed camping. On designated BLM land, you can park your rig for free, but there are strict trade-offs. There are no electrical hookups, no water connections, and no sewer dumps. You rely entirely on solar panels, small generators, and the water you can haul in 5-gallon jugs. More importantly, federal regulations strictly enforce a 14-day stay limit. Once your 14 days are up, you must pack up your entire camp and move at least 25 mi away, and you cannot return to that same district for several months. For a fit 30-year-old remote worker with an expensive lithium battery bank and an off-road four-wheel drive rig, dispersed camping is an adventurous lifestyle. For a 68-year-old retiree dealing with arthritis, managing insulin in an RV refrigerator, and needing reliable power for a CPAP machine, boondocking in the desert while packing up every 2 weeks is exhausting, physically demanding, and potentially dangerous. Other residents try to make informal arrangements with private landowners. They find a farmer or a rural homeowner with a few acres who is willing to let them park behind a barn for $300 a month in cash, running an extension cord and a garden hose out to the camper. These arrangements can work for a while, but they are inherently fragile. All it takes is one irritated neighbor calling the county zoning board to report an illegal dwelling. An inspector visits, writes a citation, and the landowner has no choice but to tell the tenant they have 48 hours to clear out. There is no legal recourse, no lease agreement, and no refund. That leaves the most desperate option, which you can see lining the industrial access roads and frontage streets outside cities like Phoenix, Las Vegas, and Portland. Campers with faded decals and flat tires parked on public asphalt, moving every 72 hours to avoid city parking tickets. At that point, the vehicle is no longer a tool for independent retirement living. It is simply an unhoused person's last shelter before sleeping on the pavement. That brings us to the next question. What can actually change this trajectory? There are a few policy discussions beginning to surface at state levels, though progress is slow. Housing advocates in several western states have pushed to amend state landlord-tenant laws to include long-term RV park residents under standard manufactured housing protections. If an RV resident signs a month-to-month lease and stays in a park for more than 30 or 60 consecutive days, those proposals would grant them the same eviction protections as a tenant in a standard apartment or mobile home park. That would mean mandatory 60-day notices for significant rent increases, clear legal procedures for lease termination, and protection against arbitrary rig limits once a resident is already established. A few rural counties are also experimenting with changing their zoning codes to allow tiny home and RV villages on private land. Recognizing that an RV pad with safe permitted utility hookups is vastly preferable to people living in cars or setting up tents along riverbanks. Whether those policy changes gain traction depends entirely on local politics. In many communities, existing homeowners strongly resist having RV parks expanded or legalized for long-term residency, fearing that high-density mobile living will lower nearby property values or strain local road and emergency services. In the meantime, anyone living in an RV full-time, or anyone considering it as a retirement plan, has to approach the road with clear eyes and defensive financial planning. First, relying on private RV parks as a cheap permanent housing solution is no longer a viable long-term strategy in most parts of the country. If you are planning to live full-time in an RV, your monthly budget must account for site fees that mirror a small apartment rents, especially in desirable climate zones. Second, maintaining mobility is the only real leverage an RV owner has. If your rig cannot move under its own power, or if you cannot afford to have it towed on short notice, you are entirely at the mercy of the park owner's rate hikes. Keeping tires fresh, wheel bearings greased, and an emergency towing fund set aside is not optional. It is the only thing standing between an unexpected rate hike and having your home impounded. Finally, older Americans considering selling their homes to live in a camper must understand the fundamental difference between depreciating assets and real estate. A house, even an older one that needs maintenance, sits on deeded land that generally holds or gains value over time. An RV is a vehicle. It loses value every year. Its components degrade rapidly under continuous full-time use, and the ground beneath it belongs to someone else who can raise the price or ask you to leave at any moment. The dream of the open road has always been a central part of American life. For decades, it represented freedom, self-reliance, and the ability to live comfortably on your own terms, even when resources were tight. Now, as investment funds purchase the gravel pads, counties rewrite the zoning maps, and monthly park fees rival traditional rent, that escape hatch is closing fast. The freedom of having a home with wheels on it only works if there is an affordable, welcoming place left to park them. If you or someone in your family has lived full-time in an RV over the past few years, what changes have you seen in your local lot rents and park rules?

metadata.title: Texas’ battery storage: a boom and bust market? | FT Energy Source
metadata.author: Financial Times
metadata.shortDescription:
Investment in battery storage systems across the US has surged in 2024, especially in Texas. The FT’s Myles McCormick looks at how climactic conditions that lead to a fluctuating power supply, combined with the state’s low-regulation, business-friendly energy market has created ideal conditions to build battery storage sites quickly and at scale. But are we looking at a boom-bust market?

See if you get the FT for free as a student (http://ft.com/schoolsarefree) or start a £1 trial: https://subs.ft.com/spa3_trial?segmentId=3d4ba81b-96bb-cef0-9ece-29efd6ef2132.

► Check out our Community tab for more stories: https://www.youtube.com/@FinancialTimes/community
►  Listen to our podcasts: https://www.ft.com/podcasts
►  Follow us on Instagram:  https://www.instagram.com/financialtimes'

segments.text: A different kind of energy rush is sweeping across America’s petroleum superstate.
Texas still holds vast oil reserves, but it also has a lot of sun, wind,
heat, and demand for electricity. It’s not a new technology. In fact, it doesn’t
actually generate energy at all, but stores and releases it, at just the right time.
Batteries are becoming a more critical and important part of our grid every day.
The batteries building up across the Lone Star state are soaking up huge amounts of
electricity from another surge, in renewable energy generation.
We have more wind than the next four states combined,
and we just passed California in terms of utility-scale solar.
It’s not because of an aggressive state push towards decarbonisation. It's because in Texas,
it's relatively easy to build infrastructure and big projects than in other states.
Renewables have added vital capacity for the state’s energy authority.
Electrically separated from the rest of the USA, it can’t rely on other states in a crisis,
but the influx of solar energy in particular has meant that the regulator has had to
juggle a fundamental switch in peak demand. It actually has shifted to later in the evening
when the sun starts to set. The solar energy has gone away, but it's still warm and hot outside,
so the air conditioning load is still very high. Those solar ramp periods have become the highest
risk periods on the grid during the summer. And that’s where batteries, or more specifically,
battery energy storage systems, can step in, discharging what can be a
grid-saving boost to electricity supplies. Just a couple of days ago, there was an outage
of a large-generation coal plant, and there are enough batteries now that they jumped in,
and batteries can deploy in microseconds, so they were able to stop any issue from
happening. The grid stayed stable. The output from this single 100MW array
could power at least 20,000 homes. Strategically positioned near the energy-sapping
data centres in the metroplex of Dallas-Fort Worth, it’s only a few years old, but already
being superseded by the next generation of larger battery systems coming online.
We're going to take excess wind and solar generation, mostly coming out of
the Texas panhandle, where there aren't as many people. That's going to be held in the battery,
and then we're going to put it back out on the grid when the need arises.
While one unit was offline, it was safe to see inside a typical battery energy storage box.
Each one of the little silver boxes is about 22 small lithium-ion battery cells.
And how many homes could a system like this power when it’s online?
A system like this could probably power about 22 homes, just for this one unit.
While California still has the most battery capacity deployed in the US,
one projection has Texas overtaking it in 2026, if and when planned systems come online.
A surplus of cheap, renewable energy is just one factor behind such explosive growth.
So, in Texas, it is going to be pretty much a pure economic play. So all of the
batteries being deployed in the state are because they can make money.
The uniquely open, deregulated nature of the whole energy market in Texas means big
profits can be made, in just a few hours. So, it’s mid-morning, the sun is up and hundreds
of solar energy projects across the state are rapidly ramping up their power production. That’s
having the impact of depressing electricity prices which means we’re naturally incentivised
to charge from that energy right now. We are then going to hold onto it for the majority of
the day. The sun goes down, people come home from work and turn on their air conditioners and we’re
going to discharge that energy for a profit. Of course, it’s not always quite that simple.
Prices can be volatile, ranging from negative territory to thousands of
dollars for the same unit of electricity. The market is constantly comparing supply and
demand and producing price signals for electricity products. We have a wholesale
power market team that is watching the forecast for solar. It's watching the forecast for wind,
and it's watching the forecast for load. And without a doubt, our net income is
dependent on their skills as traders. Those kinds of ups and downs are one of the
unique characteristics of the energy-only market, but that volatility helps to
incentivise the right type of generating resources coming onto the grid.
Juggling numbers in a constantly changing market is just one of the
variables in the battery storage game. Systems are expensive to install and maintain,
and many components have to be imported from China and other external sources, leaving operators
vulnerable to supply chain interruptions. I think that's something that all of us are
weighing a bit. We also have some political winds as well, with discussions about tariffs
on Chinese batteries. And so you have to weigh that into your calculation.
It's a constantly changing landscape. Oversaturation is another potential risk factor,
as more operators and batteries enter the easy-to-access Texas market.
Is there a risk that the bubble ultimately bursts?
The question is exactly how many batteries will come online, how quickly and how quickly relative
to some of the expected growth that we see in load and solar. We think there's enough room
for a whole lot more batteries on the grid. You know, batteries do eat their own lunch. So,
you know, they reduce high prices and increase low prices, but with the demand growth
projections we have in this state, it seems like there's a lot more room for more.
Texas has topped the tables in US population growth and become one of the
leading data centre markets in the world. Add to that the ongoing electrification of
transport and industries including oil and gas, and it’s no surprise that the
outlook for energy demand and the battery storage business it feeds, seems bright.

I think that's something that all of us are weighing a bit. We also have some political winds as well, with discussions about tariffs on Chinese batteries. And so you have to weigh that into your calculation. It's a constantly changing landscape. Oversaturation is another potential risk factor, as more operators and batteries enter the easy-to-access Texas market. Is there a risk that the bubble ultimately bursts? The question is exactly how many batteries will come online, how quickly and how quickly relative to some of the expected growth that we see in load and solar. We think there's enough room for a whole lot more batteries on the grid. You know, batteries do eat their own lunch. So, you know, they reduce high prices and increase low prices, but with the demand growth projections we have in this state, it seems like there's a lot more room for more. Texas has topped the tables in US population growth and become one of the leading data centre markets in the world. Add to that the ongoing electrification of transport and industries including oil and gas, and it’s no surprise that the outlook for energy demand and the battery storage business it feeds, seems bright.

metadata.title: Planning and Zoning for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)
metadata.author: PlanningWebcastSeries
metadata.shortDescription:
The electric energy system in our country is in the midst of dramatic changes, with new technologies deployed and infrastructural investment occurring at a speed and scale unprecedented in our nation’s history.    One example is the rapid increase in use of battery energy storage systems (BESS).  Batteries are increasingly part of consumer devices and vehicles, but also as part of “behind-the-meter” electric systems in homes and businesses, as part of utility substations and transmission systems, and incorpo-rated into solar and wind electric generation projects.  What do planners need to know about BESS when evaluating risks and nuisances?  Where might BESS be located in the community? Large-scale energy storage in liquid, gas, and solid fuels is quite common in our communities. But electric energy storage in batteries is a different thing.  Or is it?  Communities will need to consider how stationary battery storage – BESS – fits into land use plans and zoning regulations.  This webinar will describe the local benefits and risks that different battery land uses bring to the community; what communities should expect of battery developers, owners, and managers; and how planners can begin to put this new energy technology in the context of local land use decisions.

metadata.title: How a Solar Farm is Constructed From Beginning to End
metadata.author: EltonDP
metadata.shortDescription:
http://www.eltondp.com

Learn how a solar farm is constructed from start to finish.  Meet different people who work on the construction process.  See the machines that are used and learn more about the ecological works.

Shot on a Sony FS7, a Sony FS5, and a Sony A7S II with XEEN 50mm T1.5 and Sony 28-135mm f4 lenses. Edited in Final Cut Pro X. Graded with Phantom LUTs.

segments.text: In this video, we're going to show you how a solar farm is constructed from beginning to end.
We've been invited to the Elmbrook solar farm site in Schodack, NY by Eden Renewables.
This 36 acre site will produce about 11,000 megawatt hours per year of electricity
enough to power about 1,200 average homes.
That's a lot of clean energy from a small pice of land!
Here, we are at phase one of the construction process.
It begins with trucks making roads and pathways to have access
and for developing the land into a solar farm.
You've got all this earth moving equipment that's moving soil around and
as soon as soil is disturbed, it becomes sensitive to erosion, so to try to mitigate that,
the first step is to put erosion and sediment control measures in, so at your construction
entrance that might be a stone pad for the trucks to drive over so as they come out of
the construction entrance, if there is mud or dirt on their tires, it kind of gets dropped off
on the stone pad.
Don't worry, in the end they'll be replanting grasses and
wildflowers to make it even more beautiful than it ever was.
Eden ensures that building this solar farm will improve the
biodiversity here.
This land had been used for hay, and there was very little
biodiversity here, so when we build the solar farm, we're able
to implement all sorts of measures that increase the
biodiversity.
It's important to have a grid or a layout
in order for crews to work efficiently and to know
where everything will go.
The bulldozers and excavators that the contractors are using have GPS
positioning systems built right into their equipment, so they take the drawings that we
develop over the approval and permitting process, and they use a three dimensional
model of those drawings to operate the equipment.
Once all the roads have been created, and everyone can get around, they move on to
phase two, which is pounding in the pilings.
These pilings are what keep the solar panels above ground, stable, and in place.
It's important that the rows are put in the right spot for all the panels to connect in a
straight line for the arrays. That's why the workers use GPS to accurately place the
pilings in the ground.
A laser beam is used to ensure all the pilings are the correct height.
This part of the process could take a few weeks to complete.
These gears enable the solar panels to follow the sun.
As the sun moves across the sky, the angle of the panels will rotate up to
120 degrees, so they always get maximum sunlight.
They're single access tracker systems, meaning that they're oriented in the
north-south direction, the row of panels, and they rotate and face the east
to obviously face the sun in the morning and they slowly track the sun throughout
the day, facing the west at the end of the day, and then reset back to the east overnight.
These purlins and rafters are what the solar panels will attach to.
This is our golden row. A golden row is essentially a mockup for the entire system
where we build every process at once before we build it in the field.
We also have the quality control from the manufacturer as well as for electrical work
come out, check if we installed everything correctly, approve our work, and then
we continue using the same process all down the field.
Look at how far apart these rows of solar panels are placed!
They take up less than one third of the entire land on this site.
That leaves enough room for grasses, wildflowers, and natural habitat.
Say hello to BESS, the Battery Energy Storage System.
BESS stores power for when it's needed the most.
It's housed in a standard sized shipping container.
A giant crane lowers the transformers, inverters, and
battery storage containers onto the pads.
As you can see, these wires are above ground. One of the benefits is that we avoid trenching,
so we're creating a greater ecological benefit within our solar farm by not trenching and
disturbing the ground.
So we've got about 40 volts per panel out here
combined at the combiner.
The inverter inverts it to AC, and out to the road we have
around 13,000 volts going out to the road.
We plant wildflowers, seed mix, and grasses, we install bird and bat boxes around the perimeter
of the project area, we install scrapes and wood piles to support the amphibians and
reptiles, and then we focus on the vegetative screening.
At the end of the useful life of a solar farm, then there is an opportunity to remove the
panels, remove the piles, and that land will go back to whatever it was being used for
prior to the solar farm being constructed, so, that means it can be farmed again, it can
go back to wilderness, you can have trees grow back, and so, from an impact standpoint,
it's a commercial use that has very low or no contamination risk.
With the completion of this project, Eden Renewables is stacking benefits.
We're creating green electricity, we're offering a discount of that electricity to the community,
we're offering tax dollars to the community, we're implementing an education program
for the community, and we're creating a biodiverse solar farm which improves the environment.

What is BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) and why is everyone talking about it?
As renewable energy like solar and wind rapidly integrates into the power grid, new challenges are emerging — fluctuating power output, low system inertia, reactive power issues, and grid instability. In this video, filmed live from a battery manufacturing facility, we explore how BESS helps stabilize the grid and enable high renewable penetration.

You’ll learn:
• Why modern grids need battery energy storage
• Key problems caused by renewable integration
• Complete breakdown of BESS components – Batteries (LFP lithium-ion), PCS, BMS, EMS, TMS, and fire suppression systems

This video gives you a practical, real-world understanding of grid-scale energy storage systems and their role in the future power system.

segments.text: Power grid was never meant to accept the renewables, the solar and wind. Yet countries
are pushing for 100% renewable energy. So the question is how you keep your lights on
when the sun sets or the wind is not flowing. The container right here next to me can power
100 homes at the same time and importantly it can stabilize the entire power grid. This is
battery energy storage system or BESS. And today directly from the best manufacturing
facility I'll talk about what is best, why is everybody talking about it and what problems it
can solve and what are its component and I'll show you everything right from the factory.
And if you think it's just a giant battery box then you're wrong. Let me actually show you all
the components in this video. But before I open this box, it is important to understand why this
system exists and why everybody's talking about that. So first let's address that point. [music]
Now we are seeing a rapid integration of renewable power into the grid. Most of the countries have
taken [music] ambitious targets to integrate renewable energy into grid. India for example
has a target of 500 gawatt by 2030 and that's huge power. Same way you'll find a lot of countries
have taken ambitious target. Yes, renewable powers is clean but the problem with that it
is uncontrollable and it is fluctuating and power grid was never meant to accept the fluctuating
power and that basically creates a lot of issues with the power grid. Let us first talk about the
four key problems that power grid face because of renewable integration. The first problem is
fluctuating and uncontrollable output. The power output of renewable sources depends heavily on
natural conditions. For example, a solar power plant generate electricity only when the sunlight
is available. As the sun sets, the output drops to zero. Even during the day, cloud covers causes
continuous fluctuation in generation. A similar challenge exists with wind power where output
varies with wind speed. However, the traditional power grid was designed for steady and predictable
generation from conventional power plants. It is not inherently designed to handle rapid and
frequent power fluctuations which creates challenges in maintaining grid stability.
The second and the major problem is low system inertia. Conventional power plant uses large
synchronous generator with heavy rotating masses. These rotating rotors stores kinetic
energy known as inertia which helps stabilize grid frequency during disturbances. A simple
analogy is a bicycle wheel. Once it is spinning, it continues to rotate even if you stop paddling.
That stored energy is inertia. Similarly, when a generator trips or a sudden load change occurs,
the inertia of synchronous machine provides immediate support, slowing down the rate of
frequency change and giving the system time to respond. Most renewable energy sources connect
to the grid through power electronic converters which do not have mechanical rotating parts. As
renewable penetration increases, overall system inertia decreases making frequency control more
difficult and increasing the risk of rapid frequency deviations. Third problem is lack
of visibility and controllability. In conventional power system, system operator had high visibility
and centralized control over generation. Output from thermal, hydro and nuclear plants could be
scheduled and adjusted as required. Renewable generation, however, is inherently uncertain.
Accurate long-term and short-term prediction of solar and wind output is difficult because
it depends on weather conditions. Additionally, renewable plants are often distributed across the
grid, sometimes connected at weaker network points. This reduces centralized control and
make real-time coordination, dispatch, and grid management more complex for system operators.
And the fourth problem is lack of reactive power control. Now you will ask reactive power is of
no use. That's what we have learned. But that's not correct. If you go and check out the voltage
control methods that we use in power system are basically controlling reactive power. Shunt
reactors capacitor bank they basically control reactive power to get the voltage control. So
reactive power is essential for stable power grid. But with more and more renewable integration, we
are adding lot of solar inverters that basically don't produce the reactive power and the challenge
of reactive power control is now becoming more and more visible. So now we know there
are problems and these are not small problems. They are these are significant problems but we
also know we cannot go back to the conventional power sources because they are creating a lot
of pollution. So we must integrate renewable into our grid. There is no alternative to that. So what
we have to do is we have to identify a solution that can address all this problem and the solution
is energy storage technology. Battery energy storage system are not the only energy storage
option. Other technologies including pumped hydro, flywheel, thermal storage and hydrogen storage are
also there and there are other storage options also available. Each technology serves specific
purpose but none can meet all grid requirements. Pumped hydro can store large amount of energy but
it needs specific geography and has limited flexibility for fast grid services. Flywheel
responds very quickly but they can store energy only for a short duration. Thermal storage is
application specific and again depends on nature. Hydrogen storage has long-term potential but it is
still developing and faces efficiency and cost challenge. Because of all these limitation in
response time, scalability and flexibility, these technologies are not one size fit for all. Now all
the technology that we talked about cannot provide all the services that we want, all the services
that are needed for controllable power grid. But there is one technology that shines and that
potentially can address all the [music] issues and that technology is battery energy storage system.
[music] So as the name suggest in this energy storage technology we use batteries to store
electrical energy. When we have extra energy in the grid than what we need instead of wasting
that energy we can store it using the batteries and dispatch it back to the grid when we want.
Maybe during the evening period when solar is not producing or when the peak demand occurs. You can
consider this as a giant power bank. but for the entire power grid. Now Bess just don't store the
energy into it. It also interact with the grid on realtime basis. Bess is not only used for
energy storage. It goes beyond. It can be used for peak shaving, energy arbitrage, frequency support,
re output stabilization, black start capability and many other applications. And the best part
of the best they are easy to extend. So right next to me is a 250 kWh cabinet and if I want
additional power I can just add more one more cabinet to it and I have double the power that
I want. So extension uh is very flexible and easy. But if we talk about other storage technology we
don't get this flexibility and that's where the bus really shines. Now that we understand what
is bus and what application it can serve and it is very essential for having a stabilized
power grid. But a lot of people think that the bus is just a big giant power bank and that's
all. But that is not correct. This is a highly engineered piece of device and let me actually
show you what are all the components that are there placed and that makes a complete bus.
So the first component is of course the batteries. Now these are not one giant
battery. It is connected with a lot of small small cells. So small cells connected together
forms a module and that module connected together forms a battery pack or battery rack. You can see
right here these are all the modules and we have connected those in series with each other and
that's how we are getting 250 kilowatt hour of energy and this is a complete modular design.
The benefit of modular design if there is something wrong with one module we can
take out that module completely and replace it with the new one. Currently the best market is
dominated by lithium ion chemistry. The device that you see right next to me uses the lithium
ion LFP technology. Now why lithium ion dominates? Well the simple answer is it's
cost effective. It has better advantages compared to the other technology like it can store a lot
of energy into a small form factor. You can see these devices are holding 250 kowatt of
energy. But the problem with the batteries is they speak DC direct current but our grid
is having alternating current or AC because we generate we transmit and we distribute power using
alternating current. So how do we communicate between these two different uh languages? Well,
we need a converter and that's where power conversion system or PCS comes into picture.
[music] The power conversion system or PCS plays two role. The first role where it converts the
power coming from the grid into DC and acts as a rectifier. The second function it performs
the power output of the battery will again be DC and that needs to be converted in order to
connect to the grid and that is the second function. Conversion of DC into AC is also
done by the PCS and in that case it acts as an inverter. PCS can come into two configuration.
One incorporated within the same cabinet as the batteries or PCS can sit into a dedicated cabinet
or container. This is usually seen in mega best projects. Now PCS is a very crucial device. The
the PCS that you see inside this container can accept 415 volts from the grid that is
converted back into 830 volt DC using which we charge our batteries. And while giving it back
that 832 volts is again converted back into AC into 415 volts and then we can connect it back
to our grid. Now it is very important device because if PCS fails the whole unit is of no
use there won't be any charging there won't be any discharging. So it's a very important
device to keep an eye on. Now PCS is allowing the power to flow inside our batteries. But how
do we make sure that all the modules and all the cells inside the modules are equally stressed?
There is no single cell that cell that is getting stressed a lot. The the temperature of the cells
are within limit. The voltages are within limit. The currents are within limit. We need somebody
who can monitor our cells because if we don't do that this can go into a very catastrophic event
thermal runaway and that is where the battery management system or BMS comes into picture.
[music] Now the battery management system is an embedded system. Now what is embedded system? Like
let's take one example. Unlike our laptop which can perform a lot of functions, we can consider
a washing machine. Washing machine is meant to do only one single function that is to run the wash
cycles. Apart from that it will not do anything. That is basically the embedded system. The BMS
in this case is also an embedded system and it is meant to do only four function four major function
we can say. First monitoring the BMS continuously monitor the cell's temperature the voltage and
current and it gives information to all the other stakeholders in the system. The second function is
the protection function in which in case if the BMS detects something is not right with one of
the cell the BMS will immediately inform that to the distribution unit and then distribution unit
will cut down that particular module avoiding any escalations further. The third function
is performance optimization. Now PCS constantly communicates with the EMS energy management system
the PCS that we have and it decides or inform the state of charge of everything so that they
can make the right decision when to charge when to discharge and what is the capacity remaining
thereby improving on enhancing the performance of the bus and the fourth and the very important
function is the communication function. It is constantly in touch with the PCS power
conversion system and the EMS energy management system. So all the data will flow through them
and they can make the right decision. So you can say the BMS is the watchdog of complete battery
energy system especially the battery modules. But even the smartest electronic devices cannot
help if the temperature is not within limits. If the temperature is going high the BMS cannot do
anything. And that is why we also need thermal management system or [music] TMS into this.
Now there is a saying if the temperature is not suitable for human body or the human are
not comfortable in the temperature most likely the lithium ion batteries will
also not be. The lithium ion battery performs well within the temperature range of 20° to
40° and it is very important that we maintain this temperature because if the temperature
drops the performance of the battery will also drop. If the temperature increases then we have
a issue called thermal runaway that might pop up because the electrolyte within the cell will start
to heat up and it will go into thermal runaway. So that's why maintaining a constant temperature
operable temperature it is very important that we take out the heat from the system and that
is where the thermal management system comes into picture. The bus that you see right next
to me holds 250 kilowatt of R of energy and it is squeezed into in this compact form factor.
So for sure there will be heating and we need to take out that heating and that is the reason why
this device has a liquid cooling system. So you see we have at the bottom pumps which will pump
the coolings coolants inside the module and the heat will be taken out. Now there are different
methodologies. We also have HVAC systems used depending on what is the application. But when
you have a compact product, liquid cooling system makes more sense. But temperature
control is only one part of the story. We also need system that can help us in case
the event escalates into fire and that is where the fire suppression system comes into picture.
Now of course uh this is a lot of energy that we are storing. So there is a possibility that if
the event escalate uh it can result into a fire and that fire cannot be controlled. Uh it's that
bad. So that's why we have different sensors here. We have smoke sensor, off gas sensor,
temperature sensor, humidity sensor that will constantly keep an eye on everything inside the
uh container or the cabinet and then keep informed to the fire suppression system. Now in this
particular device in the module level itself we have aerosol based solutions used. So in case if
something is wrong that tube will burst and the aerosol will come out and that will contain or
limit the fire within that particular module only. So fire suppression system is very essential.
There are different methodologies available using which you can suppress the fire depending on how
big the bus is. for a bigger 20ft container the system will change. Now if you're interested to
know about what are the different fire risk in the best what are the suppression systems
available I've had a detailed discussion on this with a fire safety expert. If you're interested
uh learning about that you'll get link for that discussion down in the description. Now
we have everything in place. We have batteries we have converters we have safety systems and
all the things that we need. But how do we make the decision when to charge and when to
discharge and how do we make sure that this bus can perform the different function that
we want and that is where the EMS or energy management [music] system comes into picture.
Imagine you have taken this bus for energy arbitrage but it is charging when the electricity

Well, you you will lose the money in that, right? So to make that smart decision and

uh when to charge and when to discharge. Now depending on the application, you can change

Now all this intelligent system need a cabinet or container that can hold everything in safely and

metadata.author: Cool Wholesaling+ Land Deals-Real Estate Investing
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to learn how to quickly value vacant land using zillow?  This brief video shows you how to determine estimated retail value and how much to offer on a vacant lot.

Make better offers, faster. Use my free Multi-Offer Calculator to run your numbers and make data-driven, profitable offers: https://markcool.org/mark-cool-multi-offer-calculator/


## SOP: Finding Land Values Using Zillow

### Objective

To determine the value of vacant lots using Zillow for accurate property assessment.

### Key Steps

1. Pull up the property location on a map to understand its relation to nearby markets.
2. Use Zillow to search for the specific area, filter by land type, and zoom in and out to identify comparable properties.
3. Look for lots in the same region as the target property and analyze their sale prices.
4. Exclude high-end properties in subdivisions and focus on comparable lots for a more accurate comparison.
5. Calculate the maximum retail value based on the comparable properties found on Zillow.
6. Decide the profit you are shooting for, deduct from estimated retail, and set your offer range. \[Example; If we say we expect this to sell for max 15k retail and we want to make 5k profit, the max offer would be 10k, but we'd start at 6-7k to leave room to negotiate\].

### Cautionary Notes

- Consider the location and type of land when determining the maximum retail value.

### Tips for Efficiency

- Use the map to visually understand the property's location in relation to nearby markets.
- Filter search results on Zillow by land type to narrow down the options.
- Analyze a range of comparable properties to determine a realistic maximum retail value for the target lot.

Full Blog Post: https://retipster.com/vacant-land-valuation/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=rYCHQ59jzhY
Check out Redfin: https://retipster.com/redfin
Visit LandWatch: https://retipster.com/landwatch
Instant Data Scraper Chrome Extension: https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/instant-data-scraper/ofaokhiedipichpaobibbnahnkdoiiah
Data Miner Chrome Extension: https://dataminer.io/
Ready to get started as a land investor? Take your first steps here: https://welcome.retipster.com/5-day-email-course/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=rYCHQ59jzhY
Join Our Community: https://welcome.retipster.com/newsletter/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=rYCHQ59jzhY

There’s a common dilemma I’ve always had to wrestle with when buying vacant land. The issue boils down to valuation.

Land is a peculiar type of real estate because, in the vast majority of cases, it is EXTREMELY difficult to come up with a rock-solid, 100% reliable “market value” for this type of property (ask a professional real estate appraiser and chances are, they’re basically “winging it” in this area because the data just isn’t there).

So how are we supposed to have confidence in the value of what we’re buying?

I’ve always maneuvered through this process by following the guidelines in this blog post, which usually points to a reasonably strong conclusion, but if you’re looking for an even more quantifiable, measurable approach, I wanted to share with you an EPIC trick I learned about from Karl James, one of our faithful members of the Land Investing Masterclass.

redfin logoKarl uses a similar approach to the one I use to find sales comps on Zillow, but he goes one step further by analyzing the data with MUCH greater mathematical precision.

Karl uses Redfin, which provides much of the same information as Zillow, but allows users to download all the sales comp data in a CSV file. This may not seem significant at first glance, but trust me, it opens up all kinds of possibilities when analyzing the numbers and putting this data to work.

The video above explains how the whole process works!

0:00 - Intro
0:47 - Picking a market
1:04 - How to filter your property search
3:09 - How to download all property listings as a spreadsheet
3:32 - How to organize the spreadsheet
3:59 - How to find out the average sale price per acre
5:20 - How to average out the price per acre on all comps
5:40 - Something to remember about valuing vacant land
6:11 - How to identify and remove outliers
6:59 - What to do when Redfin won’t let you download the list
7:18 - How to use a data scraper to pull the data
8:01 - How to use instant data scraper chrome extension
9:09 - Downloading and organizing the CSV file in excel
9:37 - Deleting unneeded data and plugging in the right formulas
10:13 - Using the Find & Replace tool to eliminate unwanted text
11:30 - Finding and removing outliers
12:28 - What to do when Redfin doesn't work (go to LandWatch)
12:55 - Differences between LandWatch and Redfin
13:22 - Making sense of the scraped data from LandWatch
13:50 - The reason why Zillow doesn't work as well

🏡 **Could THIS Zillow Property Be the PERFECT Family Compound?**

I found an interesting piece of land listed on Zillow, and it got me thinking… could this property be the perfect place to build a family compound?

After asking you guys what you thought in my YouTube Short, I decided to take a deeper dive into this property!

In this video, we're breaking down what makes this land a potential family compound and some of the important things you need to consider BEFORE buying property to build multiple homes for your family.

🌲 **Here's what we'll look at:**
- Is there enough usable land for multiple homes?
- Does the property offer the privacy and space a family compound needs?
- What about road access, utilities, and infrastructure?
- Could local zoning and subdivision regulations create problems?
- What potential red flags should buyers look for?
- Would I consider buying this property for a family compound?

Buying land for a family compound is about more than finding a beautiful piece of property. It's about making sure the land actually works for your family's long-term goals.

🔥 **WANT TO BUILD YOUR OWN FAMILY COMPOUND?**

I've created resources to help families navigate the process of finding, evaluating, and planning their own family compounds.

👉 **Get started here:** https://familycompoundguide.com

📚 Learn how to evaluate land, avoid costly mistakes, and start planning your family's future.

💬 **NOW I WANT TO HEAR FROM YOU!**

Would YOU buy this property to build a family compound? What do you like about it, and what concerns would you have?

Drop your thoughts in the comments! 👇

👍 LIKE this video if you enjoy looking at potential family compound properties.

🔔 SUBSCRIBE for more videos about buying rural land, subdividing property, building family compounds, and creating a legacy for future generations.

#FamilyCompound #BuyingLand #Homestead #RuralLand #LandInvesting #FamilyHomestead #Zillow #RealEstate #MultiGenerationalLiving

metadata.shortDescription:
View vacant land deals here: https://onceuponabrick.com/ **How to Find the TRUE Value of Land in 5 Minutes (Comparable Sales & Land Comps\!)**

Looking to buy a piece of vacant land but unsure if the asking price is fair? You can find the true value of any land parcel in under five minutes by checking comparable sales, or "comps."

This video breaks down the easiest and most accurate strategies real estate professionals use to value houses, commercial property, and land:

1.  **Search the MLS/Zillow for Sold Comps:** Learn how to filter Zillow listings for only "land" in your county (e.g., Pasco County, Florida) and specifically look at recently *sold* properties that match your lot size (e.g., 1 to 10 acres).
2.  **Analyze Patterns and Average Prices:** Don't rely on just one sale. Look for a consistent average of what similar 2-acre or 3-acre parcels have recently sold for to determine your land's value.
3.  **Check Current Listings:** Once you know what similar land has sold for, look at what is *currently* for sale (current market value) in the area on the MLS.
4.  **Use County GIS or Software:** In disclosure states, you may be able to check the county's GIS map to see what neighbors paid for their lots. You can also use paid software like Land ID or Maprite.
5.  **Bonus: Call a Realtor:** Call a realtor who is listing a property nearby and ask them what they think your land is worth.

**Important:** The raw price is only half the equation. You must also evaluate the **characteristics** of the land, as these heavily affect the true value. Factors that add premium value include:

  * Is the land flat or sloping?
  * Is it a wetland or not?
  * Does it have good access/road frontage?
  * Are utilities (electric, water) nearby?

Knowing the comps and the characteristics ensures you feel confident in your land purchase\!

\#LandValue \#HowToValueLand \#LandComps \#RealEstateInvesting \#VacantLand \#Zillow

-----

Timestamps / Chapters

0:00 - Introduction: Finding the True Value of Land in Under 5 Minutes  
0:30 - How to Find the Value of Land  
0:39 - Strategy 1: Using the MLS/Zillow for Comps  
1:15 - How to Search Zillow: Unselect All But Land  
2:05 - Setting the Lot Size Filter (1 Acre to 10 Acres)  
2:30 - Filtering for Sold Listings  
2:43 - Look for Consistent Sales Patterns  
3:29 - Strategy 2: Check Current Market Listings  
4:03 - Strategy 3: Check County GIS (Disclosure States)  
4:37 - Using Paid Software (Land ID, Maprite)  
5:05 - Bonus Tip: Call a Local Realtor  
5:53 - Strategy 4: Check Non-MLS Marketplaces (LandWatch)  
6:29 - How Characteristics Affect Land Value  
6:40 - Key Characteristics: Flatness, Wetlands, Access  
7:29 - The Value of Road Frontage  
7:43 - Utility Access (Electric, Water)

Zillow can be used for a lot of different things. One thing most people don't think about is using the sold and for sale data to find comps when valuing vacant land.

Vacant land is a notoriously difficult type of property to appraise because most of the time, the information we need to establish a baseline value just isn't there... but Zillow allows you to find a lot of information that can be used to come up with a ballpark valuation.

This approach is far from perfect (for obvious reasons), but among other things, it will inform you of what kind of competition you’re dealing with (and what those sellers are hoping to get out of their property). In other words, if you were to list your subject property for sale in this market today, what other listings would you have to compete against?

Take a minute and do the math. Once you understand what price your property will have to be listed for in order to look like the best deal on the market, this will give you a better perspective of the property’s potential value in contrast to what’s currently available on the market (because if you’re offering the best deal and advertising it well, it will theoretically be the first one to sell).

Now, you see in the county, you've got 257 properties that meet our criteria. metadata.title: How I Price Land When Sold Prices Aren't Public
metadata.author: Sumner Advanced
metadata.shortDescription:
What would it take to make the next 90 days your best 90 days in land?

Book a FREE 90-Day Game Plan Call with my team. We’ll talk through where you are, what’s holding you back, and what to focus on next to get your first deal (or close more of them).

👉 Apply and book your call: https://landinvestor.co/YouTube

How do you figure out what vacant land is worth when the actual sold prices aren't publicly available?

In this LIA 2.0 coaching call, I break down how I comp land in non-disclosure states, including Texas, where the last listed price doesn't necessarily reflect the actual sale price.

We cover how to use days on market, listing history, estimated discounts, and alternative land listing websites to build a more accurate picture of property values.

You'll also learn why non-disclosure markets can create opportunities for land investors willing to put in the work to understand local pricing.

**In this video:**
- Why last list price isn't the same as sold price
- How days on market can help estimate sale prices
- When to discount active listing prices
- Using Land.com and other sources for comps
- Why non-disclosure states can be less competitive

Try Land Insights and get 1,000 free seller leads:
https://www.landinsights.co/

**About Sumner Healey**

700+ land deals flipped. Founder of Land Insights. Helped hundreds of investors through Land Investor Accelerator (LIA) and LIA 2.0.

Business. Investing. Travel. Lifestyle.

#LandInvesting #LandFlipping #VacantLand #LandComps #LandInsights

metadata.title: How to Find the Best Counties for Land Investing with Zillow
metadata.author: REtipster
metadata.shortDescription:
Full Blog Post: https://retipster.com/best-markets-land-investing/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=E9KBudZB1Do
Check out Zillow at: https://retipster.com/zillow

Most people don't realize that it's fairly easy to figure out how much a hypothetical property will sell for in any given market.

When I started investing in land, it was VERY difficult to find comparable sales data for vacant land because websites like Zillow, Trulia, and Redfin were still relatively new, and they hadn't yet grown to the highly sophisticated systems they are today.

As I explain in this blog post, most areas within these systems make it very easy to find sales data going back 3 years or more on almost any type of property you can think of. I'll show you how it works in the video above.

The beauty of this is that in many markets, Zillow allows you to see real, precise sales figures for what properties sold for in your county of choice. These numbers are much more accurate than the county's "assessed value", which is usually WAY out of bounds from reality.

When you have this kind of information at your disposal, there's really no reason to wonder how valuable properties will be in your target market - because you can see exactly what they've been selling for (and what they're currently listed for) over the past few months or years.

If you're unsure what kind of market you're getting into and whether the price ranges will be in the right place relative to your budget, a little bit of sales comp research will quickly get you up to speed!

metadata.title: Cold Calling vs Cold Texting vs Direct Mail: Which One Actually Works Best for Land Flipping?
metadata.author: Michael Bull
metadata.shortDescription:
There are three ways to find motivated land sellers — cold calling, cold texting, and direct mail. Every land investor has an opinion on which one is best.

In this video I break down all three from someone who has actually used them all. What each one costs, how they perform, where they break down, and which one I'd recommend depending on where you are in your land flipping business.

If you're just getting started and trying to figure out how to find your first deal — this video will save you a lot of time and money.

What we cover:
— How cold calling works in the land space and what kind of results to expect
— How cold texting works, what the compliance issues are, and whether it's worth it
— Why direct mail has been my primary acquisition strategy and what the numbers look like
— Cost per deal comparison across all three methods
— Which strategy makes the most sense for beginners vs experienced investors
— What I would use if I was starting from zero today

🔗 LINKS
💬 Free Discord community: https://discord.gg/xxf6ZGKwb
🌐 Website / Free resources: landflippingsimplified.com
📸 Instagram: @landflippingsimplified
📩 Questions? Drop a comment below or DM on Instagram.

If this helped you figure out how to find your first land deal — hit subscribe. Real deals, real numbers, real strategy every week.

metadata.shortDescription:
Cold Calling and Texting in Real Estate: What You Don’t Know Could Cost You BIG

In the world of real estate investing, cold calling and texting are common lead-gen tactics—but they also come with serious legal risks.

In this video, Jeff Charlton from REIPrintMail sits down with Josh Stevens, a top attorney specializing in the TCPA (Telephone Consumer Protection Act), to break down what real estate investors must know before they pick up the phone or send that next text.

Josh explains how the TCPA and Do Not Call regulations really work—including how violations happen, what constitutes “consent,” and why even if you’re buying a property (not selling), you’re still at risk.

➡️ Think you’re safe because you pulled a skip-traced list? You may want to think again.
 ➡️ Not sure if you need written consent before reaching out? This episode covers it.
 ➡️ Wondering what an “Established Business Relationship” really protects you from? Josh has answers.

You’ll also hear a cautionary tale about a real estate investor who thought he was following the rules… until it cost him over $1 million in settlements and legal fees.

This isn’t just theory—it’s real-world insight that could save your business from financial disaster.

If you're doing or planning to do any type of telemarketing—especially cold calls or texts—this video is essential viewing.

🛑 Don't make legal assumptions.
 💡 Learn what the law actually says.
 📈 Protect your business before it’s too late.

metadata.shortDescription:
Cold Calling vs Direct Mail for Real Estate Deals
#landflipping #coldcalling #realestatemarketing

Some investors think cold calling, emailing, or texting is the best way to get land or house deals. In this video, Steven and Jill explain why those methods often don’t work and how they compare to direct mail. They share real examples, talk about legal issues, and explain what actually gets results. If you're not sure how to reach sellers, this will save you time and effort.

On today's Land Academy Show, join Steven Jack Butala (https://www.linkedin.com/in/steven-butala-39853916) and Jill DeWit (https://www.linkedin.com/in/jill-dewit) break down the real-world effectiveness, and legality, of the top outreach methods investors use today. 

From awkward cold calls and ignored texts to a single strategy that actually works, they cut through the noise to reveal what’s worth your time and what could land you in hot water. If you’ve ever wondered how top land investors consistently close deals, this is the episode you’ve been waiting for.

metadata.title: How I Shoot Acreage Listings With the DJI Mavic 4 Pro - One Flight, Three Lenses
metadata.author: Next Move with Rob
metadata.shortDescription:
My agent looked at my drone shots and wrote back two words: "looks good." Here's why that bugged me, and how I fixed it.
One flight, one battery, three cameras, and the whole rural property, details and all, without ever flying over the house.

On a property with real land around it, the wide shot is the least interesting shot you've got. In this video I walk you through my one-battery, four-job flight plan with the DJI Mavic 4 Pro. I switch between its three cameras in the air: the 28mm 100MP Hasselblad wide for land and acreage, the 70mm for the facade and the details that make a country property feel like home, and the 168mm telephoto as a "distance lens" for road access, ponds, and views without hovering over a neighbor's yard. Then I roll the Infinity Gimbal to true vertical for native 9:16 clips an agent can post that same afternoon.

Along the way I share a safety tip about positioning on the wide lens (learned the hard way at some bourbon warehouses), an honesty note about not hiding a property's problems, a before-and-after of the same farm shot both ways, and the small bits of gear that make this workflow smoother.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Why "looks good" bugged me
0:59 Three cameras on the DJI Mavic 4 Pro
1:38 Is it overkill for real estate?
2:23 One battery, four jobs: the flight plan
3:04 Job 1: The wide is a map
4:17 Job 2: The 70mm portrait and detail lens
5:18 Safety tip: Reposition on the wide lens
6:38 An honesty note on details
7:03 Job 3: The 168mm distance lens
8:39 Job 4: True vertical with the Infinity Gimbal
9:42 Before and after, same farm
10:07 The Triple Lens Listing Pass
10:55 Gear I actually fly with
12:22 An honest word on buying the Mavic 4 Pro
12:44 Recap: Your next rural shoot

📋 FREE RESOURCES
Free one-page field card (shot list for all four jobs): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T4N4mAu8ppf9thvx8miQjTnRDxi-Eop7/view?usp=drive_link
Listing Pass Playbook (pricing sheet and short pitch for agents): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pembOM5iwu7a-G0mEv4-uCt6DmUtgEbv/view?usp=drive_link
My earlier video about the Mavic 4 Pro shot down in Athens, Alabama: https://youtu.be/yCWvn2sMuEI?si=pOtYzgJpBYKSvV4b

🎒 GEAR MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO - I make a small commission on anything bought through these links, at no cost to you.
DJI Mavic 4 Pro: https://link.amazon/B0gSFQ4O9
DJI eND (electronic ND) filter for the Mavic 4 Pro: https://link.amazon/B0bCNCGXY
ND filter set (ND8 / ND16 / ND32): https://link.amazon/B003P2Tba
Extra batteries + charging hub: https://link.amazon/B003P2Tba  -  https://link.amazon/B09TX6WKE

Note: DJI US stock moves in and out, and depending on where you buy, Care Refresh or a US warranty may not be available. Check live availability yourself the day you buy.

🔔 If you fly for a living or shoot listings, subscribe for more Mavic 4 Pro workflow videos. Roofs and construction progress are coming up next: YouTube.com/@NextMovewithRob/subscribe

I'm Rob, and on Next Move with Rob I help photographers and real estate agents make listings that actually showcase a property, especially rural land and farms here around Bloomfield and Nelson County, Kentucky. Next Move Media: https://nextmovemediagroup.com

metadata.title: What Happens When You Fail a Perc Test For A Septic System
metadata.author: Wells, Septic & More
metadata.shortDescription:
Hello and good afternoon, friends! In today's video, we'll be diving into the crucial topic of what happens when you don't pass a perc test for your septic system. Perc tests are essential for determining whether your property can support a septic system, especially if you're in a rural area without public sewer access.

We'll cover:

What a perk test is and why it's important.
The different types of septic systems and what happens if your soil fails the test.
Innovative and advanced septic systems versus conventional systems.
The realities and challenges of having a holding tank.
Tips on managing water usage if you're stuck with a holding tank.
Legal considerations and the potential impact on property value.
Whether you're considering buying land or you're dealing with an existing property that has septic system issues, this video is packed with valuable information. Don't forget to leave a comment with your experiences or questions about septic systems and holding tanks. Hit that like button and subscribe for more insights on well and septic systems!

Keywords: Perk Test, Septic System, Holding Tank, Septic Failure, Rural Property, Septic System Types, Wastewater Management, Property Value, Water Conservation, Legal Considerations, Home Inspection, Real Estate Tips, Septic System Maintenance

#SepticSystem #PerkTest #HomeImprovement #WaterManagement #PropertyValue #RealEstateTips

Music from #Uppbeat
https://uppbeat.io/t/sky-toes/autumn-walks
License code: DUUNNUDQGLFXT8O1

metadata.title: What the Heck is a "Perc Test" (and How Much Does it Really Matter)?
metadata.author: REtipster
metadata.shortDescription:
Full Blog Post: https://retipster.com/perc-test/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=yp6qPMTkjgE
Join Our Community: https://retipster.com/follow/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=blog&utm_content=yp6qPMTkjgE

00:00 - Intro
00:15 - What exactly is a Perc Test?
01:56 - How does the Perc Test work in most jurisdictions around the country?
03:01 - How to determine if a Perc Test is important to your specific situation
05:07 - What if the property fails the Perc Test?
05:51 - When to consider a modified septic system on the property?
06:16 - Should you hold your property even though it doesn’t have a septic system?
07:08 - Final thoughts

If you're dropping some serious cash on a parcel of vacant land, there is one issue that may seem insignificant at first glance, but it has the potential to make or break a land deal.

The “Perc Test”

A Perc Test (also known as “Perk Test,” more formally known as a Percolation Test) is a soil evaluation that tests the rate at which water drains through soil.

Perc tests are required in just about every civilized municipality in the world – because the results of this test provide crucial information required to design and install a septic system.

A perc test is conducted by drilling or digging a hole in the ground, pouring water into the hole, and then observing the rate at which the water is absorbed into the soil. In most cases, properties can easily pass a perc test when the soil has higher concentrations of sand (because sand tends to absorb water at a much faster rate than clay or silt) and when the property is situated in an area with a low water table.

Why is a Perc Test Necessary?

For all intents and purposes, a perc test (and subsequently, a septic system) is only necessary when a property does NOT have access to a municipal sewer system.

If a vacant lot is situated within reach of an existing sewer hook-up, this will usually eliminate the need for a septic system altogether. For this reason, the availability of an existing sewer system can be big "perk" (no pun intended) when evaluating a property's suitability for building a dwelling of any kind.

When there isn't an existing sewer system nearby, that's when you'll need to explore the feasibility of a septic system. Most county health departments will require a perc test to determine if a septic system is possible.

Most of the world's septic systems require a septic drain field or "leach field" to drain away any excess water. When solid waste settles in a septic tank, the excess wastewater is discharged into the septic drain field through a network of perforated pipes.

The contaminants expelled from this wastewater are then trapped and eliminated in the soil. This happens primarily through the process of percolation – and also through evaporation, transpiration, consumption by plant roots, and eventually, the remaining water re-enters the groundwater and/or surface water.

The typical drain field size is determined by the expected volume of wastewater to be discharged from the septic system (usually estimated based on the size of the proposed building).

metadata.title: Failed Perc Test? What It Means and Your Septic Options
metadata.author: Liberty Acres
metadata.shortDescription:
A failed perc test usually means the soil can't take a conventional septic drainfield, not that the land can never hold a home. Many health departments permit alternative or engineered systems, such as mounds, drip dispersal and aerobic treatment units, on sites where a conventional system won't work. Which systems are allowed is set by your state and county health department.

Read the full guide: https://libertyacres.land/guides/failed-perc-test?utm_source=youtube

Chapters:
0:00 The short answer
0:27 Alternative systems
0:55 Who decides
1:08 What to do next
1:25 State example
1:44 Land value

Sources (public official sources):
- US EPA: Types of Septic Systems: https://www.epa.gov/septic/types-septic-systems
- Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0400-48-01-.15: Alternative systems (Cornell LII): https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/tennessee/Tenn-Comp-R-Regs-0400-48-01-.15
- Ala. Admin. Code 420-3-1-.09: Engineered onsite sewage systems: https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/api/rule/420-3-1-.09

Liberty Acres is a family-owned land company based in Atlanta.

drain field, not that the land can never
hold a home.
A conventional system sends waste water
into a drain field, and the soil does
the treatment as the water moves through
it. A site usually fails because the
soil is too shallow over rock.
Groundwater sits too close to the
surface. The soil drains too slowly or
too fast. Or the slope or lot can't fit
the drain field.
EPA groups the fixes as alternative
systems, and each one fits a different
problem. A mound handles shallow soil,
high groundwater, or shallow bedrock.
Driplines sit in the top 6 to 12 inches
of soil, but need a dose tank and
electric power. Aerobic units and sand
filters treat the water further, and a
cluster system shares one system across
two or more homes. Most cost more to
build and maintain than a conventional
drain field.
Your state and local health department
decide which systems are allowed, and
not every type is approved everywhere.
Ask the permitting office for its list
of approved systems, and what it needs
from you before you pay for one.
Start with the written result, and ask
which condition failed. Soil can change
across a tract, so ask whether another
spot could be tested. Then have a soil
scientist or engineer say which systems
could fit. Ask the utility about public
sewer, and get a written estimate for
the system and its upkeep.
State rules differ, so check your own.
In Tennessee, a mound needs at least 24
inches of soil over a restrictive layer,
or 20 inches for a modified mound. The
state fee for an alternative system
permit is $500. In Alabama, any
non-conventional system needs an
engineer's design.
A failed perc test can lower land value
because a buyer who plans a home on
septic will weigh the cost and upkeep of
an alternative system. Land that can
reach public sewer, or that a buyer
would use for something that doesn't
need septic, is affected less.
Liberty Acres is a family-owned land
company based in Atlanta. Thinking about
selling land? Visit libertyacres.land.
