📥 Download your Free Relocation Guide: https://bit.ly/3VztOZV

Thinking about buying land to build your dream home or as an investment? 🏡 Before you sign, you NEED to know about the Perc Test (percolation test).

A perc test can make or break your land purchase. Without it, you may not be able to build a house or even use the land as you planned. Watch until the end so you don’t make a costly mistake!

Got questions about land or real estate? We’d love to help!
Send us an email at bqc21team@gmail.com and let’s talk.

----------

Hey everyone! Thank you for visiting my channel. As a second-generation realtor, I've been deeply involved in Virginia's real estate market since 2011. Born and raised on a farm in the Fredericksburg area, I'm fortunate enough to now help others find their dream homes in this beautiful region.

I specialize in residential properties, working primarily with first-time home buyers and seasoned investors in Virginia. My background in residential construction gives me a unique perspective, allowing me to guide clients smoothly from the initial land deals to move-in day.

Outside of real estate, I'm an avid outdoorsman. Whether you're looking to buy or sell, my dedicated team and I are here to confidently fulfill your real estate needs.

-

segments.text: out of all the topics that frequently
come up in land transactions soil and
septic are probably the most
misunderstood so this video is going to
talk about what people mean when they
talk about a perk test why it's
important for land owners to understand
and why you should care let's get
started
[Music]
the first thing about septic and soil
that you should know is that uh about
25% of all us households rely on a
septic system to manage Wastewater from
the
home and when you're in the big city
septic doesn't really come into play
because you have sewer system a
municipal sewer system that manages that
however when you get outside of the city
or even outside of a small town and
you're in the country your ability to
build on that property depends on
septic so the importance of soil and and
the perk test and how that all works
we're going to get into that but first
we have to discuss how a septic system
works in the first place so what happens
with a septic system is that Wastewater
from your home will first leave the home
through a septic line and it's going to
flow into a septic tank a septic tank is
basically a container made out of
concrete fiberglass sometimes
plastic and the Wastewater pools in a
septic tank where the the tank actually
enables initial treatment of Wastewater
through anerobic digestion is basically
a fancy way of saying that
microorganisms break down some of the
material
and remove some of the contaminants from
the
Wastewater but with the septic tank even
though it's underground usually the the
surrounding soil quality hasn't really
come into play yet because that's what
happens
next Once the waste water is pre-treated
in the septic tank what happens is that
the the treated Wastewater actually
flows out of the septic tank into what's
called a drain
field a drain field is essentially a
series of underground trenches that
distribute the
Wastewater via perforated pipes or other
permeable or semi-permeable
material the classic conventional septic
system is uses gravel trenches so the
gravel helps to distribute the waste
water into the area and the surrounding
soil basically the trenches in the drain
field allow the surrounding soil to
sponge up the Wastewater um into the
surrounding
area and once the Wastewater passes
through the drain field the soil
underground Works its
charms so no one talks about this and I
learned this just recently but soil is
basically magic now okay I know it
sounds crazy but stay with me for a
second there's this guy he's a science
fiction writer named Arthur C Clark he
wrote 2001 A Space Odyssey he has this
quote about technology that any
sufficiently advanced technology is
indistinguishable from
Magic well the fact is that no human
technology that we've developed is
Advanced enough to do what soil does
naturally in a septic system soil
purifies water it does it free of of any
cost it just does it naturally there in
your yard you know there's no monthly
bill that is applied for that soil soil
is free when you own when you own that
land but soil has to work a certain way
in order for septic to be
installed so the the function of soil is
critical because the function of soil is
what enables the Wastewater to be
disposed of naturally without without
the need for municipal sewer and without
the risk of contaminating the home or
the natural environment around the
home the slang term for perk test is um
it used to refer to a percolation test
it's kind of like an Antiquated
term the percolation referring to how
basically how water drains through the
soil but what that refers to today is a
county site inspection performed
normally by a site inspector from the
County Environmental Health office
common reasons that septic applications
and perk tests are
denied include uh soil that is too wet
or has too high of a water table perhaps
some reasons are for soil that is has
too much clay content and certain types
of soil like clay just don't drain well
they don't drain well at all a lot of
times you'll see shallow depth to rock
that below the surface of the ground you
just don't have enough soil until you
start hitting rock and then sometimes
it's the slope the terrain or Topography
of the land itself even if the soil's
good having a really steep slope makes
it difficult to install a septic system
a lot of times it's just a combination
of all those variables and they play in
together and they can change on a dime
you know 10 ft in any direction soil
characteristics can change just because
the house next door has a septic system
and the house on the other side has one
too doesn't mean that your vacant lot in
the middle is necessarily going to
qualify so at the end of the day if
you're a landowner and your property
requires septic to be used as a home
site it doesn't matter what the realtor
says it doesn't matter what the
appraiser says if you don't know what's
going on with the soil under the ground
of your property you'll never fully know
what the property is really worth and
the good news though is that you can
find out and it's pretty simple uh in
terms of how what I'd recommend is that
you consider hiring a soil scientist to
perform a preliminary soil evaluation of
your property they'll go out they'll
take a sample of soil across the entire
property they'll tell you with a general
mapping you know literally a map a
mapped report of your property and
they'll show you you know where the soil
is good for septic and where it's
not the downside of the working with
soil scientists is that they're more
expensive than working with the county
but um the POS the positive benefit is
that they'll take more of a distributed
sample of your entire property so they
they can sometimes go go through as an
extra ex ra service and they'll actually
get you a permit as well when you're
ready to do
construction but to know what the soil
will give you you don't really need a
permit a soil evaluation with a good uh
soil map is really all that you need so
a lot of times sellers you'll you know
sellers will be told from real estate
agents oh yeah don't worry about it you
know the buyer is going to pay for this
anyway and that's true however if you
have it done in advance what's going to
happen when you go to sell is that you
just have way more leverage with your
buyer you just have way more pricing
power and confidence in the market of
the product that you're actually
offering and what it's really going to
be worth so I'd recommend considering
that investment if you're a land owner
you want to find out what your property
is really worth but you need to install
septic for resid residential
construction soil evaluation is going to
be a good bet so I hope this video
demystifies the perk test what it is and
how septic and soil are really important
to land owners
[Music]

2021: Voted by my peers as North Carolina Weekly's Rising Star. Started serving on the board as the attorney for the Lake Norman Homebuilders Association.
2023: Voted by my peers as a Super Lawyers Rising Star (an award I've won in 2024 and 2025 as well).
2025: Invited to speak on Yahoo Finance as a live guest about the state of the real estate market. Our firm has now closed nearly 10,000 real estate transactions.

Today: I serve on multiple boards including the South Iredell Economic Development Committee, Iredell Economic Development Committee, and as board chair for Hope of Mooresville (a local non-profit). I've been invited to speak on national stages to share insights on real estate law with attorneys and real estate agents across the country.

Thomas & Webber operates three offices across the Lake Norman area. We handle residential real estate closings, estate planning, and business law. But what we're really known for is actually keeping our clients informed throughout the process—which shouldn't be revolutionary, but apparently it is.

Why do I make these videos?

Because I've seen too many people show up to closing confused, stressed, and blindsided by costs or terms they didn't understand. I've seen buyers lose thousands of dollars because they didn't know their rights during due diligence. I've seen property owners accept lowball offers from the DOT because they didn't know they could negotiate.

Real estate law shouldn't be complicated. It shouldn't require a law degree to understand what you're signing. And you shouldn't have to chase down your attorney just to find out what's happening with your closing.

So I'm putting everything I know into free videos—breaking down closing disclosures, explaining due diligence timelines, showing you how to protect yourself from wire fraud, teaching you your rights in eminent domain cases—all in plain English.

If you're buying or selling property in North Carolina, you're in the right place.

To everyone navigating real estate transactions: You're making one of the biggest financial decisions of your life. You deserve to understand every step of the process. You deserve an attorney who keeps you informed. And you deserve to walk into closing confident, not confused.

Keep learning. Keep asking questions. And never sign something you don't understand.

See you in the next video,
Tiffany

segments.text: I never thought I would spend my Tuesday
morning staring down three smug HOA
board members who somehow believed they
owned the rights to what lay beneath my
property. But there I was holding a
Manila folder that was about to blow
their entire scam wide open. My name is
James Peterson and I bought my house in
Broken Arrow, Oklahoma 3 years ago. It
was a modest ranchstyle home on 2 acres,
far enough from the Tulsa metro area to
feel rural, but close enough to commute
to my engineering job.
The neighborhood, Pine Ridge Estates,
was relatively new, established about 15
years ago when some developer decided to
carve up an old cattle ranch into 30
upscale lots. When I purchased the
property, I did my due diligence, had
the home inspected, reviewed all the
paperwork, and yes, I read through the
HOA covenant. It was standard stuff
about lawn maintenance, fence heights,
and paint colors. Nothing seemed too
restrictive, so I signed on the dotted
line. Life was peaceful for those first
three years. I kept my grass mowed, paid
my dues on time, and generally avoided
the HOA drama. I had heard horror
stories about the board president, a
woman named Patricia Hris, would
occasionally send passive aggressive
emails about minor violations, but
nothing that really got under my skin.
She was in her late 50s, always wore
designer sunglasses, even indoors, and
had that particular hairstyle that
somehow screamed, "I need to speak to
your manager," without her saying a
word. Everything changed last spring
when an energy company sent me a letter.
Breenidge Energy Resources wanted to
discuss a potential mineral lease on my
property. According to their geological
surveys, the area beneath Pineriidge
Estates sat at top a promising natural
gas formation. They were contacting all
property owners in the vicinity to
negotiate mineral rights leases. The
offer was substantial, potentially worth
hundreds of thousands of dollars
depending on what they found. I was
stunned. I had known Oklahoma was oil
and gas country, but I never imagined my
little slice of suburbia would attract
corporate attention. I called my real
estate attorney, Marcus Chen, to make
sure everything was legitimate. He
reviewed the letter and confirmed it was
real. Then he asked me the crucial
question. Do you actually own the
mineral rights to your property?
I think so, I said. Wouldn't they have
come with the house?
Marcus explained that in many states,
particularly Oklahoma and Texas, mineral
rights can be severed from surface
rights. Previous owners could have sold
the minerals while keeping the land or
vice versa. He recommended we pull my
deed and trace the title history to be
absolutely certain.
We spent two weeks going through county
records at the Creek County Courthouse.
The chain of title was complex, going
back to the original land grant in the
1890s when Oklahoma was still Indian
territory. But every single transfer
clearly stated that both surface and
mineral rights were being conveyed
together. There was no severance
anywhere in the chain. According to
every legal document we could find, I
owned not just my house and yard, but
everything beneath it down to the center
of the earth, as the old common law
saying goes. Armed with this
information, I contacted Breenidge
Energy and began negotiating a lease.
They offered a signing bonus of $50,000
and an 18% royalty on any gas produced
from my property. It was not quite
life-changing money, but it would pay
off my mortgage and fund some long
overdue home improvements. Or that is
when Patricia showed up at my door. It
was a Saturday morning in early April,
and I was having my coffee on the back
porch when I heard aggressive knocking
on the front door. I opened it to find
Patricia flanked by two other board
members, Dennis Kowalsski, the treasurer
who ran a used car dealership, and
Sharon Martinez, the secretary who
taught elementary school. All three
looked angry. "We need to talk about
your little scheme, James," Patricia
said, pushing past me into my living
room without invitation. "Excuse me," I
said, too surprised to stop her. "What
scheme?" "Don't play dumb," Dennis said,
following her inside. "We know about the
energy company. We know what you're
trying to do. Sharon at least had the
decency to look uncomfortable about the
home invasion.
James, the HOA, received notification
from Breenidge Energy about activity in
our subdivision. As the governing body
for Pineriidge Estates, we need to
coordinate any mineral extraction that
might occur here. I closed my door and
crossed my arms. I appreciate your
concern, but this is between me and the
energy company, my property, my mineral
rights.
Patricia laughed, an ugly sound without
any humor. Your mineral rights? Is that
what you think? Did you even read the
HOA covenants when you bought here? Yes,
I read them. There was nothing about
mineral rights. Page 47, section 12,
subsection D, Patricia said
triumphantly. She pulled out a printed
document from her massive purse. All
natural resources within the boundaries
of Pineri Ridge estates, including but
not limited to water, minerals, oil,
gas, and timber of commercial value are
considered common assets of the
community and fall under the management
authority of the HOA board. She shoved
the paper at me. I scanned it quickly,
feeling a cold weight settle in my
stomach. The language was there, buried
in a section about community resource
management that I had honestly skipped
over during my initial review. who reads
every subsection of a 49page HOA
covenant. This doesn't mean what you
think it means, I said slowly. This is
talking about management authority, not
ownership. There is a legal difference.
Not according to our attorney, Dennis
said. We have already consulted with
legal counsel. When you signed the
covenant, you agreed to seed control of
subsurface resources to the HOA. Any
money from mineral leases comes to the
community and gets distributed according
to the bylaws,
which means the board determines how it
gets used," Patricia added with a thin
smile for the good of everyone in
Pineriidge Estates. I was furious, but
tried to keep my voice level. I have
reviewed my deed extensively with my
attorney. I own the mineral rights to
this property. A HOA covenant cannot
supersede a recorded deed. That is not
how property law works.
We will see what a judge says," Patricia
replied. "But until this is resolved,
you need to cease all negotiations with
Breen Ridge Energy immediately. The
board will handle communications with
them from now on. If you continue with
this unauthorized lease, we will sue you
for breach of covenant and seek
damages." They left after that and I
immediately called Marcus Chen. He
listened to my explanation and asked me
to email him the relevant section of the
HOA covenant. This is interesting, he
said after reviewing it. They are
absolutely wrong about the law, but I
can see why they think they have a case.
The language is deliberately vague. Can
they actually sue me? They can file a
lawsuit. Yes, anyone can sue anyone for
anything. The question is whether they
would win, and the answer is almost
certainly no. Mineral rights are real
property interests that run with the
land. They are recorded with the county
and cannot be taken away by a private
contract like an HOA covenant. At most,
the covenant might give them some say in
how extraction occurs, like requiring
certain environmental protections or
limiting noise, but ownership? No way.
So, what do I do? Keep negotiating with
Breenidge. Document everything with the
HOA. If they sue, we will fight it and
probably counters sue for legal fees. In
the meantime, I'm going to do some more
research on this particular covenant.
Something smells off about this. Marcus'
instincts were correct. Over the next
week, he discovered something
fascinating. The community resource
management section had been added to the
Pineriidge Estates Covenant only 7 years
ago, long after the subdivision was
established. Original homeowners had
been sent a notice about updated
community guidelines and told that
failure to respond within 30 days would
constitute acceptance of the changes.
Most people, including those who had
since sold their homes, probably tossed
the notice in the trash without reading
it. Even more interesting, the amendment
had been pushed through shortly after
Patricia became HOA president. Marcus
found the meeting minutes from that
year. Only 12 of the 30 homeowners had
attended the meeting where the amendment
was discussed. Patricia had presented it
as protecting our community's natural
resources from exploitation and the
handful of people present had voted to
approve without much discussion.
This is a taking, Marcus explained. You
cannot use a HOA covenant to seize
someone's property rights without
compensation, even if they technically
agreed to the covenant. It violates both
Oklahoma law and constitutional
principles. If they had wanted to do
this legitimately, they would have
needed to purchase the mineral rights
from each homeowner individually.
Why would Patricia go to all this
trouble? I asked. What is she getting
out of this? That is what we need to
find out. The situation escalated
quickly. I continued negotiating with
Breenidge Energy and by late April, we
had a draft lease agreement ready to
sign. That is when I received a formal
cease and desist letter from the HOA's
attorney, a guy named Victor Bramwell,
who ran a small practice in Tulsa. The
letter demanded I halt all mineral lease
activities and threatened litigation if
I proceeded. Marcus sent back a response
explaining why the HOA's legal theory
was nonsense and inviting them to sue if
they wanted to waste everyone's time and
money. We thought that might be the end
of it. Surely, they would consult with
their attorney and realize they had no
case. We were wrong. In early May, the
HOA filed a lawsuit in Creek County
District Court seeking declaratory
judgment that the mineral rights under
Pine Ridge Estates were community
assets. They also requested a temporary
restraining order, blocking me from
signing any lease agreements pending the
outcome of the case. The TTRO hearing
was scheduled for a Wednesday afternoon.
Marcus and I showed up at the courthouse
with three file boxes full of
documentation, my deed, the complete
title history going back to the 1890s,
Oklahoma statutes on mineral rights,
case law on HOA authority, and expert
analyses on property law. The HOA's
attorney, Victor Bramwell, showed up
with Patricia, Dennis, and Sharon, plus
a binder containing the HOA covenant and
some cherrypicked cases that he thought
supported their position. Judge Raymond
Foster, a stern man in his 60s who had
been on the bench for 20 years, listened
to both sides present their arguments.
Bramwell went first, explaining the
HOA's interpretation of the covenant and
arguing that I had voluntarily agreed to
community control of mineral resources
when I bought my house. Then Marcus
stood up and methodically destroyed
their argument. He walked the judge
through the title history, showing clear
ownership of mineral rights passing
through every transaction. He cited
Oklahoma statutes that protected mineral
rights as real property interests that
could not be taken without due process
and just compensation.
He referenced a dozen cases where courts
had struck down HOA attempts to control
subsurface resources. Judge Foster did
not take long to decide. The temporary
restraining order is denied, he said
firmly. Based on the preliminary
evidence, it appears Mr. Peterson has
clear title to the mineral rights
beneath his property. The HOA covenant,
regardless of its language, cannot
supersede a recorded deed. The
declaratory judgment action can proceed,
but I am not going to stop Mr. Peterson
from exercising his property rights in
the meantime. If the HOA ultimately
prevails, which seems unlikely, damages
can be sorted out later. Patricia looked
like she wanted to explode. Her face
turned red and she started whispering
furiously to Bramwell who could only
shrug helplessly.
We left the courthouse and I felt
victorious.
The next day, I signed the lease
agreement with Breenidge Energy. The
signing bonus hit my bank account within
a week. I paid off my mortgage and
started planning renovations. But
Patricia was not done. Not even close.
The HOA began hitting me with violation
notices for everything imaginable. My
grass was a/4 in too long. My mailbox
was the wrong shade of black. I had left
my garage door open past 8:00 in the
morning, which apparently violated a
garage appearance rule buried in the
Covenant. Each violation came with a
fine, usually $50 or $100. I ignored
them. Marcus advised that we were
building a case for harassment, and
every petty fine just strengthened our
position. The HOA could find me all they
wanted, but they had no actual
enforcement mechanism unless they sued,
and they had already shown their hand in
court. Then things got weird. In midMay,
I came home from work to find surveyor
stakes in my yard. They were marked with
orange flags and appeared to be
measuring something. I had not
authorized any surveying. I called the
surveyor's company identified on a
business card stuck to one of the
stakes. They told me the HOA had hired
them to conduct a boundary survey of the
entire Pineriidge Estate subdivision.
When I pressed for details, they clammed
up and said I would need to speak with
their client. Marcus found this
suspicious. They are looking for
something, he said. My guess is they are
trying to find any excuse to challenge
your property boundaries or find some
technicality in your deed.
He was partially right, but the truth
was even stranger.
A week later, the HOA called an
emergency community meeting. I almost
did not go, but Marcus insisted I
attend. "We need to see what they are up
to," he said. The meeting was held at
Dennis's car dealership in a conference
room that smelled like air freshener and
desperation.
About 20 homeowners showed up, which was
a good turnout for Pine Ridge Estates.
Most people avoided HOA meetings like
the plague. Patricia stood at the front
of the room next to a projector screen.
She waited until everyone was seated,
then began her presentation.
Thank you all for coming, she said in a
saccharine voice. I know everyone is
busy, so I will get right to the point.
The board has discovered something
incredible about our community. Beneath
Pineriidge Estates lies a substantial
natural gas deposit potentially worth
millions of dollars. She clicked to show
a geological map with our subdivision
highlighted. An energy company has been
trying to exploit these resources by
making private deals with individual
homeowners. One person in particular has
already signed a lease without
consulting the community.
Everyone looked at me. I kept my face
neutral. The board has been working to
protect all of our interests. Patricia
continued, "Our HOA covenant clearly
states that mineral rights are community
property. We have filed a lawsuit to
enforce this. And while that proceeds,
we are exploring options to ensure that
if any extraction occurs, the benefits
are shared equally. Dennis stood up. We
have been in negotiations with multiple
energy companies. If we can consolidate
the mineral rights for the entire
subdivision, we can negotiate a much
better deal than any individual could
get a loan. We are talking about
potentially $20 million or more. A
murmur went through the crowd. $20
million split 30 ways was still over
600,000 per household. People were
listening now. Sharon pulled up a
spreadsheet. The board has created a
proposal. If every homeowner agrees to
assign their mineral rights to the HOA,
we will establish a trust. Any money
from leases will be distributed equally
minus a management fee to cover
administrative costs. How much is the
management fee? Someone asked. 10%,
Patricia said quickly. very reasonable
for this type of arrangement. I raised
my hand. I have a question. If the
mineral rights are already community
property according to the covenant like
you've been claiming in your lawsuit,
why do you need us to assign them to the
HOA?
The room went silent. Patricia's
expression hardened. That is a legal
formality, Victor Bramwell said,
standing up from the back of the room.
To streamline the process and avoid
further litigation costs. Or, I said
standing up as well. It is because you
know your legal position is garbage. And
this is a lastditch effort to get people
to voluntarily hand over their rights so
you can collect your 10% management fee
on a $20 million deal. $2 million is a
nice payday for the board. That is
completely inappropriate. Patricia
snapped. The management fee would go to
the HOA for community improvements.
Really? Is that in writing? Can you show
us the proposed trust documents?
Patricia glanced at Bramwell, who looked
uncomfortable.
The documents are still being drafted.
Convenient, I said. Look, everyone here
should know the facts. I had an attorney
research this thoroughly. In Oklahoma,
mineral rights are real property. If
they came with your house when you
bought it, they are yours. The HOA
cannot take them through a covenant.
Judge Foster already agreed with this
preliminary assessment when he denied
their restraining order against me. If
an energy company wants to lease your
mineral rights, you can negotiate
directly and keep 100% of the money
minus taxes. You don't need the HOA
playing middleman and skimming 2 million
off the top. This is why individual
negotiations are bad, Dennis said. You
are sabotaging the community for your
own greed. I am not sabotaging anything.
I signed a fair lease that pays me for
my property rights. If everyone else
wants to do the same, the energy
companies will work with you. If you
want to band together and negotiate
collectively, you can do that without
signing your rights over to the HOA
board, form your own trust with
transparent terms, and keep the fees
minimal. But don't let them scare you
into giving up your property. The
meeting devolved into arguments after
that. Some homeowners were angry at me
for going rogue and possibly reducing
the collective negotiating power. Others
were skeptical of the HOA's motivations,
especially after I pointed out the
management fee.
Patricia tried to regain control, but
the unity she had hoped for was
fractured. After the meeting, several
neighbors approached me with questions.
I gave them Marcus's contact information
and encouraged them to get independent
legal advice. A few thanked me, others
walked away shaking their heads. Marcus
and I left feeling cautiously
optimistic.
You threw a wrench in their plans, he
said. But Patricia does not strike me as
someone who gives up easily. He was
right. The harassment intensified. The
HOA sent me a bill for over $3,000 in
accumulated fines for various
violations. When I did not pay, they
filed a lean against my property. They
also sent notices to my neighbors
claiming I was jeopardizing everyone's
financial interests through my reckless
individual lease. In late May, Breenidge
Energy contacted me with concerning
news. The HOA had sent them a cease and
desist letter claiming that my lease was
invalid and that any extraction based on
it would expose the company to
litigation. While Breenidge's legal team
was confident they were in the right,
the uncertainty was causing problems
with their financing and permitting. We
are not backing out, the company
representative assured me. But this
might delay drilling operations by
several months while we sort out the
legal mess. I was furious. Even though
the HOA was wrong, they were still
managing to cost me money and time
through sheer obstinacy.
Marcus filed a motion to expedite the
declaratory judgment case, arguing that
the HOA's frivolous legal actions were
causing real economic harm. Judge Foster
agreed and scheduled a full hearing for
late June. Both sides would present
their complete cases and he would issue
a final ruling on whether the HOA had
any legitimate claim to the mineral
rights. In the meantime, I decided to
dig deeper into Patricia's motivations.
Something about this whole situation
felt personal beyond simple greed.
I started asking around the
neighborhood, talking to longtime
residents who had been there since the
beginning. I hit the jackpot when I
spoke with Randall Hughes, a retired oil
and gas engineer who lived at the far
end of the subdivision. Randall was in
his 70s and had worked in the energy
industry for 40 years before retiring to
Broken Arrow. "You want to know about
Patricia?" he said when I stopped by his
house one evening. She has been obsessed
with those mineral rights for years.
Started right around when her husband
left her. I did not know she was
divorced. Oh, yeah. Nasty split about 8
years ago. Her ex Thomas was a
geologist, worked for one of the big oil
companies. They lived in Tulsa, but
Thomas always talked about how this area
had potential. He had done some
preliminary surveys on his own time and
thought there might be gas deposits
around here. Patricia used to brag about
it at parties, how they were going to
strike it rich someday.
What happened? Randall shrugged. Thomas
left her for a younger woman, a
colleague from his company. Patricia got
the divorce settlement and used some of
the money to buy into Pineriidge
Estates. She ran for HOA president
almost immediately. I always thought it
was a power trip, you know, filling the
void in her life. But now I wonder if
she had an ulterior motive. The mineral
rights, I said. Exactly. Think about it.
Thomas had told her about the potential
here. She gets on the HOA board and
pushes through that covenant amendment
about community resources. If she could
consolidate control over the mineral
rights for the whole subdivision, she
could make millions, more than she got
in the divorce settlement, it would be
her way of proving she did not need
Thomas.
This added a whole new dimension to the
situation. Patricia was not just greedy,
she was trying to vindicate herself
using our mineral rights as the vehicle.
I shared this information with Marcus.
It does not change the legal situation,
he said, but it might be useful context.
It shows she had a personal motivation
to engineer the scheme. As June
progressed, I prepared for the hearing.
Marcus had me gather every piece of
documentation related to my property
purchase. We also hired an expert
witness, Dr. Linda Cortez, a professor
of property law at the University of
Oklahoma. She would testify about HOA
authority and the limits of covenants.
Then Marcus suggested something that
turned out to be a gamecher.
We should get a geologist, he said.
someone who can testify about the
mineral deposits and the value we're
talking about. It would help the judge
understand the stakes and why Patricia
is so motivated to pull this scam. I
remembered Randall mentioning that he
had worked in oil and gas. When I asked
if he knew any geologists who might
help, he made a call and connected me
with Dr. Raymond Walsh, a geology
professor at the University of Tulsa.
Dr. Walsh had decades of experience in
petroleum geology and had served as an
expert witness in numerous mineral
rights disputes. I met with Dr. Walsh at
his office on campus. He was a lanky man
in his late 50s with a graying beard and
an enthusiasm for rocks that was almost
infectious. Broken Arrow area, you said?
He asked, pulling up geological maps on
his computer. Yes, there is definitely
potential there. You're sitting on the
edge of what we call the Cherokee
platform. natural gas formations
primarily. Based on recent drilling data
from surrounding areas, I would estimate
significant reserves.
Can you testify about this? Sure. If it
helps establish the value of what is at
stake. Mineral rights disputes often
hinge on whether the rights in question
are worth fighting over. In your case,
they absolutely are. We are talking
about potentially hundreds of thousands
to millions of dollars in royalties over
the life of a well. I hired Dr. Walsh
and felt a surge of confidence. We had
the law. We had the title history. We
had expert witnesses. There was no way
the HOA could win. The hearing was
scheduled for June 23rd. As the date
approached, Patricia seemed to get more
desperate. She sent a neighborhoodwide
email accusing me of stealing from the
community and claiming I had bribed
public officials to support my position.
The allegations were completely false
and defamatory.
Marcus sent her a letter threatening a
liel lawsuit if she did not retract the
statements. She ignored it. 3 days
before the hearing, something happened
that changed everything. I was at work
buried in a project deadline when I got
a call from Randall Hughes. He sounded
shaken. James, you need to hear this. I
was going through some old boxes in my
garage, stuff from when I used to work
in the industry. I found a survey report
from 1998. It is about Pine Ridge
Estates back before it was developed.
You are not going to believe who
commissioned it. Who? Patricia's
ex-husband, Thomas Hrix. He was
evaluating the land for mineral
potential before the developer bought
it. According to the report, he
identified substantial natural gas
deposits and recommended against selling
the mineral rights if the land was
developed. My heart was pounding. Does
the report say anything about who owned
the land then? Yeah, it was the Morrison
family. They had owned the ranch for
generations. According to Thomas's
notes, he advised them to retain the
mineral rights when they sold to the
developer. There is a handwritten note
in the margin that says potential value
10 million plus. Randall, this is huge.
Can I get a copy of that report? I am
scanning it right now. I will email it
to you and your attorney. James, there
is something else. There is a letter
attached from Thomas to Patricia dated
about 6 months before their divorce. He
tells her about the survey and says they
should try to buy property in Pineriidge
Estates once the mineral potential
becomes public. He says they could make
a fortune if they played it right. So,
Patricia has known about this the entire
time. Not just known, she's been
planning it for years. This was not a
spontaneous scam. She bought into the
subdivision specifically to position
herself to steal the mineral rights. I
thanked Randall and immediately called
Marcus. He was stunned by the
revelation. "Uh, this is fraud," he
said. "Diberate, premeditated fraud. If
Patricia amended the HOA covenant
specifically to seize mineral rights
that she knew were valuable, and if she
concealed her knowledge from the other
homeowners, that is not just a civil
matter. It could be criminal. What do we
do? First, we use this at the hearing.
It goes to motivation and shows bad
faith. Second, depending on how the
hearing goes, we might need to contact
law enforcement. This could be theft by
deception, fraud, maybe even
racketeering if she involved the other
board members knowingly. The next two
days were a whirlwind. Marcus subpoenaed
Patricia's financial records and
correspondence with Victor Bramwell. We
wanted to know if she had ever disclosed
her prior knowledge about the mineral
deposits to the HOA or to Bramwell. We
also prepared Dr. Walsh to testify not
just about the geology, but about the
1998 survey and what it meant. The
morning of the hearing, I barely slept.
I put on my best suit and met Marcus at
the courthouse. Dr. Cortez and Dr. Walsh
were already there reviewing their
notes. Randall Hughes had also come to
watch, sitting in the gallery with a
folder containing the original survey
report. Patricia arrived with her
entourage, Dennis, Sharon, and Victor
Bramwell. She wore an expensive dress
and had her hair done up. She looked
confident like she thought she still had
a chance.
The courtroom was one of the older ones
in the Creek County Courthouse with wood
paneling and high ceilings. Judge Foster
took the bench at 9:00 sharp.
This is a declaratory judgment action
regarding mineral rights ownership, he
began. The HOA claims that a covenant
grants them control over subsurface
resources. Mr. Peterson claims clear
ownership through his deed. Let us
proceed. Mr. Bramwell, you may call your
first witness. Bramwell called Patricia
to the stand. She testified about the
HOA covenant, the amendment process, and
her interpretation that mineral rights
were community property. Under direct
examination, she came across as
reasonable and community-minded,
painting me as a greedy individual,
undermining the neighborhood. Then
Marcus stood up for cross-examination.
Ms. Hendrix, when did you first become
aware that there might be valuable
mineral deposits under Pineriidge
Estates? Patricia hesitated. I suppose
when Breenidge Energy contacted us.
Really? Not before then. I mean, I knew
this was Oklahoma. There is oil and gas
everywhere. But you had no specific
knowledge about Pineriidge Estate
specifically? No. Marcus walked over to
our table and picked up a document. Your
honor, I would like to introduce
plaintiff's exhibit A. This is a
geological survey report dated 1998,
commissioned by Thomas Hrix regarding
the land that would become Pineriidge
Estates. He handed a copy to the judge
and to Bramwell, whose face went pale as
he scanned it. Miss Hendris, Thomas
Hendrickx is your ex-husband, correct?
Yes, Patricia said quietly. And he is a
geologist with extensive experience in
oil and gas exploration.
Yes, this report identifies substantial
natural gas deposits beneath the land.
Were you aware of this report?
Patricia's jaw tightened. I might have
known about it years ago. I do not
remember. Let me refresh your memory.
Marcus produced another document. This
is a letter from Thomas Hrix to you
dated 8 years ago, shortly before your
divorce. In it, he specifically mentions
the Pineriidge Estate Survey and
suggests you both invest in property
there to capitalize on future mineral
extraction. Did you receive this letter?
I do not recall. You do not recall your
ex-husband writing to you about a
potential multi-million dollar
investment opportunity. It was a
difficult time. The divorce was
contentious.
Ms. Hrix, you purchased your home in
Pineriidge Estates 7 years ago, shortly
after the divorce. Is that correct? Yes.
And you ran for HOA president
immediately after moving in? Yes. I
wanted to be involved in the community.
And one of your first acts as president
was to push through a covenant amendment

But don't let them scare you into giving up your property. The meeting devolved into arguments after that. Some homeowners were angry at me for going rogue and possibly reducing the collective negotiating power. Others were skeptical of the HOA's motivations, especially after I pointed out the management fee. Patricia tried to regain control, but the unity she had hoped for was fractured. After the meeting, several neighbors approached me with questions. I gave them Marcus's contact information and encouraged them to get independent legal advice. A few thanked me, others walked away shaking their heads. Marcus and I left feeling cautiously optimistic. You threw a wrench in their plans, he said. But Patricia does not strike me as someone who gives up easily. He was right. The harassment intensified. The HOA sent me a bill for over $3,000 in accumulated fines for various violations. When I did not pay, they filed a lean against my property. They also sent notices to my neighbors claiming I was jeopardizing everyone's financial interests through my reckless individual lease. In late May, Breenidge Energy contacted me with concerning news. The HOA had sent them a cease and desist letter claiming that my lease was invalid and that any extraction based on it would expose the company to litigation. While Breenidge's legal team was confident they were in the right, the uncertainty was causing problems with their financing and permitting. We are not backing out, the company representative assured me. But this might delay drilling operations by several months while we sort out the legal mess. I was furious. Even though the HOA was wrong, they were still managing to cost me money and time through sheer obstinacy. Marcus filed a motion to expedite the declaratory judgment case, arguing that the HOA's frivolous legal actions were causing real economic harm. Judge Foster agreed and scheduled a full hearing for late June. Both sides would present their complete cases and he would issue a final ruling on whether the HOA had any legitimate claim to the mineral rights. In the meantime, I decided to dig deeper into Patricia's motivations. Something about this whole situation felt personal beyond simple greed. I started asking around the neighborhood, talking to longtime residents who had been there since the beginning. I hit the jackpot when I spoke with Randall Hughes, a retired oil and gas engineer who lived at the far end of the subdivision. Randall was in his 70s and had worked in the energy industry for 40 years before retiring to Broken Arrow. "You want to know about Patricia?" he said when I stopped by his house one evening. She has been obsessed with those mineral rights for years. Started right around when her husband left her. I did not know she was divorced. Oh, yeah. Nasty split about 8 years ago. Her ex Thomas was a geologist, worked for one of the big oil companies. They lived in Tulsa, but Thomas always talked about how this area had potential. He had done some preliminary surveys on his own time and thought there might be gas deposits around here. Patricia used to brag about it at parties, how they were going to strike it rich someday. What happened? Randall shrugged. Thomas left her for a younger woman, a colleague from his company. Patricia got the divorce settlement and used some of the money to buy into Pineriidge Estates. She ran for HOA president almost immediately. I always thought it was a power trip, you know, filling the void in her life. But now I wonder if she had an ulterior motive. The mineral rights, I said. Exactly. Think about it. Thomas had told her about the potential here. She gets on the HOA board and pushes through that covenant amendment about community resources. If she could consolidate control over the mineral rights for the whole subdivision, she could make millions, more than she got in the divorce settlement, it would be her way of proving she did not need Thomas. This added a whole new dimension to the situation. Patricia was not just greedy, she was trying to vindicate herself using our mineral rights as the vehicle. I shared this information with Marcus. It does not change the legal situation, he said, but it might be useful context. It shows she had a personal motivation to engineer the scheme. As June progressed, I prepared for the hearing. Marcus had me gather every piece of documentation related to my property purchase. We also hired an expert witness, Dr. Linda Cortez, a professor of property law at the University of Oklahoma. She would testify about HOA authority and the limits of covenants. Then Marcus suggested something that turned out to be a gamecher. We should get a geologist, he said. someone who can testify about the mineral deposits and the value we're talking about. It would help the judge understand the stakes and why Patricia is so motivated to pull this scam. I remembered Randall mentioning that he had worked in oil and gas. When I asked if he knew any geologists who might help, he made a call and connected me with Dr. Raymond Walsh, a geology professor at the University of Tulsa. Dr. Walsh had decades of experience in petroleum geology and had served as an expert witness in numerous mineral rights disputes. I met with Dr. Walsh at his office on campus. He was a lanky man in his late 50s with a graying beard and an enthusiasm for rocks that was almost infectious. Broken Arrow area, you said? He asked, pulling up geological maps on his computer. Yes, there is definitely potential there. You're sitting on the edge of what we call the Cherokee platform. natural gas formations primarily. Based on recent drilling data from surrounding areas, I would estimate significant reserves. Can you testify about this? Sure. If it helps establish the value of what is at stake. Mineral rights disputes often hinge on whether the rights in question are worth fighting over. In your case, they absolutely are. We are talking about potentially hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars in royalties over the life of a well. I hired Dr. Walsh and felt a surge of confidence. We had the law. We had the title history. We had expert witnesses. There was no way the HOA could win. The hearing was scheduled for June 23rd. As the date approached, Patricia seemed to get more desperate. She sent a neighborhoodwide email accusing me of stealing from the community and claiming I had bribed public officials to support my position. The allegations were completely false and defamatory. Marcus sent her a letter threatening a liel lawsuit if she did not retract the statements. She ignored it. 3 days before the hearing, something happened that changed everything. I was at work buried in a project deadline when I got a call from Randall Hughes. He sounded shaken. James, you need to hear this. I was going through some old boxes in my garage, stuff from when I used to work in the industry. I found a survey report from 1998. It is about Pine Ridge Estates back before it was developed. You are not going to believe who commissioned it. Who? Patricia's ex-husband, Thomas Hrix. He was evaluating the land for mineral potential before the developer bought it. According to the report, he identified substantial natural gas deposits and recommended against selling the mineral rights if the land was developed. My heart was pounding. Does the report say anything about who owned the land then? Yeah, it was the Morrison family. They had owned the ranch for generations. According to Thomas's notes, he advised them to retain the mineral rights when they sold to the developer. There is a handwritten note in the margin that says potential value 10 million plus. Randall, this is huge. Can I get a copy of that report? I am scanning it right now. I will email it to you and your attorney. James, there is something else. There is a letter attached from Thomas to Patricia dated about 6 months before their divorce. He tells her about the survey and says they should try to buy property in Pineriidge Estates once the mineral potential becomes public. He says they could make a fortune if they played it right. So, Patricia has known about this the entire time. Not just known, she's been planning it for years. This was not a spontaneous scam. She bought into the subdivision specifically to position herself to steal the mineral rights. I thanked Randall and immediately called Marcus. He was stunned by the revelation. "Uh, this is fraud," he said. "Diberate, premeditated fraud. If Patricia amended the HOA covenant specifically to seize mineral rights that she knew were valuable, and if she concealed her knowledge from the other homeowners, that is not just a civil matter. It could be criminal. What do we do? First, we use this at the hearing. It goes to motivation and shows bad faith. Second, depending on how the hearing goes, we might need to contact law enforcement. This could be theft by deception, fraud, maybe even racketeering if she involved the other board members knowingly. The next two days were a whirlwind. Marcus subpoenaed Patricia's financial records and correspondence with Victor Bramwell. We wanted to know if she had ever disclosed her prior knowledge about the mineral deposits to the HOA or to Bramwell. We also prepared Dr. Walsh to testify not just about the geology, but about the 1998 survey and what it meant. The morning of the hearing, I barely slept. I put on my best suit and met Marcus at the courthouse. Dr. Cortez and Dr. Walsh were already there reviewing their notes. Randall Hughes had also come to watch, sitting in the gallery with a folder containing the original survey report. Patricia arrived with her entourage, Dennis, Sharon, and Victor Bramwell. She wore an expensive dress and had her hair done up. She looked confident like she thought she still had a chance. The courtroom was one of the older ones in the Creek County Courthouse with wood paneling and high ceilings. Judge Foster took the bench at 9:00 sharp. This is a declaratory judgment action regarding mineral rights ownership, he began. The HOA claims that a covenant grants them control over subsurface resources. Mr. Peterson claims clear ownership through his deed. Let us proceed. Mr. Bramwell, you may call your first witness. Bramwell called Patricia to the stand. She testified about the HOA covenant, the amendment process, and her interpretation that mineral rights were community property. Under direct examination, she came across as reasonable and community-minded, painting me as a greedy individual, undermining the neighborhood. Then Marcus stood up for cross-examination. Ms. Hendrix, when did you first become aware that there might be valuable mineral deposits under Pineriidge Estates? Patricia hesitated. I suppose when Breenidge Energy contacted us. Really? Not before then. I mean, I knew this was Oklahoma. There is oil and gas everywhere. But you had no specific knowledge about Pineriidge Estate specifically? No. Marcus walked over to our table and picked up a document. Your honor, I would like to introduce plaintiff's exhibit A. This is a geological survey report dated 1998, commissioned by Thomas Hrix regarding the land that would become Pineriidge Estates. He handed a copy to the judge and to Bramwell, whose face went pale as he scanned it. Miss Hendris, Thomas Hendrickx is your ex-husband, correct? Yes, Patricia said quietly. And he is a geologist with extensive experience in oil and gas exploration. Yes, this report identifies substantial natural gas deposits beneath the land. Were you aware of this report? Patricia's jaw tightened. I might have known about it years ago. I do not remember. Let me refresh your memory. Marcus produced another document. This is a letter from Thomas Hrix to you dated 8 years ago, shortly before your divorce. In it, he specifically mentions the Pineriidge Estate Survey and suggests you both invest in property there to capitalize on future mineral extraction. Did you receive this letter? I do not recall. You do not recall your ex-husband writing to you about a potential multi-million dollar investment opportunity. It was a difficult time. The divorce was contentious. Ms. Hrix, you purchased your home in Pineriidge Estates 7 years ago, shortly after the divorce. Is that correct? Yes. And you ran for HOA president immediately after moving in? Yes. I wanted to be involved in the community. And one of your first acts as president was to push through a covenant amendment regarding mineral rights. Is that correct? It was about protecting our natural resources. Protecting them for whom? The community or for you personally? Marcus' voice was sharp now. You knew about the gas deposits. You knew they were worth millions. You bought into this subdivision specifically to position yourself to control those rights. Then you used your position as HOA president to amend the covenant in a way that would let you seize everyone's mineral rights. Is not that the truth? No, that is not what happened. Then explain to the court why you never disclosed your prior knowledge about the mineral deposits when you proposed the Covenant Amendment. Explain why you did not tell your neighbors that your ex-husband had identified $10 million in potential value beneath their properties. Patricia was flustered now, her composure cracking. I was trying to protect the community from being exploited by big energy companies. By exploiting them yourself, by taking control of their property rights without compensation? Objection. Bramwell finally found his voice. Argumentative. Sustained. Judge Foster said, "But I think we have heard enough. Mr. Bramwell, do you have any other witnesses?" Bramwell looked like he wanted to crawl under the table. "No, your honor. Then let us hear from Mr. Peterson's side." "Mr. Chen," Marcus called me first. I testified about purchasing my property, reviewing the deed, discovering the mineral rights, and negotiating with Breenidge Energy. I explained how I had researched the title history and confirmed ownership. Then Marcus introduced the deed and title documents, walking through the complete chain of ownership. Every transfer clearly conveyed both surface and mineral rights together. There was no severance, no ambiguity. Next came Dr. Cortez, the property law professor. She gave a methodical explanation of how mineral rights work in Oklahoma, the limits of HOA authority, and why a covenant could not take someone's property without due process. She cited case after case supporting our position. Bramwell barely bothered with cross-examination. Finally, Dr. Walsh took the stand. He explained the geology of the area, the natural gas formations, and the potential value of the deposits. He discussed the 1998 survey and confirmed that it was a professional, thorough analysis that accurately identified the mineral potential. In your opinion, Dr. Walsh. Would someone with geological knowledge like Thomas Hrix have understood the significance of this survey? Absolutely. Doctor Walsh said this is a textbook evaluation. Anyone in the industry would recognize that this land was sitting on a valuable resource. And if someone had access to this information and then took steps to gain control over the mineral rights without disclosing what they knew, what would that suggest to you? Objection. Bramwell stood. Dr. Walsh is not here to speculate about motives. I'm asking about industry standards and ethics. Marcus said, "Dr. Walsh has testified as an expert in mineral rights disputes for 20 years. He is qualified to discuss appropriate conduct." I will allow it. Judge Foster said, "Answer the question." Dr. Walsh. In the oil and gas industry, there are strict ethical guidelines about disclosure. Dr. Walsh said, "If someone has material information about mineral value and uses it to acquire rights without disclosing that information, it is considered fraud. We have seen cases where leases were voided and individuals faced criminal charges for that kind of deception." The courtroom was silent. Patricia looked like she might be sick. Marcus rested our case. Bramwell offered a half-hearted closing argument about the plain language of the covenant and the need to respect HOA authority. Marcus delivered a passionate rebuttal about property rights, the rule of law, and Patricia's fraudulent scheme. Judge Foster did not even take a recess to deliberate. "Ah, I have heard enough," he said. "This is one of the clearest cases I have seen. Mr. Peterson has demonstrated unambiguous ownership of the mineral rights beneath his property through a properly recorded deed and clear chain of title. The HOA covenant, even if it attempted to seize those rights, would be invalid as an unconstitutional taking without just compensation. Furthermore, the evidence presented today suggests that the Covenant Amendment was procured through fraud and concealment of material information. He turned to Patricia. Ms. Hrix, I do not know if you fully understood the legal implications of what you were attempting, but it amounts to theft. You tried to use your position of authority to steal valuable property from your neighbors. Your honor, I never intended, Patricia started. I do not want to hear it, Judge Foster cut her off. I am ruling in favor of Mr. Peterson. The declaratory judgment will state that he has clear title to the mineral rights beneath his property and that the HOA has no authority over those rights. I am also awarding attorneys fees and costs to Mr. Peterson to be paid by the HOA. And Ms. Hendrickx, I'm referring this matter to the Creek County District Attorney's Office for investigation into possible criminal fraud. Patricia stood up, her face red. You cannot do this. I was protecting the community. Sit down, Miss Hendris. Baiff, please escort her out if she cannot control herself. Patricia looked around wildly, as if expecting someone to support her. Dennis and Sharon were both staring at the floor. Victor Bramwell was packing his briefcase, clearly wanting to distance himself from his client as quickly as possible. Patricia finally stormed out of the courtroom, her heels clicking loudly on the tile floor. Dennis and Sharon followed more slowly, looking shell shocked. Marcus and I shook hands with Dr. Cortez and Dr. Walsh, thanking them for their testimony. Randall Hughes came up and congratulated me. "You did it," he said. "You beat her." "We all did," I replied. "If you had not found that survey, we might not have been able to prove her intent." Outside the courthouse, Marcus and I discussed next steps. Judge Foster referred this to the DA. He said, "That means there will be a criminal investigation. They will look at whether Patricia committed fraud, theft, or any other crimes. Given the dollar amounts involved, this could be serious. What about Dennis and Sharon? They went along with this. That depends on what they knew. If Patricia deceived them too, they might not face charges. But if they knew about the survey and the fraud, they could be considered accompllices. Over the next few weeks, the story spread through Pine Ridge Estates. Several other homeowners contacted me and Marcus asking about their own mineral rights. We helped them understand their ownership and put them in touch with Breenidge Energy. Some negotiated individual leases, others formed a voluntary cooperative to negotiate collectively with transparent terms and no management fees. The Creek County District Attorney, a sharp woman named Rebecca Thornton, opened a formal investigation into Patricia's conduct. She subpoenaed HOA records, Patricia's personal emails, and financial documents. What she found was damning. Patricia had not just known about the mineral potential. She had been actively planning to exploit it for years. She had consulted with multiple attorneys about how to structure the HOA covenant to maximize her control. She had even drafted agreements with energy companies that would have funneled the management fees into accounts she controlled, not into community improvements. Dennis and Sharon were interviewed extensively. It turned out they had been mostly clueless. Patricia had told them the Covenant Amendment was about environmental protection and giving the community a voice in any extraction operations. She had never mentioned the 1998 survey or her ex-husband's assessment. When they learned the truth, both resigned from the HOA board immediately. In August, the district attorney filed criminal charges against Patricia, theft by deception, fraud, and abuse of fiduciary duty. Each charge was a felony carrying potential prison time. The case went to trial in October. I testified as did Marcus Randall, Dr. Walsh, and several other neighbors. The prosecution presented overwhelming evidence of Patricia's scheme. the 1998 survey, the letter from her ex-husband, the Covenant Amendment, her secret negotiations with energy companies, the hidden accounts, it all painted a picture of calculated premeditated fraud. Patricia's defense attorney tried to argue that she had genuinely believed the covenant was legal and that she was acting in the community's best interests, but the evidence of her prior knowledge and the concealed accounts made that defense untenable. The jury deliberated for less than 3 hours. They found Patricia guilty on all counts. In November, she was sentenced to 5 years in prison with the possibility of parole after two. She was also ordered to pay restitution to the HOA and to me personally for the legal fees and stress she had caused. The judge made it clear that he was sending a message. People in positions of authority cannot use their power to steal from those they are supposed to serve. Patricia's last words before being led away were bitter. This is all your fault, James. If you had just played along, everyone would have benefited. I did not respond. There was nothing to say to someone who still did not understand that stealing is wrong, even if you dress it up as community service. By December, my life had returned to a comfortable routine. The declaratory judgment was recorded with the county, making my ownership of the mineral rights a matter of permanent public record. Breenidge Energy completed their drilling operations on my property and two neighboring lots. The wells were productive and royalty checks started arriving monthly. The Pine Ridge Estates HOA elected a new board with Randall Hughes as president. One of their first acts was to repeal the community resource management section of the covenant. They also implemented new transparency requirements and term limits to prevent anyone from consolidating too much power again. I used some of my mineral royalties to renovate my house, finally updating the kitchen and bathrooms that had been on my wish list for years. I also set aside money for my niece's college fund and made donations to legal aid organizations that help homeowners fight HOA abuse. Marcus Chen and I became good friends through the ordeal. He told me that the case had become something of a legend in property law circles, a cautionary tale about HOA overreach and a reminder that some rights are too fundamental to be bargained away. Dr. Walsh occasionally emailed me updates about the geology of the area. The gas formations were proving even more productive than initially estimated. Based on current production, my lifetime royalties would likely exceed $2 million. Other homeowners in Pineriidge Estates who had leased their mineral rights were seeing similar success. I sometimes wondered what Patricia thought about sitting in her prison cell. Did she regret her choices? Did she understand that her obsession with proving herself to her ex-husband had destroyed her life? Or did she still believe she was the victim, unfairly persecuted for trying to help the community? In the end, it did not matter. Justice had been served. The law had protected property rights against someone who tried to abuse their position of authority, and I had learned valuable lessons about vigilance, the importance of reading contracts carefully, and the need to stand up for what is right, even when powerful people try to intimidate you. On a cold evening in late December, I stood in my backyard and looked out over my two acres. Somewhere far beneath my feet, natural gas was flowing through rock formations that had existed for millions of years. That gas belonged to me because the law recognized that when you own land, you own what lies beneath it. Not because a HOA said so, not because it was convenient, but because property rights are fundamental to a free society. I thought about all the homeowners across America who face HOA abuse, who are fined for trivial violations, whose lives are made miserable by petty tyrants on neighborhood boards. Most never fight back because the legal costs seem too high or the opposition too powerful. But sometimes you have to fight. Sometimes you have to stand up and say, "No, this is mine and you cannot take it from me." Sometimes you have to show up with your original deed and a geologist and prove that the law is on your side. I went back inside, poured myself a drink, and sat down at my kitchen table. My laptop was open to an email from Marcus, another homeowner, this one in Texas, had reached out after hearing about my case. His HOA, was trying to claim ownership of water rights on his property. Marcus wanted to know if I would be willing to share my experience and maybe testify as a witness about HOA overreach. I smiled and typed a reply. Absolutely. Let me know what you need. The fight was not over. It never really is. But at least I had shown that it was possible to win, that property rights still mattered, and that no HOA board was above the law. As winter settled over Broken Arrow, I felt a deep sense of satisfaction. My mortgage was paid off. My house was mine truly and completely from the roof down to the center of the earth. And somewhere in a state prison, Patricia Hris was learning that you cannot steal what does not belong to you, no matter how clever you think your scheme is. Justice had prevailed. The mineral rights were mine, and I had the original deed and a geologist to prove it. I raised my glass in a silent toast to property rights, to good lawyers, to helpful neighbors like Randall, and to the simple truth that sometimes standing up for yourself is the most important thing you can do. The story had started with a threatening visit from a HOA board president who thought she could intimidate me into surrendering valuable property. It ended with that same president behind bars and me sitting comfortably in my debt-free home, collecting royalty checks from the minerals I rightfully owned. It was a good reminder that in America, despite all its flaws, the law still protects individual rights against those who would abuse power for personal gain. The system worked slowly and expensively. But it worked. Judge Foster had seen through Patricia's scheme. The jury had delivered justice, and the community had learned a valuable lesson about the dangers of giving too much authority to HOA boards without proper oversight. I finished my drink and closed my laptop. Tomorrow, I would call Marcus and tell him I was happy to help the Texas homeowner. Tonight, I would enjoy the peace of knowing that my home, my land, and my mineral rights were secure. No HOA could take them away. No fraudulent covenant could supersede a properly recorded deed. The law was clear, and I had the documents to prove it. Outside, snow began to fall, dusting the Oklahoma landscape with white. Inside, my house was warm and paid for. Deep underground, natural gas continued to flow, generating wealth that belonged to me by right and by law. And in the county records office, my deed sat in a file, a permanent testament to the principle that property rights are not subject to the whims of neighborhood associations or the schemes of wouldbe thieves. It had been a long fight, but I had won. And that victory meant something not just for me, but for every homeowner who would face similar challenges in the years to come. The precedent was set. The message was clear. Your property is yours, and no HOA can take it away without facing the full force of the law. I turned off the lights and headed to bed, content in the knowledge that justice, though sometimes delayed, eventually arrives for those patient and brave enough to demand

metadata.shortDescription:
What are deed restrictions in real estate? Deed restrictions are rules recorded with a property that limit what an owner can do with it, like paint colors, landscaping, or parking. 
📘 Real Estate Exam Crash Course 👉 https://www.usrealtytraining.com/exam-prep-crash-course?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=youtube&utm_campaign=deedrestrictions&utm_id=youtube
🧮 Free Math Cheat Sheet 👉 https://www.usrealtytraining.com/real-estate-math-cheat-sheet?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=youtube&utm_campaign=deedrestrictions-mathsheet&utm_id=youtube

They're a type of encumbrance, often found in planned or gated communities as CC&Rs. This video explains why they exist and how buyers and agents can find them before closing.

In this video, you'll learn:
✅ What deed restrictions are
✅ Why they count as an encumbrance
✅ What CC&Rs are and why communities use them
✅ Common examples, like paint colors and parking
✅ How to find deed restrictions before you buy

QUICK ANSWERS

What are deed restrictions?
Deed restrictions are recorded rules that limit how a property can be used or changed. They stay with the property when it's sold.

Are deed restrictions an encumbrance?
Yes. An encumbrance is any claim or limit on a property. Deed restrictions limit its use, so they count as one.

What are CC&Rs?
CC&Rs stands for covenants, conditions, and restrictions. They're recorded rules for a community, often enforced by an HOA (homeowners association), covering things like exterior colors, landscaping, and parking.

Why do communities have deed restrictions?
In this video's example, a community uses them to keep homes consistent and protect the neighborhood's look and value.

How do you find out if a home has deed restrictions?
Order a title report from a title company, which lists recorded restrictions. You can also search the property's recorded documents at the county recorder's office.

Are all deed restrictions enforceable?
No. Restrictions that discriminate, such as old racial covenants, are illegal and can't be enforced under fair housing laws.

metadata.title: Did you know, NO HOA does not mean NO Rules? #hoa #landrestrictions #landusepolicy #land
metadata.author: Danielle Dojcak
metadata.shortDescription:
DID YOU KNOW? No HOA does NOT necessarily mean no restrictions!

This is one I see agents and buyers misunderstand all the time.

A property may have no HOA and still have restrictive covenants recorded in the land records that could affect what an owner can do with the property.

Thinking about chickens? 
A detached garage?
A fence?
An RV or boat?
Running a business from home?
Subdividing the property?

Before telling a client, “There’s no HOA, so you’re good,” remember:

NO HOA ≠ NO RESTRICTIONS

The goal isn’t to know every answer. It’s to recognize when you need to stop, verify and know who to ask.

And remember, restrictive covenants aren’t the only consideration. Zoning, easements, permits and other regulations may also affect how a property can be used.

Agents: What’s another “Did You Know?” topic you think agents should be talking about? Drop it in the comments!

This content is for educational purposes only and is not intended as legal advice. Agents should consult their managing/principal broker regarding specific transactions and seek appropriate legal or professional guidance when necessary.

#RealEstateTips #RealtorEducation #RealEstateAgents #DidYouKnow #RealEstateTraining
Danielle Dojcak
C21 Redwood Realty
540-533-1279
Licensed Broker; VA, WV, MD & PA
